docs.title: Causes of Death in Conventional Land Warfare

raw_front_matter.title: Causes of Death in Conventional Land Warfare
raw_front_matter.description: In conventional land warfare, overall mortality is driven far more by early battlefield deaths from hemorrhage and CNS trauma than by late complications, so research and system design must prioritize…
raw_front_matter.authors: Ronald F. Bellamy
raw_front_matter.tags: combat casualty care, hemorrhagic shock, trauma, battlefield medicine, exsanguination, craniocerebral trauma, sepsis, evacuation time, prehospital care, military medicine, shock resuscitation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In conventional land warfare, overall mortality is driven far more by early battlefield deaths from hemorrhage and CNS trauma than by late complications, so research and system design must prioritize powerful, practical hemorrhage control and resuscitation capabilities at the point of wounding and in forward echelons.
key_points: Most combat deaths occur on the battlefield before reaching medical treatment; for every death from wounds after evacuation, up to nine die prior to evacuation.
Exsanguination accounts for roughly half of deaths in conventional land warfare, while central nervous system (CNS) trauma causes about one-third and sepsis/multiple organ failure less than 10%.
Rapid evacuation as practiced in Vietnam (≈1–2 hours) greatly reduces mortality compared with World War I–II style delays, but further gains require improved field care, not only faster transport.
Delays of 6–24 hours in evacuation markedly increase the proportion of casualties who die before reaching definitive care, primarily from hemorrhage.
A substantial subset of otherwise fatal hemorrhages arises from sites where simple first aid (pressure, tourniquet, MAST) could have provided temporary control.

Research and system redesign should prioritize forward resuscitation capabilities (medic and battalion surgeon) focused on hemorrhage control, shock resuscitation, and basic airway/chest interventions.

Improving ICU or operative management of sepsis and multiple organ failure, while important, will have only modest impact on overall combat mortality compared with improving battlefield hemorrhage control and early CNS trauma management.

docs.title: Pyruvate Enhancement of Cardiac Performance

raw_front_matter.title: Pyruvate Enhancement of Cardiac Performance
raw_front_matter.description: Supraphysiologic pyruvate administration enhances myocardial energetics, Ca²⁺ handling, and antioxidant/anti-inflammatory defenses, translating from robust preclinical cardioprotection in ischemia–re…
raw_front_matter.authors: Robert T. Mallet, Albert H. Olivencia-Yurvati, Rolf Bǘnger
raw_front_matter.tags: pyruvate, cardioprotection, ischemia-reperfusion, hemorrhagic shock, cardiopulmonary bypass, cardiac arrest, heart failure, septic shock, myocardial energetics, oxidative stress, inflammation, erythropoietin signaling, calcium handling

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Supraphysiologic pyruvate administration enhances myocardial energetics, Ca²⁺ handling, and antioxidant/anti-inflammatory defenses, translating from robust preclinical cardioprotection in ischemia–reperfusion and shock models to early clinical benefit in heart failure, cardiopulmonary bypass, and septic shock, and warranting larger therapeutic trials.
key_points: Pyruvate is a metabolic substrate with combined inotropic, antioxidant, and anti-inflammatory actions that enhance cardiac performance, especially in ischemia–reperfusion injury.
At supraphysiologic plasma levels (≈3–6 mM), pyruvate increases myocardial free energy of ATP hydrolysis more than glucose, lactate, or fatty acids.
Pyruvate improves sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺ uptake and release, increases myofilament Ca²⁺ sensitivity, and restores β-adrenergic responsiveness in stunned myocardium.
Through direct scavenging of reactive oxygen/nitrogen species and boosting NADPH–glutathione systems, pyruvate preserves redox balance and limits post-ischemic inflammation.
Preclinical large-animal studies in cardiopulmonary bypass, cardiac arrest–resuscitation, and hemorrhagic shock show improved hemodynamics, energetics, and reduced tissue injury with pyruvate.

Early clinical trials demonstrate safety and functional benefit of pyruvate given intracoronary for heart failure and cardiogenic shock, as cardioplegia fortification during CPB, and intravenously for septic shock.
Receiver operating characteristic analyses show strong concordance between isolated-heart data and clinical CPB outcomes, supporting translational validity and the need for phase III trials.

docs.title: Amiodarone in Hemorrhagic VF Arrest (Pig Model)

raw_front_matter.title: Amiodarone in Hemorrhagic VF Arrest (Pig Model)
raw_front_matter.description: In a porcine model of hemorrhagic ventricular fibrillation arrest, adding early low-dose amiodarone to vasopressin-based resuscitation significantly improved 3‑hour survival, hemodynamic stability, a…
raw_front_matter.authors: Frank Zoerner, Egidijus Semenas
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac arrest, ventricular fibrillation, amiodarone, vasopressin, open-chest CPR, porcine model, postresuscitation hemodynamics, myocardial injury
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a porcine model of hemorrhagic ventricular fibrillation arrest, adding early low-dose amiodarone to vasopressin-based resuscitation significantly improved 3‑hour survival, hemodynamic stability, and markers of myocardial and organ injury compared with vasopressin alone.
key_points: In a piglet model of hemorrhagic ventricular fibrillation arrest, adding low-dose amiodarone to vasopressin-based resuscitation improved 3‑hour survival compared with vasopressin alone.
Amiodarone-treated animals had better postresuscitation hemodynamics, with higher arterial pressures and coronary perfusion pressure and lower heart rates.
Biomarkers and urine output indicated less myocardial injury and better organ perfusion in the amiodarone group.
The study used early, low-dose amiodarone (1 mg/kg) administered before defibrillation in the setting of severe hypovolemia.
No increase in defibrillation success during CPR was demonstrated, but post-ROSC stability and survival were better with amiodarone.
The model combines controlled hemorrhage, electrically induced VF, open-chest CPR, vasopressin, and hypertonic-hyperoncotic resuscitation to mimic hypovolemic cardiac arrest.

docs.title: Shock Plus Pneumonectomy Causes Right Heart Failure

raw_front_matter.title: Shock Plus Pneumonectomy Causes Right Heart Failure
raw_front_matter.description: In a porcine model of traumatic hemorrhagic shock requiring pneumonectomy, death results from extreme pulmonary vascular resistance that precipitates right ventricular failure, severely limits left v…
raw_front_matter.authors: H. Gill Cryer, Constantine Mavroudis, Jun Yu, Andrew M. Roberts, Jorge I. Cue, J. David Richardson, Hiram C. Polk Jr.
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, pneumonectomy, right ventricular failure, pulmonary vascular resistance, trauma surgery, cardiopulmonary physiology, large animal model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a porcine model of traumatic hemorrhagic shock requiring pneumonectomy, death results from extreme pulmonary vascular resistance that precipitates right ventricular failure, severely limits left ventricular preload, and prevents successful resuscitation despite aggressive fluid and blood replacement.
key_points: Emergency pneumonectomy in the setting of hemorrhagic shock produces a pathophysiologic synergy that frequently leads to death from right ventricular failure.
In a porcine model, neither hemorrhagic shock alone nor pneumonectomy alone impaired cardiac output after resuscitation, but their combination did.
Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) rose to extremely high levels after shock plus pneumonectomy, exceeding the additive effects of each insult alone.
Right ventricular compensation (increased pressure, dilation, tachycardia) reached apparent maximal limits and then failed, causing loss of cardiac index and hypotension.
Failure of resuscitation was accompanied by persistent lactic acidosis and failure of arterial pH and lactate to normalize.
The mechanism of death is impaired left ventricular preload secondary to right ventricular failure from excessive afterload.
Effective treatment will likely require strategies that lower pulmonary vascular resistance or provide temporary mechanical support.

docs.title: Atrial Arrhythmias in ICU Trauma Patients

raw_front_matter.title: Atrial Arrhythmias in ICU Trauma Patients
raw_front_matter.description: In ICU trauma patients, atrial arrhythmias occur in about 6%, are strongly age-associated and independently linked to higher mortality, while beta-blocker therapy in those who develop arrhythmias is…
raw_front_matter.authors: Pantelis Hadjizacharia, Terence O'Keeffe, Carlos V.R. Brown, Kenji Inaba, Ali Salim, Linda S. Chan, Demetrios Demetriades, Peter Rhee
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, intensive care, atrial fibrillation, atrial arrhythmias, cardiac complications, beta-blockers, mortality risk, intracranial hemorrhage

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In ICU trauma patients, atrial arrhythmias occur in about 6%, are strongly age-associated and independently linked to higher mortality, while beta-blocker therapy in those who develop arrhythmias is associated with significantly improved survival.
key_points: Atrial arrhythmias occur in about 6% of trauma patients admitted to the surgical ICU.
Older age (>55 years) is the only independent risk factor identified for developing atrial arrhythmias after trauma.
Development of an atrial arrhythmia independently doubles mortality risk in ICU trauma patients.
Atrial arrhythmia patients are more often older, female, severely injured, and more likely to have intracranial hemorrhage and blunt trauma.
Beta-blocker therapy in trauma patients with atrial arrhythmias is associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality.
Beta-blocker exposure is also associated with improved survival in trauma patients with traumatic brain injury.
Atrial arrhythmias likely reflect greater injury severity and physiologic stress rather than being a direct primary cause of death.

docs.title: Hemorrhage-Induced Endotoxemia and rBPI21 in Rats

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhage-Induced Endotoxemia and rBPI21 in Rats
raw_front_matter.description: In a rat model of prolonged hemorrhagic shock, gut-derived endotoxin and bacterial translocation drive organ injury and mortality, and treatment with the LPS-binding protein fragment rBPI21 neutraliz…
raw_front_matter.authors: Yong-Ming Yao, Soheyl Bahrami, Guenther Leichtfried, Heinz Redl, Guenther Schlag
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endotoxemia, bacterial translocation, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), multiple organ failure, bactericidal/permeability-increasing protein (BPI), rBPI21, gut barrier, sepsis pathogenesis, rat model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of prolonged hemorrhagic shock, gut-derived endotoxin and bacterial translocation drive organ injury and mortality, and treatment with the LPS-binding protein fragment rBPI21 neutralizes systemic endotoxin, reduces intestinal and pulmonary damage, and trends toward improved survival without suppressing TNF, indicating both a key role for endotoxemia and additional, endotoxin-independent pathways of cytokine activation.
key_points: Prolonged hemorrhagic shock in rats leads to transient systemic endotoxemia and frequent bacterial translocation from the gut.
Recombinant BPI fragment rBPI21 nearly neutralized circulating endotoxin after resuscitation without significantly altering TNF levels.
rBPI21 treatment reduced histologic organ damage (especially lung and intestine) and showed a strong trend toward improved 48‑hour survival.
TNF elevation after hemorrhage appeared largely independent of circulating endotoxin neutralized by rBPI21, suggesting other induction pathways.
Data support a pathogenic role of gut-derived endotoxin/bacteria in post-hemorrhagic organ injury and mortality.
rBPI21 may disrupt a vicious cycle between endotoxemia and further bacterial translocation via combined LPS-binding and bactericidal effects.

docs.title: Transmural Glycolytic Enzyme Gradients in Normal LV (Dog)

raw_front_matter.title: Transmural Glycolytic Enzyme Gradients in Normal LV (Dog)
raw_front_matter.description: In anesthetized dogs with globally normal myocardial metabolism, the left ventricular subendocardium and papillary muscles already exhibit distinct glycolytic enzyme activity patterns consistent with…
raw_front_matter.authors: P. Lundsgaard-Hansen, C. Meyer, H. Riedwyl
raw_front_matter.tags: myocardial metabolism, glycolysis, transmural gradients, left ventricle, subendocardial ischemia, oxygen supply, canine model, enzyme activities

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized dogs with globally normal myocardial metabolism, the left ventricular subendocardium and papillary muscles already exhibit distinct glycolytic enzyme activity patterns consistent with chronic adaptation to lower oxygen supply, underscoring significant transmural metabolic heterogeneity that standard coronary sinus measurements may obscure.
key_points: In anesthetized open-chest dogs with globally normal hemodynamics and blood metabolites, the left ventricular wall is not metabolically homogeneous.
Seven of nine measured glycolytic-related enzymes show significant transmural activity gradients between subendocardial (inner) and subepicardial (outer) layers.
Inner (subendocardial) myocardium and papillary muscle generally show a pattern of enzyme activities consistent with higher reliance on glycolysis under limited oxygen.
The pattern of transmural enzyme differences resembles the enzyme redistribution previously described in hypoxic or failing hearts in a heart–lung preparation.
Results support the concept that, even in the apparent normal state, subendocardium operates in a “pre-insufficient” or chronically adapted metabolic state due to lower oxygen tension.
No significant gradients were found along the apex–base axis; differences were radial (transmural) only.
Conventional coronary sinus measurements may miss subendocardial metabolic distress because of these intrinsic heterogeneities.

docs.title: Hemodynamic & Neurohumoral Responses to Acute Hypovolemia

raw_front_matter.title: Hemodynamic & Neurohumoral Responses to Acute Hypovolemia
raw_front_matter.description: Acute hypovolemia in conscious mammals produces a biphasic response in which initial arterial baroreflex-mediated sympathetic vasoconstriction preserves pressure until a cardiopulmonary- and centrall…
raw_front_matter.authors: James C. Schadt; John Ludbrook
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hypovolemia, circulatory failure, vasovagal syncope, baroreflex, cardiopulmonary receptors, sympathetic nervous system, vasopressin, renin-angiotensin system, catecholamines, neuropeptide Y, opioids, serotonin, anesthesia effects, conscious animal models
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Acute hypovolemia in conscious mammals produces a biphasic response in which initial arterial baroreflex-mediated sympathetic vasoconstriction preserves pressure until a cardiopulmonary- and centrally mediated opioid/serotonin-dependent sympathoinhibitory phase abruptly causes vasodilation and hypotension, with humoral systems mainly supporting recovery rather than preventing collapse.
key_points: Acute central hypovolemia in conscious mammals elicits a biphasic response: an initial sympathoexcitatory, pressure-maintaining phase followed by an abrupt sympathoinhibitory, hypotensive phase.
Phase 1 is dominated by arterial baroreflex-mediated sympathetic activation and vasoconstriction that largely preserves arterial pressure despite falling cardiac output.

Phase 2 begins when blood volume loss reaches ~30% (species-dependent) and is characterized by withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor drive, relative/absolute bradycardia, and precipitous hypotension.
Cardiopulmonary (often ventricular) afferents appear to trigger the sympathoinhibitory phase in rabbits, rats, and cats, whereas the key signal in dogs and humans remains uncertain.

Humoral systems (renin–angiotensin and vasopressin) rise progressively with blood loss but play a secondary and mainly compensatory role, becoming more important for recovery than for initial pressure maintenance.

Endogenous central opioid and serotonergic mechanisms contribute importantly to the phase 2 sympathoinhibition; naloxone or serotonergic blockade can prevent or reverse this decompensatory phase in several species.

General anesthesia markedly distorts these patterns, usually blunting phase 1 vasoconstriction and often obscuring or altering phase 2, so conscious models are essential to understand clinically relevant responses.

docs.title: Effects of Hemorrhagic Shock on the Dog Heart

raw_front_matter.title: Effects of Hemorrhagic Shock on the Dog Heart
raw_front_matter.description: In anesthetized dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock preserves coronary flow and myocardial oxygen consumption via sympathetic-driven vasodilation and increased oxygen extraction but severely deranges m…
raw_front_matter.authors: Donavp B. Hackel, Walter T. Goodale
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial metabolism, coronary circulation, cardiac efficiency, subendocardial injury, sympathetic activation, canine model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock preserves coronary flow and myocardial oxygen consumption via sympathetic-driven vasodilation and increased oxygen extraction but severely deranges myocardial carbohydrate metabolism—especially pyruvate uptake—reduces mechanical efficiency, and can produce subendocardial injury, implicating intrinsic metabolic failure rather than simple underperfusion as a key driver of terminal cardiac dysfunction in shock.
key_points: In intact anesthetized dogs, 3 hours of controlled hemorrhagic hypotension profoundly altered myocardial carbohydrate metabolism, especially pyruvate handling.
Despite severe systemic hypotension and low cardiac output, coronary blood flow and total myocardial oxygen consumption were maintained via increased oxygen extraction and coronary vasodilation.
Myocardial oxygen extraction coefficients rose markedly, indicating relative myocardial hypoxia even though global oxygen use remained near normal.
Mechanical efficiency of the left ventricle fell sharply because oxygen consumption stayed high while external work dropped.
Subendocardial hemorrhage or necrosis of the left ventricle occurred in a subset of animals after hemorrhagic shock.
No clear correlation emerged between metabolic changes, survival, and the presence or type of myocardial pathology.
The authors attribute the pattern of changes to marked sympathetic hyperactivity and elevated circulating catecholamines in severe hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Plasma Succinate and Mortality After Critical Injury

raw_front_matter.title: Plasma Succinate and Mortality After Critical Injury
raw_front_matter.description: In severely injured trauma patients, plasma succinate—reflecting hypoxic mitochondrial dysfunction and ischemia-reperfusion—rises dramatically and predicts mortality more powerfully and specifically…
raw_front_matter.authors: D’Alessandro A, Moore HB, Moore EE, Reisz JA, Wither MJ, Ghasabyan A, Chandler J, Silliman CC, Hansen KC, Banerjee A
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, hemorrhagic shock, critical care, metabolomics, succinate, lactate, biomarkers, mortality prediction, mitochondrial dysfunction, ischemia-reperfusion
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In severely injured trauma patients, plasma succinate—reflecting hypoxic mitochondrial dysfunction and ischemia-reperfusion—rises dramatically and predicts mortality more powerfully and specifically than lactate, offering a promising biomarker for assessing shock severity and guiding resuscitation.
key_points: Plasma succinate rises markedly after severe trauma and hemorrhagic shock and is strongly associated with mortality.
Succinate outperforms lactate as a mortality predictor, with a higher ROC AUC and larger fold-change between survivors and non-survivors.
Succinate elevation reflects hypoxic mitochondrial dysfunction and ischemia-reperfusion biology, not just generic anaerobic metabolism.
Patients with early high succinate who survived typically showed rapid normalization with successful resuscitation.
Persistently elevated or rising succinate after initial resuscitation was characteristic of patients who died.
Succinate appears more specific for death from hemorrhagic trauma than for death from non-hemorrhagic causes.
High-throughput mass spectrometry platforms can quantify succinate rapidly enough to be potentially useful as an ED point-of-care tool.

docs.title: Dopamine Mechanisms in Endotoxin Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Dopamine Mechanisms in Endotoxin Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In canine endotoxin shock, dopamine preserves venous return and improves survival primarily by mobilizing pooled blood from the hepatosplanchnic bed and enhancing cardiac performance, highlighting th…
raw_front_matter.authors: Linda L. Shanbour
raw_front_matter.tags: endotoxin shock, septic shock, hemorrhagic shock model, dopamine, hepatosplanchnic circulation, venous return, cardiac output, canine model
raw_front_matter.journal: Technical Report, University of Oklahoma Medical Center; Office of Naval Research Contract N00014-68-A-0496

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine endotoxin shock, dopamine preserves venous return and improves survival primarily by mobilizing pooled blood from the hepatosplanchnic bed and enhancing cardiac performance, highlighting the liver’s central role in the circulatory collapse of septic shock.
key_points: Endotoxin (septic) shock in dogs is characterized by decreased total peripheral resistance, reduced cardiac output, and profound hepatosplanchnic venous pooling that lowers venous return and arterial pressure.
Dopamine has complex, dose-dependent cardiovascular actions, including renal vasodilation, positive inotropy, and variable systemic vascular effects that differ by species and vascular bed.
In canine endotoxin shock, continuous dopamine infusion prevents the typical hepatosplanchnic pooling of blood and helps maintain venous return and cardiac output.
Dopamine’s protective effect is more pronounced when given as pretreatment and continued through the post-endotoxin period, rather than as rescue therapy alone.
Isolated perfused liver experiments show that dopamine markedly reduces liver volume and portal venous pressure and prevents the large liver swelling usually induced by endotoxin.
Survival studies in intact dogs suggest improved survival and better maintenance of blood pressure, heart rate, and venous pH with dopamine infusion during endotoxin shock.

The data support a mechanistic model in which dopamine simultaneously enhances cardiac performance and mobilizes pooled blood from the hepatosplanchnic bed to sustain venous return in endotoxin shock.

docs.title: Acute Coronary Insufficiency from Hemorrhage

raw_front_matter.title: Acute Coronary Insufficiency from Hemorrhage
raw_front_matter.description: In patients with acute hemorrhage—especially those with underlying heart disease—rapid blood loss, hypotension, tachycardia, and shock frequently precipitate reversible or sometimes necrotizing suben…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur M. Master, Simon Dack, Henry Horn, Bernard I. Freedman, Leonard E. Field
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, acute coronary insufficiency, myocardial ischemia, subendocardial necrosis, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, cardiac failure, electrocardiography, coronary circulation
raw_front_matter.journal: American Heart Journal (Mount Sinai Hospital series)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In patients with acute hemorrhage—especially those with underlying heart disease—rapid blood loss, hypotension, tachycardia, and shock frequently precipitate reversible or sometimes necrotizing subendocardial myocardial ischemia without coronary occlusion, making early ECG monitoring and aggressive blood transfusion critical to prevent hemorrhage‑induced coronary insufficiency and cardiac failure.
key_points: In 103 patients with moderate or severe acute hemorrhage, 57% developed clinical or ECG evidence of acute coronary insufficiency.
Coronary insufficiency occurred particularly in patients with pre‑existing cardiovascular disease but was also seen in young individuals with structurally normal hearts.
Electrocardiographic changes (T‑wave inversion and RS‑T depression) were frequent, could precede symptoms, and were often reversible after blood replacement.
Severity and rapidity of blood loss, hypotension, tachycardia, and shock were strongly associated with coronary insufficiency, sometimes independently of marked anemia.
Autopsies demonstrated subendocardial myocardial necrosis without acute coronary artery occlusion, localised mainly to the left ventricular subendocardium and papillary muscles.
Hemorrhage could precipitate or worsen congestive heart failure; heart failure developed in about 10% of cases.
Early, adequate blood transfusion is emphasized as both prophylaxis and treatment for hemorrhage‑induced coronary insufficiency, especially in patients with underlying heart disease.

docs.title: Intestinal Factor in Irreversible Endotoxin Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Intestinal Factor in Irreversible Endotoxin Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of lethal endotoxin shock, irreversible cardiovascular failure is driven largely by sympathomimetic-induced intestinal ischemia and hemorrhagic necrosis, which can be prevented by a…
raw_front_matter.authors: Richard C. Lillehei, Lloyd D. MacLean
raw_front_matter.tags: endotoxin shock, septic shock, hemorrhagic shock, intestinal ischemia, vasoconstriction, sympathomimetic agents, adrenergic blockade, hydrocortisone, vasopressors, canine model, microcirculation, plasma volume, hemorrhagic necrosis

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of lethal endotoxin shock, irreversible cardiovascular failure is driven largely by sympathomimetic-induced intestinal ischemia and hemorrhagic necrosis, which can be prevented by adrenergic blockade or hydrocortisone but is worsened or unimproved by vasopressors and isolated volume replacement.
key_points: Irreversible endotoxin shock in dogs is closely associated with hemorrhagic necrosis of the intestinal mucosa, large plasma volume losses, rising hematocrit, and increasing plasma free hemoglobin.
Endotoxin acts largely via intense, prolonged vasoconstriction in the mesenteric circulation, leading to critical bowel ischemia and capillary leak.

Adrenergic blocking agents (chlorpromazine, Dibenzyline) and high-dose hydrocortisone largely prevent bowel necrosis, plasma loss, and death, whereas vasopressor drugs (metaraminol, norepinephrine) worsen or fail to improve outcome.
Surgical removal of most of the intestine prolongs survival after endotoxin despite severe coagulopathy, implicating the gut as a major determinant of irreversibility.
Intestinal sterilization with oral antibiotics, systemic neomycin, hypothermia, and plasma-volume replacement do not prevent irreversible endotoxin shock.

The bowel appears to be the prime organ driving the irreversible phase of endotoxin shock, likely via ischemic injury and release of endogenous toxic products, rather than via luminal bacteria per se.

docs.title: Myocardial Response to Acute Oligemic Hypotension

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Response to Acute Oligemic Hypotension
raw_front_matter.description: In this canine model of severe acute oligemic hypotension, death follows progressive loss of effective venous return and arterial pressure while myocardial contractile force remains largely preserved…
raw_front_matter.authors: M. G. Weidner Jr., Loren Roth, F. A. Simeone
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, oligemic hypotension, myocardial function, cardiac output, animal model, venous return, hemodynamics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In this canine model of severe acute oligemic hypotension, death follows progressive loss of effective venous return and arterial pressure while myocardial contractile force remains largely preserved until terminal collapse, indicating that the failing circulation—not intrinsic myocardial failure—is the primary limiting factor.
key_points: In anesthetized dogs, rapid severe oligemic hypotension (mean arterial pressure 25–30 mm Hg) causes an immediate ~50% drop in myocardial contractile force.
Despite progressive hypotension and eventual death in many animals, myocardial contractile force generally remains near normal after reinfusion until terminal collapse.
Cardiac output falls markedly and arterial pressure deteriorates after prolonged hypotension even though left atrial and vena caval pressures stay near normal until late.
Electrocardiographic signs of ischemia appear quickly with bleeding but largely normalize after blood reinfusion, indicating substantial myocardial recovery capacity.
The authors conclude that in this model death is not primarily due to intrinsic myocardial failure but to inadequate venous return, likely from peripheral blood pooling.
Small additional blood withdrawals during established hypotension transiently increase contractile force, consistent with sympathetic compensation.
The heart appears capable of maintaining contractile force as long as an adequate volume of blood is delivered to it, even after prolonged severe hypotension.

docs.title: Adrenergic Blockade in Experimental Haemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Adrenergic Blockade in Experimental Haemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine haemorrhagic shock model, alpha- or combined alpha–beta adrenergic blockade improved tolerance and markedly reduced metabolic acidosis—largely via better preservation of circulating blood…
raw_front_matter.authors: G. Zierott, P. Lundsgaard-Hansen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, adrenergic blockade, alpha blockade, beta blockade, combined blockade, microcirculation, metabolic acidosis, dog model, cardiovascular physiology
raw_front_matter.journal: British Journal of Surgery (Proceedings of the Surgical Research Society Joint Meeting)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine haemorrhagic shock model, alpha- or combined alpha–beta adrenergic blockade improved tolerance and markedly reduced metabolic acidosis—largely via better preservation of circulating blood volume—while beta-blockade alone worsened outcomes, underscoring the central role of adrenergic tone in shock pathophysiology and therapy.
key_points: Prolonged adrenergic activation in haemorrhagic shock is harmful, prompting evaluation of alpha-, beta-, and combined adrenergic blockade in a controlled animal model.
Alpha-blockade reduced external blood loss, extended the tolerated duration of shock, and lessened metabolic derangements compared with untreated controls.
Beta-blockade alone worsened tolerance to shock, shortening the tolerated period and aggravating metabolic sequelae despite similar initial blood loss.
Combined alpha- and beta-blockade minimized metabolic consequences of shock while maintaining tolerated shock duration comparable to alpha-blockade alone.
Blocked animals exhibited plasma refill during shock, in contrast to plasma loss in controls, so true circulating volume differences exceeded what external blood loss suggested.
A roughly 10% difference in circulating blood volume was associated with about a 100% difference in metabolic acidosis severity.
These data help explain reported protective effects of adrenergic blockade and illuminate discrepancies between clinical and experimental haemorrhagic shock regarding metabolic acidosis.

docs.title: Control of BP in Hemorrhagic/Hypovolemic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Control of BP in Hemorrhagic/Hypovolemic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: This review outlines the integrated neural, hormonal, and endothelial regulation of central and peripheral blood pressure in hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock and highlights centhaquine as a novel venoco…
raw_front_matter.authors: Amaresh K. Ranjan, Anil Gulati
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hypovolemic shock, central blood pressure, peripheral blood pressure, autonomic regulation, RAAS, endothelium, centhaquine, vasopressors, cardiorenal protection

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: This review outlines the integrated neural, hormonal, and endothelial regulation of central and peripheral blood pressure in hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock and highlights centhaquine as a novel venoconstrictive, centrally acting α2‑agonist that improves hemodynamics, reduces mortality, and protects organs when added to standard resuscitation.
key_points: Central blood pressure (CBP) more directly reflects pressures in the heart and brain than peripheral blood pressure (PBP), and the two can diverge substantially due to pulse pressure amplification.
Blood pressure is regulated by tightly integrated neural, hormonal, osmotic, and endothelial mechanisms acting on heart rate, stroke volume, and systemic vascular resistance.

In hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock, early compensatory baroreflex and neurohumoral responses preserve perfusion, but failure of these mechanisms leads to abrupt decompensation, metabolic acidosis, and multiorgan failure.
Current resuscitation options (crystalloids, colloids, blood products, HBOCs, plasma) each have significant limitations regarding efficacy, safety, and logistical feasibility.

Centhaquine (Lyfaquin) is a novel resuscitative agent that selectively induces venoconstriction (α2B) and central sympatholysis (α2A), improving venous return, cardiac output, MAP, and tissue perfusion without arterial vasoconstriction.
Phase II/III trials in hypovolemic shock show centhaquine reduces vasopressor requirements, improves hemodynamics and lactate/base deficit, and decreases 28‑day mortality versus standard care.
Preclinical data suggest centhaquine also preserves renal perfusion and limits hemorrhage‑induced acute kidney injury via HIF‑1α upregulation and reduced injury/apoptosis markers.

docs.title: Arterial Isovolumic Contraction Period in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Arterial Isovolumic Contraction Period in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: Ventilation-induced variation in the arterially determined left ventricular isovolumic contraction period closely tracks hemorrhagic shock severity and fluid responsiveness, correlates with PPV and S…
raw_front_matter.authors: Marc J. van Houwelingen, Daphne Merkus, Jan Hofland, Jan Bakker, Robert Tenbrinck, Maaike te Lintel Hekkert, Geert van Dijk, Arnold P. G. Hoeks, Dirk J. Duncker
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac function, left ventricle, isovolumic contraction period, pre-ejection period, stroke volume variation, pulse pressure variation, hemodynamic monitoring, mechanical ventilation, swine model
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology - Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Ventilation-induced variation in the arterially determined left ventricular isovolumic contraction period closely tracks hemorrhagic shock severity and fluid responsiveness, correlates with PPV and SVV, and can be measured in a site-independent manner from arterial pressure waveforms without ECG, making it a promising timing-based index for shock assessment.
key_points: Ventilation-induced preload changes during graded hemorrhage mainly alter the left ventricular isovolumic contraction period, not electromechanical delay or arterial pulse travel time.

The ventilatory variation in arterially determined isovolumic contraction period (ΔAIC) tracks hemorrhage severity and resuscitation similarly to pulse pressure variation (PPV) and stroke volume variation (SVV).
ΔAIC measured in the ascending aorta and carotid artery are interchangeable, suggesting site independence for this timing-based shock index.
Pre-ejection period variation (ΔPEP) also reflects fluid responsiveness but is measurement-site dependent and confounded by pulse travel time.
AIC can be derived solely from the arterial pressure waveform, unlike PEP which requires simultaneous ECG, potentially simplifying monitoring.
Neither ventilatory variation in electromechanical delay (ΔEMD) nor in pulse travel time (ΔPTT) changed meaningfully with hemorrhage or resuscitation.

docs.title: Changing Incidence of Ventricular Fibrillation in Cardiac Arrest

raw_front_matter.title: Changing Incidence of Ventricular Fibrillation in Cardiac Arrest
raw_front_matter.description: Declining ventricular fibrillation incidence in cardiac arrest—driven by improved cardiovascular prevention and device therapy—has shifted the burden toward pulseless electrical activity, a mechanist…
raw_front_matter.authors: Steven P. Keller, Henry R. Halperin
raw_front_matter.tags: cardiac arrest, ventricular fibrillation, pulseless electrical activity, out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, implantable cardioverter-defibrillator, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, shockable vs non-shockable rhythms, heart failure, sepsis, critical care
raw_front_matter.journal: Current Treatment Options in Cardiovascular Medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Declining ventricular fibrillation incidence in cardiac arrest—driven by improved cardiovascular prevention and device therapy—has shifted the burden toward pulseless electrical activity, a mechanistically complex, non-shockable rhythm with poor outcomes that demands renewed focus on underlying pathophysiology and perfusion-focused resuscitation strategies.
key_points: The incidence of ventricular fibrillation (VF) as the presenting rhythm in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) has declined markedly over recent decades in multiple populations.
Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole now account for the majority of both in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrests and have far worse survival than VF/pulseless VT.
Improved coronary heart disease management, widespread beta‑blocker use, and expansion of implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) likely reduce VF incidence and may shift some events to PEA.

PEA represents a spectrum from pseudo‑PEA with residual ventricular wall motion to true electromechanical dissociation with no effective contraction, often driven by severe ischemia and disordered calcium handling.
An aging population with more multiorgan failure, sepsis, and non-cardiac causes of shock likely contributes to the increasing relative burden of PEA arrests.

Current treatment of PEA centers on high-quality CPR, rapid identification and reversal of underlying causes, and selective use of adjunctive mechanical CPR devices, targeted temperature management, and ECMO.
Despite advances in VF management, PEA outcomes remain poor, underscoring the need for mechanistic research and optimization of circulatory support strategies during arrest.

key_points: Plasma free iodide levels increase markedly in human trauma patients with hemorrhagic shock and in sepsis patients compared with healthy controls.
Hibernating Arctic ground squirrels show substantial increases in circulating iodide during late torpor and interbout arousals.
In a mouse hindlimb ischemia–reperfusion model, iodide accumulates in injured tissue and reduces local muscle damage and remote organ injury.
Iodide likely derives from deiodination of thyroid hormones and may represent a conserved stress-response mechanism.
Iodide acts as a catalytic antioxidant against hydrogen peroxide, distinct from sacrificial antioxidants such as vitamins C and E.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In swine, uncontrolled aortic hemorrhage causes a much larger fall in blood pressure for a given blood loss than controlled hemorrhage, demonstrating that the presence of an active vascular injury fundamentally alters the hemodynamic response to hemorrhage and limits the clinical realism of standard controlled-bleeding models.
key_points: Uncontrolled aortic hemorrhage produces a disproportionately large fall in mean arterial pressure (MAP) relative to blood loss compared with controlled hemorrhage.
To match the MAP profile of uncontrolled hemorrhage, controlled hemorrhage required significantly greater blood volume loss.
When blood loss was matched, MAP during controlled hemorrhage remained substantially higher than during uncontrolled hemorrhage.
Cardiac output, heart rate, and total peripheral resistance showed broadly similar directional changes across models, but their relationships to blood volume and pressure differed.
Central venous pressure fell more during uncontrolled hemorrhage for a given blood loss, suggesting greater preload reduction.
Metabolic derangements (lactate rise, acidosis) were similar across groups at comparable times, despite differing hemodynamics.
The pressure–volume relationship is fundamentally altered in the presence of an uncontrolled vascular injury, implying different reflex and vascular control mechanisms.

key_points: Simultaneous left ventricular outflow and aortic root pressures were recorded in anesthetized dogs using dual intracardiac manometers.
Under normal conditions, ventricular and aortic pressure peaks are congruent, and catheter position changes in the outflow tract do not alter contour.
During hemorrhagic circulatory shock (mean arterial pressure < 50 mmHg), a marked dissociation between ventricular and aortic pressure waveforms appears.
In shock, left ventricular pressure can reach 120–200 mmHg while aortic pressure falls abruptly after a modest peak of 50–60 mmHg.
These findings are interpreted as evidence that the left ventricle continues to contract isometrically after ejecting an abnormally small blood volume.
The abnormal isometric phase is especially prominent during certain stages of adrenergic (adrenaline) influence in shock.
Prolonged high-force isometric contraction in a poorly filled ventricle may explain the high incidence of subendocardial hemorrhages in prolonged shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Regional ischemia–reperfusion in cardiomyocyte monolayers produces subcellular mitochondrial membrane potential instability that creates a heterogeneous, pro‑reentrant electrophysiologic substrate, and pharmacologic stabilization of the mitochondrial network with 4′‑chlorodiazepam markedly suppresses these post‑ischemic arrhythmias.
key_points: Regional ischemia–reperfusion in neonatal rat ventricular myocyte (NRVM) monolayers produces complex, two-phase mitochondrial depolarization followed by highly unstable recovery of mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm).
Reperfusion after 1 hour of ischemia consistently elicits subcellular ΔΨm oscillations (“flickers”) across the reperfused zone, coinciding with a window of vulnerability to reentrant arrhythmias.
Heterogeneous recovery of electrical excitability upon reperfusion leads to stray wavelets, micro‑reentry, and sustained spiral wave reentry anchored near the ischemic border.

The benzodiazepine-site ligand 4′‑chlorodiazepam (4′‑Cl‑DZP) suppresses ΔΨm oscillations, improves glutathione (GSH) redox recovery, preserves conduction, and markedly reduces reperfusion-induced reentry.
Cyclophilin D–sensitive permeability transition pore (PTP) opening does not mediate early ΔΨm oscillations but appears to contribute to late, widespread mitochondrial collapse during reperfusion.

KATP channel blockade does not prevent IR-induced ΔΨm instability and, in this model, fails to reduce reperfusion arrhythmias, indicating that mitochondrial stabilization, rather than KATP inhibition alone, is critical.
The data support a causal link between mitochondrial network instability during reperfusion and the genesis of post-ischemic tachyarrhythmias.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Intracoronary pyruvate infusion produces a reversible positive inotropic effect that significantly improves regional function in both normal and stunned canine myocardium, likely by enhancing myocardial energetics rather than simply increasing adrenergic drive.
key_points: Pyruvate exerts an acute positive inotropic effect on both normal and post-ischemic stunned myocardium in vivo.
In a canine LAD occlusion model, intracoronary pyruvate infusion improved depressed regional systolic wall thickening after reperfusion.
The inotropic effect of pyruvate was present only during active infusion and was fully reversible after its cessation.
Pyruvate enhanced function in the ischemia–reperfused region without altering function in non-ischemic control regions.
Findings support the concept that stunned myocardium retains substantial contractile reserve that can be recruited by metabolic interventions.
Because pyruvate is a key oxidative substrate, its benefits may derive from improving myocardial energy state rather than simply increasing oxygen demand.

key_points: Hemorrhagic shock produces characteristic abnormalities in myocardial extraction of pyruvate, lactate, and oxygen.
Reinfusion of shed blood within ~1–1.5 hours of shock can largely normalize myocardial metabolic disturbances.
If shock is prolonged to 3 hours or more at very low arterial pressures, myocardial metabolic abnormalities become functionally irreversible to transfusion.
Short-duration shock shows restoration of both systemic blood pressure and myocardial substrate extraction after transfusion.
Prolonged shock shows blunted blood pressure recovery and persistent or worsened myocardial metabolic derangements after transfusion.
Findings support a role for irreversible myocardial injury and enzyme dysfunction in the irreversibility of prolonged hemorrhagic shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Once hemorrhagic shock has progressed to a state unresponsive to adequate transfusion, no combination of volume expansion, pressor, or metabolic therapy can reverse it, and experimental preservation of liver perfusion shows that preventing prolonged hepatic underperfusion is crucial to avoiding this irreversible phase.
key_points: Irreversible traumatic/hemorrhagic shock cannot be cured by restoring blood or plasma volume alone once a critical period of severe hypotension has elapsed.
High hematocrit and blood viscosity aggravate shock hemodynamics, especially in tourniquet shock, but are secondary in importance to volume deficiency.
A broad range of fluids, pressor agents, metabolic substrates, and alkali fail to reverse hemorrhagic shock once it is unresponsive to adequate transfusion.
Intermediary carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism, while quantitatively disturbed, remains functionally capable even in irreversible shock and does not pinpoint the onset of irreversibility.
Selective preservation of liver perfusion during prolonged hemorrhagic shock prevents the development of irreversibility to transfusion and permits survival.
Findings implicate severe, prolonged hepatic underperfusion/anoxia as a primary, preventable determinant of the transition to irreversible shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic hypotension, beta-adrenergic blockade with pronethalol restores depressed systolic coronary blood flow and reduces myocardial lesions without altering systemic pressure or output, implicating excessive positive inotropy—and the resulting systolic mechanical impedance of coronary transmyocardial vessels—as a key cause of subendocardial ischemia when perfusion pressure is low.
key_points: Hemorrhagic hypotension markedly depresses coronary blood flow, with a disproportionate loss of systolic flow during early shock.
Beta-adrenergic blockade with pronethalol in hemorrhagic hypotension significantly increases total coronary blood flow without changing arterial pressure or cardiac output.
The improvement in coronary flow with pronethalol is almost entirely due to restoration of systolic flow rate; diastolic flow is largely unchanged.
Pretreatment with pronethalol partially preserves coronary blood flow during the onset of hemorrhagic hypotension compared with untreated animals.
Beta-sympathetic blockade reduces the myocardial lesions (subendocardial hemorrhage and necrosis) otherwise seen in hemorrhagic shock, independent of heart rate.
Findings support a major role for intense positive inotropic sympathetic stimulation in dynamically impeding coronary flow and producing subendocardial injury when perfusion pressure is low.

The study is foundational for later concepts of shock-induced cardiomyopathy.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A standardized 30%-blood-loss swine model of hemorrhagic shock at a target MAP of ~45 mmHg produces reproducible hemodynamic depression, metabolic acidosis, and reduced oxygen delivery with relatively preserved oxygen consumption, offering a robust platform for evaluating monitoring tools and resuscitation therapies.
key_points: A reproducible large-animal (swine) model of controlled hemorrhagic shock was established by removing 30% of blood volume and maintaining shock for 90 minutes.
Mean arterial pressure was standardized to ~45 mmHg to define the degree of shock and allow comparability with prior work.
Hemorrhagic shock caused progressive decreases in blood pressure, cardiac output, oxygen delivery, and urine output, with compensatory tachycardia and increased pulmonary vascular resistance.
Oxygen delivery declined significantly during shock, whereas oxygen consumption remained relatively stable until late phases, indicating preserved global oxygen uptake over a wide delivery range.
Progressive metabolic acidosis developed (fall in pH and bicarbonate) while hematocrit and hemoglobin remained relatively stable.
The model is suitable for evaluating invasive monitoring techniques (e.g., Swan–Ganz, oximetry) and new resuscitation strategies such as hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, hyperbaric oxygen markedly reduces hypoxia-driven subendocardial myocardial and renal tubular injury but does not affect mechanically mediated myocardial zonal lesions, supporting distinct pathophysiologic mechanisms for these lesion types.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in dogs produces two major myocardial lesion types: subendocardial hemorrhage/necrosis and focal zonal lesions.
Treating dogs with 100% oxygen at 2.36 ATA during hemorrhagic shock markedly reduced severe left ventricular subendocardial hemorrhage and necrosis.
The incidence and severity of subendocardial hemorrhage inversely correlated with venous oxygen content at the end of shock.
Hyperbaric oxygen did not alter the occurrence or severity of myocardial zonal lesions.
Severe acute renal tubular necrosis was absent in hyperbaric oxygen–treated dogs but present in controls.
Lesions in liver, intestine, spleen, and lungs were similar in treated and control animals, implying limited benefit where flow is critically reduced.
Findings support distinct etiologies: subendocardial lesions are primarily hypoxic, whereas zonal lesions are mainly mechanical in origin.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A controlled human LBNP model reveals that tolerance to hemorrhage hinges on robust sympathetic tachycardia, vasoconstriction, and oscillatory cardio-cerebral hemodynamics, with respiratory and neurocirculatory dynamics offering promising targets for earlier diagnosis and intervention in hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Lower body negative pressure (LBNP) in conscious humans is a valid, repeatable laboratory model of progressive hemorrhage to the point of early decompensatory shock.
Healthy humans show large inter-individual variability in tolerance to central hypovolemia, allowing classification into high-tolerant (HT) and low-tolerant (LT) phenotypes.
Maintenance of arterial pressure and cerebral perfusion during blood volume loss depends critically on sympathetically mediated tachycardia, vasoconstriction, and oscillations in pressure and flow.
Dynamic oscillations in arterial pressure and cerebral blood flow, rather than absolute mean values, are strongly associated with higher tolerance to simulated hemorrhage.
The respiratory pump can be therapeutically harnessed (intrathoracic pressure regulation, IPR) to improve cardiac filling, arterial and cerebral perfusion, and tolerance to central hypovolemia.

Transition from compensation to decompensatory shock occurs in two phases: metabolically driven vasodilation at still-adequate pressures, followed by abrupt bradycardia and sympathetic withdrawal causing rapid hypotension and presyncope.
Standard vital signs alone are unreliable for early diagnosis of hemorrhagic shock; integrated measures of compensatory reserve and dynamic hemodynamics offer superior insight.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, the myocardium begins producing rather than extracting pyruvate due to a shock-related peripheral circulating factor, and this metabolic disturbance is not adequately explained by reduced coronary perfusion alone but is modulated by systemic hemodynamics.
key_points: In hemorrhagic shock, the canine myocardium switches from net extraction to net production of pyruvate despite preserved ventricular contractile function.
This metabolic shift is not explained solely by reduced coronary artery perfusion pressure or coronary hypotension.
Maintaining normal systemic arterial pressure and flow delays or modifies the onset of myocardial pyruvate production.
Cross-transfusion from normotensive dogs partially reduces pyruvate production in shocked myocardium, implicating a circulating peripheral factor.
Myocardial lactate extraction and oxygen extraction generally increase during early shock, while overall uptake falls as coronary flow declines.
Extended cardiopulmonary bypass at normal coronary pressure can itself be associated with delayed myocardial pyruvate production.
Findings support the existence of a shock-derived peripheral factor affecting myocardial metabolism, analogous to known myocardial depressant factors.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a large cohort of severely injured trauma patients, admission catecholamine surges—especially adrenaline—drive endothelial glycocalyx and cell damage, with syndecan-1 and thrombomodulin emerging as strong independent predictors of early and late mortality, underscoring endotheliopathy as a central mechanistic and therapeutic target in hemorrhagic trauma.
key_points: In 424 severely injured trauma patients, admission adrenaline levels strongly and independently correlated with syndecan-1, indicating catecholamine-driven endothelial glycocalyx degradation (“endotheliopathy of trauma”).
Adrenaline and syndecan-1 were independent predictors of early (<24 h) and late (7- and 28-day) mortality after adjustment for injury severity and physiological status.
Noradrenaline independently predicted <24-hour mortality, while soluble thrombomodulin, a marker of endothelial cell damage, independently predicted 7- and 28-day mortality.
Endothelial activation marker soluble E-selectin neither correlated with catecholamines nor predicted mortality in this cohort.
Endotheliopathy severity (high syndecan-1) was greatest in patients with the highest adrenaline, most severe injuries, most profound shock, and highest transfusion requirements.
Findings validate earlier smaller-cohort and experimental work linking sympathoadrenal activation to endothelial injury, coagulopathy, and poor outcome in trauma.
Results support targeting sympathoadrenal overactivation and protecting/restoring the endothelium as potential therapeutic strategies in hemorrhagic trauma.

key_points: Capture myopathy (CM) in hooved mammals is proposed as an evolutionary and mechanistic model for human stress cardiomyopathy, including Takotsubo syndrome.
CM is evolutionarily labile among ungulates, with gains and losses of susceptibility occurring repeatedly across the phylogeny.
Life history traits associated with predation avoidance—greater maximum running speed, larger brains, larger minimum group size, and longer maximum longevity—are linked to reported CM susceptibility.
Fear and acute autonomic activation, rather than physical exertion alone, are central to the pathophysiology of CM.
The study highlights how adaptations that reduce predation risk may inadvertently increase vulnerability to stress-induced cardiac and muscular failure.
Comparative patterns in CM susceptibility may help generate hypotheses about human variability in vulnerability to Takotsubo cardiomyopathy.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In controlled swine exsanguination, early shock is driven by preload loss but terminal cardiac arrest occurs only after coronary perfusion collapses at very low arterial pressures, highlighting coronary perfusion as a critical and currently under-addressed resuscitation target in hemorrhagic cardiac arrest.
key_points: In a swine model of controlled exsanguination, two distinct phases were observed: early preload failure and late coronary perfusion failure leading to asystole.
Asystole occurred after shedding about half of the total blood volume, with organized cardiac activity persisting until terminal arrest and no dysrhythmias.
Coronary blood flow was relatively preserved despite profound shock until mean arterial pressure (MAP) fell below about 20 mm Hg, at which point flow precipitously declined and asystole ensued.
Early hemodynamic deterioration (first ~15 minutes) was marked by sharp decreases in SBP, cardiac output, stroke volume, and LV end-diastolic volume.
Metabolic acidosis, rising lactate, and hyperkalemia developed progressively during exsanguination, consistent with worsening tissue hypoperfusion.
A strong linear relationship was found between coronary (LAD) flow and left ventricular ejection fraction, linking coronary perfusion directly to systolic performance.
Existing trauma resuscitation strategies focused on preload/afterload support and thoracotomy likely fail in late exsanguination because they do not adequately restore coronary perfusion.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In rabbit hearts, the metabolic damage incurred during the agonal period, particularly with asphyxial death, is at least as important as warm ischemia duration in determining postmortem myocardial viability, underscoring the need to control preterminal cardiac metabolism to optimize cadaver heart preservation and resuscitation.
key_points: The metabolic state of the heart after death is strongly influenced by the agonal period (mode of dying), not only by the postmortem warm ischemia interval.
Among tested death modes, exsanguination under anesthesia preserved myocardial energy stores far better than ether overdose or asphyxia.
Asphyxial death produced the most severe depletion of high‑energy phosphates and glycogen, and the greatest edema, despite similar postmortem intervals.
Postmortem myocardial glycolysis is markedly activated, but substantial loss of glycolytic products and adenine nucleotides from the cell occurs, especially after asphyxia.
Myocardial glycogen content strongly correlates with residual high‑energy phosphate levels, indicating that high pre‑ and perimortem energy demand predicts poor resuscitability.
Key glycolytic control steps (e.g., phosphofructokinase) lose their rate‑limiting character during the agonal and early postmortem period, reflecting major metabolic deregulation.
Strategies to modulate cardiac metabolism before and during the agonal phase may be as critical for successful cadaver heart resuscitation as minimizing warm ischemia time.

Seven of nine measured glycolytic and related dehydrogenase enzymes show statistically significant transmural activity gradients.
Inner (subendocardial) layers and papillary muscles display an enzyme pattern resembling that of hearts stressed toward failure or hypoxia in prior work.
The observed gradients are consistent with chronic metabolic adaptation of subendocardium to lower oxygen tension and blood flow.
Standard coronary sinus measurements can therefore mask important regional metabolic heterogeneity within the left ventricle.
No significant base-to-apex (longitudinal) gradients in enzyme activities were detected.
Isocitrate and malate dehydrogenase behavior was equivocal and not clearly interpretable.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a goat model of hemorrhagic shock with tourniquet-induced limb ischemia, pyruvate-fortified Ringer’s solution provided superior post-resuscitation blood pressure stability, reduced myocardial nitrosative stress, and blunted systemic neutrophilic inflammation compared with conventional lactated Ringer’s.
key_points: In a goat model of hemorrhagic shock plus hindlimb ischemia-reperfusion, pyruvate-fortified Ringer’s (PR) was compared with conventional lactated Ringer’s (LR) for resuscitation.
PR more effectively maintained mean arterial pressure during the post-resuscitation period than LR.
PR improved systemic acid–base status, augmenting arterial bicarbonate and base excess relative to LR.
LR resuscitation was associated with increased myocardial nitrotyrosine, indicating elevated nitrosative stress, which was markedly reduced by PR.
PR blunted the post-resuscitation increase in circulating neutrophils seen with LR, suggesting reduced systemic inflammation.
Both LR and PR increased myocardial lactate, but PR better preserved myocardial pyruvate content and a more favorable lactate/pyruvate ratio.
Findings support pyruvate-enriched crystalloid as a potentially superior resuscitation fluid in traumatic hemorrhagic shock with limb ischemia-reperfusion.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rabbit model of hemorrhagic shock, low-dose combined alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade optimally preserves metabolic stability while minimizing the reduction in tolerated blood loss, making it a useful regimen for experimental studies of shock and cardiac protection.
key_points: Alpha-adrenergic blockade during controlled hemorrhagic hypotension reduces metabolic acidosis but also decreases tolerated blood loss.
Pure beta-adrenergic blockade worsens the course of experimental hemorrhagic shock metabolically.
Combining low-dose alpha- and beta-blockade preserves the metabolic benefits of alpha-blockade while limiting the reduction in tolerated blood loss.
Arterial lactate/pyruvate ratios indicate improved tissue perfusion at all levels of alpha-blockade, unaffected by added beta-blockade.
Three hours after retransfusion, metabolic recovery (pH, base excess) is better with low-dose combined blockade than with alpha-blockade alone.
The combination of 1.0 mg/kg phenoxybenzamine and 0.1 mg/kg Trasicor is proposed as an optimal regimen for experimental hemorrhagic shock studies.

raw_front_matter.authors: P. Lundsgaard-Hansen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial metabolism, oxygen supply, lactate, pyruvate, coronary circulation, dog model, cardiac failure, redox state

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In hemorrhagic shock in dogs, coronary sinus oxygenation and lactate/pyruvate–based redox markers show that the heart generally does not shift to overt anaerobic metabolism, arguing against critical global myocardial oxygen deficiency as the primary cause of cardiac failure in this setting.
key_points: In anesthetized open-chest dogs subjected to hemorrhagic shock (mean BP ~32 mmHg), the heart did not show a consistent shift to anaerobic metabolism by modern lactate/pyruvate criteria.
Coronary sinus oxygen content and saturation fell during shock but remained above experimentally defined critical levels that trigger anaerobic glycolysis in myocardium.

Myocardial lactate and pyruvate extraction decreased in shock and sometimes reversed to net output, but excess lactate and calculated anaerobic metabolic rate across the heart were not significantly different from zero.
Arterial blood showed marked increases in lactate, pyruvate, and lactate/pyruvate ratio, indicating systemic (extra-cardiac) anaerobic metabolism and metabolic acidosis.
Redox potential changes of the blood lactate dehydrogenase system across the heart were small and not consistent with a major switch to anaerobic myocardial metabolism.
The findings argue against critical global myocardial oxygen deficiency as the primary cause of cardiac deterioration in prolonged experimental hemorrhagic shock.
The author favors peripheral factors (e.g., circulating toxic/metabolic substances, systemic acidosis) as key contributors to myocardial impairment in shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of hemorrhagic shock, conventional resuscitation normalizes systemic and mesenteric macro-hemodynamics but leaves intestinal microvascular perfusion markedly impaired, indicating that standard resuscitation endpoints may fail to capture ongoing mesenteric ischemia.
key_points: A large-animal swine model was developed to directly measure mesenteric arterial, venous, and intestinal microvascular physiology during hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation.

Controlled hemorrhage to a systolic blood pressure <50 mmHg produced significant reductions in SMA, portal vein, and IVC pressures and flows, with associated intestinal hypoperfusion and rising lactate.
Conventional resuscitation with autologous blood, crystalloids, calcium, dextrose, and norepinephrine restored systemic and mesenteric macro-hemodynamics to near-baseline values.
Despite normalized MAP and SMA/IVC/portal pressures and flows, intestinal microvascular perfusion (LDF) recovered to only about half of baseline after 120 minutes of resuscitation.
Lactate decreased but did not fully return to baseline, supporting ongoing mesenteric/end-organ ischemia despite apparent hemodynamic correction.
Norepinephrine increased SMA and IVC pressures and flows but did not improve intestinal perfusion, highlighting a dissociation between macro-circulatory metrics and microvascular flow.
The study suggests that reliance on systemic endpoints alone may underestimate persistent mesenteric injury after hemorrhagic shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of severe hemorrhage, Wiggers and Ingraham define irreversible hemorrhagic shock as a distinct, largely nonrecoverable state diagnosable by specific hemodynamic, hematologic, and gastrointestinal criteria, emphasizing the need to differentiate it from earlier, reversible stages of hemorrhagic hypotension and impending shock.
key_points: The authors propose a three-stage classification of hemorrhage-related circulatory disturbances: simple hemorrhagic hypotension, impending shock, and irreversible hemorrhagic shock.
Irreversible hemorrhagic shock is defined as a state from which recovery is unlikely even after full restoration of blood volume.
Five physiological criteria are identified that reliably diagnose the irreversible shock state in the experimental setting.
Transition from impending to irreversible shock occurs during sustained severe hypotension and may not be evident from blood pressure or outward behavior alone.
Persistent hemodilution during hypotension is associated with survival, whereas early arrest of dilution and hemoconcentration signal poor prognosis.
Borderline cases exist in which animals ultimately die of shock without clearly manifesting the defined criteria.
The paper emphasizes the need for precise terminology and staging in both experimental and clinical discussions of hemorrhagic shock.

raw_front_matter.description: This review synthesizes seven major whole-body cardiovascular models relevant to hemorrhagic shock, highlighting how differing emphases on baroreflex, renal control, and fluid–oxygen dynamics yield c…
raw_front_matter.authors: Luciano Curcio; Laura D'Orsi; Andrea De Gaetano
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiovascular modeling, systems physiology, baroreflex, renal control, hemodynamics, hypovolemia, lumped-parameter models
raw_front_matter.journal: Computational and Mathematical Methods in Medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: This review synthesizes seven major whole-body cardiovascular models relevant to hemorrhagic shock, highlighting how differing emphases on baroreflex, renal control, and fluid–oxygen dynamics yield complementary but incomplete tools, and calling for simpler, better-validated models that more fully represent fluid balance and can realistically support clinical decision-making.
key_points: The review compares seven influential whole-body mathematical models of the cardiovascular system that can simulate responses to hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock.
Models span from minimal Windkessel afterload representations to highly comprehensive frameworks such as the Guyton-Coleman model and the Beard long-term pressure control model.
Most models are lumped-parameter (0D) systems using electrical analogies to represent resistances, compliances, and inertances of the circulation.

Different models prioritize different mechanisms: short-term baroreflex control, long-term renal and renin–angiotensin regulation, microvascular autoregulation, or oxygen delivery during fluid resuscitation.
Validation against experimental or clinical data is uneven; many models are only partially validated and often only for short time windows or limited variables.
Transcapillary refill and body-fluid balance—crucial in hemorrhage—are incompletely represented in most models, constituting an identified gap.
The authors implemented web-accessible versions of the Guyton and Zenker models and argue that simpler models like Zenker’s may be more suitable for direct clinical support.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: By adding a physiologic transcapillary refill mechanism to a compact baroreflex-controlled cardiovascular model, the ZenCur framework can reproduce key hemodynamic patterns of severe hemorrhage in swine and offers a computationally simple basis for predicting shock progression and transfusion needs.
key_points: The authors present ZenCur, an upgraded version of the Zenker 5-ODE cardiovascular model, tailored to simulate hemorrhagic shock.
ZenCur adds an explicit transcapillary refill mechanism to better capture post-hemorrhage hemodynamics.
The model is calibrated and tested against detailed data from four anesthetized swine subjected to severe controlled hemorrhage (~30–35% blood volume) without resuscitation.
ZenCur reproduces time courses of mean arterial pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output during and after hemorrhage with reasonable accuracy.
Sensitivity analysis highlights venous unstressed volume and peripheral resistance control as dominant determinants of model behavior during shock.
The framework is intended as a simple, computationally efficient decision-support tool to anticipate shock, survival windows, and massive transfusion needs.
Despite limitations (small sample size, anesthesia effects, simplified baroreflex and circulation), the model captures key qualitative patterns of compensatory cardiovascular responses.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Exsanguination cardiac arrest in this swine model progresses from early preload failure to late coronary perfusion failure, with abrupt loss of coronary flow below a MAP of ~20 mm Hg triggering asystole, indicating that future resuscitation strategies must directly restore coronary perfusion to improve survival.
key_points: Progressive exsanguination in swine shows two distinct phases: early preload-driven instability and late coronary perfusion–driven myocardial failure.
Cardiac rhythm remains organized without dysrhythmias until abrupt asystole, despite profound shock.
Coronary (LAD) flow is relatively preserved until mean arterial pressure (MAP) falls below ~20 mm Hg, after which flow collapses and asystole occurs.
Initial hemodynamic deterioration is dominated by reductions in preload, cardiac output, and stroke volume rather than primary pump failure.
There is a strong linear relationship between coronary flow and left ventricular ejection fraction during exsanguination.
Current resuscitative strategies (volume, aortic occlusion, chest compressions) do not directly restore coronary perfusion in late exsanguination.
Endovascular techniques that augment coronary perfusion (e.g., selective aortic arch perfusion) may be necessary to salvage late-stage exsanguination cardiac arrest.

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Carbohydrate Metabolism in Dogs
raw_front_matter.description: In intact dogs, the heart’s use of glucose, lactate, and pyruvate is tightly linked to their arterial levels—with glucose requiring a threshold, lactate and pyruvate being avidly extracted at low lev…
raw_front_matter.authors: Walter T. Goodale, M.D.; Donald B. Hackel, M.D.
raw_front_matter.tags: myocardial metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, lactate, pyruvate, glucose, hyperglycemia, starvation, respiratory quotient, coronary sinus catheterization, canine model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In intact dogs, the heart’s use of glucose, lactate, and pyruvate is tightly linked to their arterial levels—with glucose requiring a threshold, lactate and pyruvate being avidly extracted at low levels, and starvation shifting the myocardium from carbohydrate to fat oxidation—so that circulating substrate availability primarily governs myocardial fuel choice and oxidative balance.
key_points: In intact, lightly anesthetized dogs, myocardial extraction of oxygen, glucose, lactate, and pyruvate is closely proportional to each metabolite’s arterial concentration and largely independent of the others.
Lactate and pyruvate show high myocardial extraction coefficients even at very low arterial levels but contribute less than half of energy needs at normal resting concentrations.
Glucose displays a clear utilization threshold (~54 mg/dL); above this, especially at 70–120 mg/dL, it can provide the major oxidative fuel for the heart.
Approximately two-thirds of myocardial oxidative energy in postabsorptive normal dogs is supplied by carbohydrate (lactate, pyruvate, glucose), with the remainder likely from fat.

During starvation, myocardial respiratory quotient falls to ~0.70 and carbohydrate extraction is markedly reduced, indicating predominant fat utilization and a functional block in carbohydrate oxidation.

Under induced hyperglycemia, myocardial respiratory quotient can exceed 1.0, and extracted carbohydrate can exceed the concurrent oxidative requirement, implying storage or nonoxidative use of carbohydrate.

raw_front_matter.authors: Harold C. Wiggers, Raymond C. Ingraham
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, irreversible shock, acidosis, sodium bicarbonate, sodium lactate, resuscitation, canine model, hemodynamic failure, microcirculation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of severe hemorrhagic shock, continuous sodium bicarbonate infusion during the hypotensive period effectively prevented acidosis and significantly reduced progression to irreversible shock, whereas sodium lactate did not, underscoring acidosis as a key, treatable driver of lethal shock.
key_points: In a dog model of standardized hemorrhagic hypotension, continuous sodium bicarbonate infusion during shock reduced mortality compared with no treatment, whereas sodium lactate did not.
Prevention of metabolic acidosis during the low-pressure period was closely associated with avoidance of progression to irreversible shock.
Sodium lactate failed to adequately correct acidosis under severe hemorrhagic-hypotensive conditions, likely due to impaired hepatic metabolism in anoxia.
Sodium bicarbonate maintained plasma CO2 capacity near or above control levels in survivors, indicating effective buffering.
Uncorrected acidosis appears to hasten the transition from impending to irreversible hemorrhagic shock.
Several physiological criteria (spontaneous BP decline, bloody diarrhea, marked tachycardia after reinfusion) were validated as reliable indicators of established irreversible shock.
The authors advocate more frequent clinical use of intravenous sodium bicarbonate plus glucose in severe hemorrhage when acidosis is present or anticipated.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, coronary circulation, cardiac failure, coronary blood flow, vascular resistance, canine model, hemodynamics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In hemorrhagic shock, coronary vascular resistance falls and coronary flow becomes supranormal after reinfusion, indicating that post-shock circulatory failure stems not from inadequate coronary perfusion but from intrinsic myocardial damage sustained during the preceding hypotensive period.
key_points: The study quantified coronary blood flow during standardized hemorrhagic hypotension and subsequent shock in anesthetized dogs.
Coronary flow fell to roughly 30–60% of control values during sustained arterial hypotension at 50 and 30 mm Hg.
After reinfusion and restoration of mean aortic pressure, coronary flow markedly overshot control, reaching 121–420% of baseline.
During circulatory failure (shock), coronary flow at a given aortic pressure was generally equal to or higher than in the pre-shock state.
Coronary vascular resistance consistently decreased during hypotension and remained below control during shock, implying active vasodilation.
The authors conclude that post-reinfusion circulatory failure is not due to inadequate coronary flow, but more likely to intrinsic myocardial metabolic injury incurred during hypotension.

raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, hemorrhagic shock, cardiac dysfunction, myocardial injury, mouse model, inflammation, necroptosis, AIF, echocardiography-guided resuscitation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Severe trauma-hemorrhagic shock in mice produces rapid, progressive myocardial injury and intrinsic cardiac dysfunction driven by acute inflammation and mitochondria-dependent, caspase-independent cell death, providing a clinically relevant model and mechanistic basis for targeting post-traumatic cardiac failure.
key_points: A clinically relevant murine model of trauma-hemorrhagic shock (THS) reproduces the cardiac dysfunction observed in severely injured patients.
Severe trauma plus pressure-controlled hemorrhage (MAP 30–40 mmHg) rapidly induces myocardial injury, evidenced by marked elevations in H-FABP and troponin I.
Despite echocardiography-guided volume resuscitation to restore stroke volume, cardiac output and LV volumes progressively fall over 3 hours, indicating intrinsic cardiac dysfunction.
THS triggers acute myocardial inflammation with neutrophil and pro-inflammatory monocyte/macrophage infiltration into the heart.
Ultrastructural analyses show widespread sarcomere disorganization, mitochondrial swelling and damage, and nuclear chromatin changes consistent with irreversible cardiomyocyte injury.
Biochemical and localization data suggest mitochondria-driven, caspase-independent cell death involving apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) rather than classic caspase-8–dependent apoptosis.
This model provides a platform to dissect mechanisms of trauma-associated cardiac failure and to test cardioprotective interventions after hemorrhagic shock.
