McGrew, Charles T. Harris, Robert Reily, Mimi Sammarco, Partha K. Chandra, Derek Pociask, Jay Kolls, Prasad V. Katakam, Alison Smith, Sharven Taghavi, Juan Duchesne, Olan Jackson-Weaver
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, trauma, endotheliopathy, endothelial glycocalyx, coagulopathy, succinate, succinate dehydrogenase, mitochondrial ROS, membrane lipids, lysophospholipids, phospholipase A2, MMP24, MMP25, lung injury, kidney injury

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Acute succinate accumulation and SDH-dependent mitochondrial ROS in endothelial cells remodel plasma membrane lipids to bring MMP24/25 into contact with glycocalyx components, driving rapid glycocalyx shedding, trauma-induced coagulopathy, and organ injury that can be prevented by targeting succinate metabolism or membrane reorganization.
key_points: Acute traumatic hemorrhage causes rapid endothelial glycocalyx shedding that drives coagulopathy and organ dysfunction, but the upstream mechanisms were previously unclear.
Succinate accumulation and its metabolism via succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) in endothelial cells trigger mitochondrial ROS production, lipid oxidation, and membrane reorganization.
These membrane changes promote interaction of membrane-bound MMP24 and MMP25 with glycocalyx components such as syndecan-1, causing proteolytic shedding.

In a rat hemorrhage–resuscitation model, inhibition of SDH or phospholipase A2, or disruption of membrane organization, prevented glycocalyx damage, coagulopathy, and reduced organ injury and mortality.
Intravenous succinate or lysophosphatidylcholine alone were sufficient to induce glycocalyx shedding and coagulopathy in otherwise healthy rats, in an SDH- and PLA2-dependent manner.

In trauma patients, plasma succinate levels correlated strongly with syndecan-1 (glycocalyx shedding), prothrombin time, and endothelial MMP24–syndecan-1 interaction, and were a better correlate than lactate.
Succinate-driven mechanisms also contributed to glycocalyx damage in endothelial cells exposed to LPS and H1N1, suggesting a shared pathway across critical illness states.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized dogs with fixed-pressure hemorrhagic shock, beta-receptor blockade—especially with cardiodepressant propranolol—shortens the compensable shock period and worsens metabolic and myocardial derangements, indicating that conventional beta-blockers are harmful rather than protective in this setting.
key_points: Beta-receptor blockade during fixed-pressure hemorrhagic shock in dogs shortened the compensable shock period and worsened metabolic derangements despite reduced blood loss.
Both CIBA 39'089 Ba and propranolol increased myocardial oxygen extraction (lower coronary sinus O2 saturation) during shock compared with non-medicated controls.
Propranolol produced more severe hemodynamic and metabolic impairment than CIBA 39'089 Ba, consistent with additional nonspecific cardiodepressive effects.
Beta-blockade largely abolished shock-induced hyperglycemia but increased lactate accumulation and metabolic acidosis.
Coronary sinus measurements indicated higher myocardial lactate extraction and CO2 gradients under beta-blockade, despite preserved coronary sinus O2 above ischemic thresholds.

Gross inspection showed marked ventricular dilatation and poor myocardial tone with propranolol, milder changes with CIBA 39'089 Ba, and generally preserved tone but more subendocardial hemorrhages in controls.

raw_front_matter.authors: James C. Schadt

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In conscious rabbits, the abrupt hypotension of acute hemorrhage reflects an active, centrally mediated withdrawal of sympathetic vasoconstrictor tone—likely involving endogenous opioid peptides—which can be reversed by naloxone to restore vascular resistance and arterial pressure.
key_points: In conscious rabbits, the transition from compensated hemorrhage to hypotension is associated with an active generalized vasodilation rather than a simple failure of compensatory mechanisms.
Early during blood loss, sympathetic activation maintains arterial pressure via increased vascular resistance and heart rate despite falling cardiac output.
At ~20–25% blood volume loss, arterial pressure drops abruptly in parallel with decreases in total peripheral resistance, heart rate, and sympathetic indices.
Peripheral sympathetic norepinephrine (NE) release declines at the onset of hypotension, while adrenal epinephrine release markedly increases.
Naloxone reverses established hemorrhagic hypotension primarily by increasing vascular resistance through enhanced sympathetic outflow and NE release.
Blocking opioid receptors before or after hemorrhage prevents or reverses the characteristic sympathoinhibition and hypotension.
Findings implicate endogenous opioid peptides, acting centrally, in mediating the late sympathoinhibition and hypotension of acute hemorrhage.

docs.title: The Heart in Shock

raw_front_matter.title: The Heart in Shock
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhagic shock induces both hypoxia-driven subendocardial necrosis and hypovolemia-associated reversible zonal lesions, which, together with humoral cardiodepressant factors and sympathetic overac…
raw_front_matter.authors: Donald B. Hackel, Norman B. Ratliff, Eileen Mikat
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, subendocardial hemorrhage, myocardial necrosis, zonal lesions, myocardial depressant factor, catecholamines, myocardial ischemia, pathophysiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock induces both hypoxia-driven subendocardial necrosis and hypovolemia-associated reversible zonal lesions, which, together with humoral cardiodepressant factors and sympathetic overactivity, progressively disrupt myocardial contractile function and culminate in cardiac failure.
key_points: Cardiac dysfunction is a central and progressive component of the shock syndrome and contributes importantly to terminal cardiovascular collapse.
Hemorrhagic shock produces two distinct types of myocardial lesions: subendocardial hemorrhagic-necrotic lesions and nonlethal “zonal lesions.”
Subendocardial hemorrhage and necrosis are primarily hypoxia-driven and are favored in the vulnerable subendocardial region under low perfusion pressure.
Zonal lesions represent localized myocyte hypercontraction and structural distortion near intercalated discs and are characteristic of hypovolemia rather than hypoxia.
Sympathetic overactivity and catecholamines both aggravate myocardial damage and can be experimentally modulated to prevent or attenuate lesions.
Humoral cardiotoxins such as myocardial depressant factor, arising from splanchnic ischemia, add a functional component of cardiac depression to structural injury.
The combination of anatomic injury (necrotic and zonal lesions) and circulating cardiotoxins drives the progression to myocardial failure in prolonged shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a hamster hemorrhagic shock model, succinate dehydrogenase inhibition with itaconate transiently increased venular oxygen saturation during resuscitation—consistent with reduced tissue oxygen consumption and ROS generation—demonstrating both the therapeutic potential of itaconate and the utility of hyperspectral imaging to track microvascular oxygen utilization.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock induces microcirculatory ischemia and sets the stage for reperfusion-driven ROS formation.
Itaconate inhibits succinate dehydrogenase, thereby limiting ROS generation during reperfusion.
Hyperspectral imaging was applied to quantify hemoglobin oxygen saturation in microvessels during hemorrhage and resuscitation.
Increasing doses of itaconate transiently restored venular HbO2 saturation during resuscitation from hemorrhagic shock.
SDH inhibition led to succinate accumulation and reduced tissue oxygen utilization, consistent with lower ROS formation.
The protective effects on venular oxygen saturation diminished over time, indicating a temporary benefit.
Itaconate has potential as an adjunct to resuscitation strategies to reduce reperfusion-related tissue injury after trauma or surgery.

raw_front_matter.authors: William C. Stanley, Gary D. Lopaschuk, Jennifer L. Hall, James G. McCormack
raw_front_matter.tags: myocardial metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, fatty acid oxidation, ischemia, reperfusion, heart failure, pyruvate dehydrogenase, glycolysis, pharmacologic metabolic modulation, lactate, CPT-I inhibitors, insulin, malonyl-CoA

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Reciprocal regulation between fatty acid and carbohydrate metabolism—centered on PDH, malonyl-CoA, and CPT-I—critically shapes myocardial responses to ischemia and reperfusion, and targeted pharmacologic shifts from fatty acid toward glucose oxidation can improve efficiency and outcomes in ischemic heart disease.
key_points: In the normally perfused heart, fatty acids are the dominant oxidative fuel, with glucose and lactate contributing less but critically to efficient energy production.
High rates of fatty acid oxidation suppress glycolysis, glucose uptake, and pyruvate oxidation via reciprocal regulation centered on pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) and malonyl-CoA–CPT-I signaling.
During ischemia, dependence on anaerobic glycolysis rises, lactate and H+ accumulate, and fatty acids remain the predominant oxidative substrate when there is residual flow.

On reperfusion, there is a characteristic overshoot of fatty acid oxidation with impaired pyruvate oxidation, producing a marked mismatch between glycolysis and glucose oxidation and excess H+ generation.

Plasma substrates and insulin strongly modulate myocardial fuel selection: high FFAs inhibit carbohydrate oxidation, while insulin both stimulates glucose utilization and indirectly suppresses fatty acid oxidation.
Pharmacologic strategies that inhibit fatty acid oxidation or activate PDH can shift metabolism toward glucose oxidation, improving mechanical efficiency and functional recovery after ischemia.

Metabolic therapies (e.g., glucose–insulin–potassium, dichloroacetate, CPT-I inhibitors, carnitine derivatives, trimetazidine, ranolazine) show promise, particularly in settings of partial ischemia and reperfusion where oxidative metabolism can still proceed.

docs.title: Oxidative Stress, Diabetes, and Myocardial Ischemia

raw_front_matter.title: Oxidative Stress, Diabetes, and Myocardial Ischemia
raw_front_matter.description: In diabetes mellitus, chronic oxidative stress disrupts redox-sensitive coronary ion channel function that normally couples cardiac metabolism to coronary blood flow, driving microvascular dysfunctio…
raw_front_matter.authors: Paolo Severino, Andrea D’Amato, Lucrezia Netti, Mariateresa Pucci, Fabio Infusino, Viviana Maestrini, Massimo Mancone, Francesco Fedele
raw_front_matter.tags: diabetes mellitus, ischemic heart disease, oxidative stress, coronary microvascular dysfunction, ion channels, coronary blood flow, heart failure, coronary artery disease

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In diabetes mellitus, chronic oxidative stress disrupts redox-sensitive coronary ion channel function that normally couples cardiac metabolism to coronary blood flow, driving microvascular dysfunction and ischemic heart disease, but this pathway also offers multiple ion channel– and redox-targeted therapeutic opportunities.
key_points: Ischemic heart disease in diabetes arises from both obstructive coronary artery disease and coronary microvascular dysfunction, often in the absence of epicardial stenosis.
Oxidative stress links diabetes to vascular injury by driving both atherosclerosis and coronary microvascular dysfunction via ROS, AGEs, and inflammatory signaling.
Coronary ion channels (especially K+, Ca2+, Na+ and TRP channels) are key end-effectors coupling myocardial metabolism to coronary blood flow and are redox-sensitive.
Physiological levels of ROS (notably H2O2) act as metabolic vasodilators via activation of K+ channels, while excessive ROS in diabetes disrupt these signaling pathways.
Specific Kv (Kv1.5, Kv1.3), KATP, BKCa, TRPV1, and ENaC channels are directly altered by oxidative modifications, contributing to ischemia and diastolic dysfunction.

Targeting ion channels and upstream oxidative pathways (e.g., NOX inhibition, Nrf2 activation, antioxidants, KATP/BKCa/TRP modulators) represents a therapeutic strategy against diabetic ischemic heart disease.
Microvascular dysfunction and altered coronary flow reserve are central mechanisms in diabetic heart failure, particularly diastolic dysfunction, even without large-vessel CAD.

docs.title: Endothelial Mitochondria in Vascular Disease

raw_front_matter.title: Endothelial Mitochondria in Vascular Disease
raw_front_matter.description: Although endothelial cells rely little on mitochondrial ATP production, their mitochondria serve as pivotal redox and metabolic signaling organelles whose dysfunction drives endothelial injury and ma…
raw_front_matter.authors: Xiaoqiang Tang, Yu-Xuan Luo, Hou-Zao Chen, De-Pei Liu
raw_front_matter.tags: review, endothelium, mitochondria, reactive oxygen species, vascular biology, atherosclerosis, diabetes, pulmonary arterial hypertension, systemic hypertension, senescence, mitophagy, cardiovascular disease

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Although endothelial cells rely little on mitochondrial ATP production, their mitochondria serve as pivotal redox and metabolic signaling organelles whose dysfunction drives endothelial injury and major vascular diseases, but which can be therapeutically targeted with mitochondria-focused antioxidants and metabolic interventions such as caloric restriction mimetics.
key_points: Endothelial cells contain relatively few mitochondria and rely mainly on glycolysis for ATP, yet mitochondrial signaling is central to endothelial homeostasis and dysfunction.

Mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (mROS), calcium handling, and dynamics (fusion, fission, biogenesis, mitophagy) critically regulate endothelial NO bioavailability, senescence, apoptosis, and barrier function.

Excess mROS and impaired mitochondrial quality control contribute to endothelial dysfunction in major vascular diseases including atherosclerosis, diabetic vasculopathy, pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and systemic hypertension.

Mitochondrial pathways integrate diverse vascular risk factors—aging, hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hypoxia, high salt, and angiotensin II—into redox and metabolic signals that drive vascular remodeling.
Endothelial mitochondrial dysfunction promotes both local vascular pathology and remote organ injury (e.g., podocyte loss and renal failure) via NO depletion and oxidative stress.

Mitochondria-targeted antioxidants and caloric restriction (and its mimetics such as resveratrol, metformin, and rapamycin) can improve endothelial mitochondrial function and ameliorate experimental vascular disease.
Unresolved issues include how mitochondrial signals alter nuclear epigenetics and how mitochondrial control of senescence, apoptosis, and mitophagy is coordinated in endothelium.

docs.title: Myocardium of the Dog in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardium of the Dog in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In dogs subjected to controlled hemorrhagic shock, early reversible subendocardial "zonal" myocardial lesions rapidly appear and, with prolonged hypotension, evolve into distinct necrotic and microin…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur M. Martin Jr., Donald B. Hackel
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial failure, cardiac histopathology, histochemistry, canine model, microinfarction, subendocardial hemorrhage, myocardial metabolism

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs subjected to controlled hemorrhagic shock, early reversible subendocardial "zonal" myocardial lesions rapidly appear and, with prolonged hypotension, evolve into distinct necrotic and microinfarct patterns, providing anatomical support for a major role of progressive myocardial damage in the development of irreversible shock.
key_points: In a canine model of standardized hemorrhagic shock, distinct, time‑linked myocardial lesions were identified histochemically and morphologically.
An early, characteristic "zonal" lesion appears within minutes of hypotension and is largely confined to subendocardial regions and papillary muscles.
Later "segmental" and "advanced" lesions represent true myocardial necrosis and microinfarction, often but not always overlapping with areas of subendocardial hemorrhage.
The early zonal lesion appears reversible when shock is not prolonged, whereas later necrotic lesions progress to scarring and calcification.
Myocardial changes occur in parallel with severe but largely reversible hepatic, renal, and gastrointestinal injury after shock.
Findings support a significant role for intrinsic myocardial damage in the pathogenesis of irreversible hemorrhagic shock, alongside central nervous system and intestinal factors.

docs.title: CPP and ROSC after Prolonged Cardiac Arrest

raw_front_matter.title: CPP and ROSC after Prolonged Cardiac Arrest
raw_front_matter.description: In a swine model of prolonged ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest, return of spontaneous circulation required markedly higher preshock coronary perfusion pressure—both peak and cumulative—than hi…
raw_front_matter.authors: Joshua C. Reynolds, David D. Salcido, James J. Menegazzi
raw_front_matter.tags: coronary perfusion pressure, CPP threshold, cardiac arrest, ventricular fibrillation, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, CPR hemodynamics, animal model, swine, vasopressors, resuscitation physiology, ROSC predictors

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of prolonged ventricular fibrillation cardiac arrest, return of spontaneous circulation required markedly higher preshock coronary perfusion pressure—both peak and cumulative—than historically cited, indicating that robust augmentation of coronary perfusion during early CPR is crucial for successful defibrillation.
key_points: In a swine model of prolonged ventricular fibrillation arrest (8–11 minutes untreated), animals that achieved ROSC had substantially higher preshock coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) than those that did not.
The CPP threshold associated with ROSC early in resuscitation was approximately 35–40 mmHg, higher than the historically cited 15–25 mmHg.
Both peak CPP (maxCPP) and the cumulative "dose" of CPP (area under the CPP curve, AUC) before the first defibrillation shock independently predicted ROSC.
Animals that failed to achieve ROSC were physiologic "hyporesponders" to vasopressor administration, with shallower CPP increases after drugs.
Traditional short-duration arrest animal models and late-phase human measurements likely underestimate CPP requirements in modern out-of-hospital cardiac arrest scenarios.
Conceptualizing CPP as both a threshold and a time-integrated dose may better capture the hemodynamic prerequisites for successful defibrillation.

docs.title: Hematocrit Ratio and Susceptibility to Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Hematocrit Ratio and Susceptibility to Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In dogs subjected to fixed severe hypotension, resistance to irreversible hemorrhagic shock is maximal at an intermediate hematocrit (~35%), with both marked anemia and high hematocrit accelerating p…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jack W. Crowell, Sara H. Bounds, W. W. Johnson
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hematocrit, irreversible shock, microcirculation, oxygen delivery, buffer capacity, canine model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs subjected to fixed severe hypotension, resistance to irreversible hemorrhagic shock is maximal at an intermediate hematocrit (~35%), with both marked anemia and high hematocrit accelerating progression to irreversible shock, likely via effects on flow, oxygen delivery, and tissue buffering.
key_points: In 67 anesthetized dogs, susceptibility to irreversible hemorrhagic shock varied non‑linearly with hematocrit from 12% to 56%.
Time to need for blood reinfusion at a fixed arterial pressure of 30 mmHg was used as an index of resistance to irreversible shock.
Raising hematocrit from about 12% to ~35% increased resistance to irreversible shock roughly fivefold.
Hematocrit values above ~35% were associated with decreasing resistance; very high and very low hematocrits produced similarly rapid deterioration.
The relationship appears continuous across naturally occurring and experimentally manipulated hematocrit ranges.
Authors interpret the optimum around 35% as reflecting a balance between blood flow, oxygen-carrying capacity, and buffering capacity.
They propose that tissue acidosis and buffering capacity are central determinants of progression to irreversible shock.

docs.title: l-Norepinephrine, Myocardial O₂ Tension, and Survival in Acute Hemorrhagic Hypotension

raw_front_matter.title: l-Norepinephrine, Myocardial O₂ Tension, and Survival in Acute Hemorrhagic Hypotension
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of acute hemorrhagic hypotension, l-norepinephrine rapidly restores myocardial oxygen tension and improves survival when given within 5 minutes of shock onset, but its benefit is tr…
raw_front_matter.authors: F. A. Simeone, E. A. Husni, M. G. Weidner Jr.
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, acute hemorrhagic hypotension, norepinephrine, myocardial oxygen tension, coronary circulation, canine model, resuscitation timing, sympathomimetic agents

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of acute hemorrhagic hypotension, l-norepinephrine rapidly restores myocardial oxygen tension and improves survival when given within 5 minutes of shock onset, but its benefit is transient and contingent on timely volume restoration.
key_points: Rapid hemorrhagic hypotension markedly reduces myocardial oxygen tension despite decreased cardiac work.
Intravenous l-norepinephrine acutely restores myocardial oxygen tension by raising systemic arterial pressure during oligemia.
Survival after severe hemorrhagic hypotension is significantly improved when l-norepinephrine is given within 5 minutes of onset.
The beneficial effect of norepinephrine is highly time-dependent and may disappear or reverse with delayed administration.
Definitive correction of hemorrhagic hypotension still requires restoration of blood volume; vasopressors are only temporary adjuncts.
Data support the existence of an early reversible phase of shock beyond which vascular responsiveness and tissue viability are lost.

docs.title: Iodide Protection in Myocardial Reperfusion Injury

raw_front_matter.title: Iodide Protection in Myocardial Reperfusion Injury
raw_front_matter.description: Acute administration of reduced iodide, but not iodate, markedly limits myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury and improves cardiac function in mice in a thyroid-dependent manner, highlighting iodide…
raw_front_matter.authors: Akiko Iwata, Michael L. Morrison, Mark B. Roth
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, myocardial ischemia-reperfusion, reperfusion injury, iodide, halogens, thyroid function, cardioprotection, mouse model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Acute administration of reduced iodide, but not iodate, markedly limits myocardial ischemia–reperfusion injury and improves cardiac function in mice in a thyroid-dependent manner, highlighting iodide as a promising, safe cardioprotective agent around the time of reperfusion.
key_points: Intravenous sodium iodide given just before reperfusion reduces myocardial infarct size by up to ~75% in a mouse ischemia–reperfusion model.
The protective effect is specific to the reduced form iodide; oxidized iodate does not confer benefit.
Iodide treatment improves functional recovery, reduces neutrophil accumulation, and lowers circulating troponin I after reperfusion.
Oral iodide given in drinking water for two days prior to ischemia also significantly decreases infarct size.
Bromide provides modest protection, but less than iodide, suggesting halogen-specific and possibly thyroid-related mechanisms.
Iodide’s benefit is lost in mice with experimentally reduced thyroid function, implying a requirement for normal thyroid activity.
Acute iodide administration transiently lowers heart rate, CO₂ production, and core temperature, consistent with reduced metabolic demand.

docs.title: Myocardial Contractile Force in Experimental Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Contractile Force in Experimental Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In experimental hemorrhagic shock in dogs, direct measurement of myocardial contractile force shows that early combined blood replacement and pressor support can restore cardiac function and survival…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jack C. Cooley, C. L. McIntosh
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac function, myocardial contractility, irreversible shock, canine model, levarterenol, blood transfusion, hemodynamics
raw_front_matter.journal: Presented at the 20th Annual Meeting of the Central Surgical Association; likely published in JAMA network journal

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In experimental hemorrhagic shock in dogs, direct measurement of myocardial contractile force shows that early combined blood replacement and pressor support can restore cardiac function and survival, but once contractile force has sharply declined, shock becomes irreversible despite aggressive therapy, highlighting acute cardiac failure as the key determinant of outcome.
key_points: Direct measurement of left ventricular myocardial contractile force (LVCF) reveals it is more stable than systemic blood pressure during progressive hemorrhagic shock.
Irreversibility and impending death closely follow a sharp decline in myocardial contractile force, even if blood pressure has been low for some time.
Levarterenol (norepinephrine) alone produces only modest improvement in blood pressure and almost no meaningful recovery of contractile force after hemorrhage.
Partial blood replacement (60% of shed blood) improves both blood pressure and contractile force more than levarterenol alone but cannot reverse advanced myocardial depression.

Combined therapy with levarterenol plus 60% blood replacement yields the largest and most sustained recovery of blood pressure and contractile force, especially at severe blood loss (50–60% of blood volume).
Timing of therapy is critical: treatment initiated before severe depression of contractile force can salvage animals, whereas late treatment after major contractile force loss is ineffective.
Findings support the concept that acute cardiac failure plays a central role in determining irreversibility in hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Myocardial Glycolytic Enzymes in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Glycolytic Enzymes in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of standardized hemorrhagic shock, left ventricular glycolytic enzyme patterns reveal widespread but partly beta-blocker–reversible metabolic and structural myocardial alterations w…
raw_front_matter.authors: P. Lundsgaard-Hansen, C. Meyer, H. Riedwyl, G. Zierott
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, beta-blockade, propranolol, myocardial metabolism, glycolytic enzymes, dog model, subendocardial ischemia, cardiac failure

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of standardized hemorrhagic shock, left ventricular glycolytic enzyme patterns reveal widespread but partly beta-blocker–reversible metabolic and structural myocardial alterations without clear evidence of additional subendocardial oxygen deprivation, highlighting catecholamine injury, acidosis, and systemic toxic factors as key drivers of shock-related cardiac dysfunction.
key_points: Nine glycolytic and related enzymes were mapped across the left ventricular wall in dogs under normal conditions, after untreated hemorrhagic shock, and after beta-blockaded hemorrhagic shock.
Global myocardial oxygen supply appeared adequate in all groups, despite severe systemic metabolic acidosis during both forms of shock.
Distinct transmural enzyme activity gradients in normal myocardium are compatible with chronic adaptation to lower subendocardial oxygen tension.
Prolonged untreated hemorrhagic shock disrupted normal enzyme distribution patterns and activity correlations, particularly in the subendocardium.
Beta-receptor blockade with propranolol prevented many, but not all, shock-induced alterations in enzyme activities and their correlations.
Transmural enzyme gradients during shock did not support the presence of a hidden subendocardial oxygen deficit under these experimental conditions.
Findings support a role for catecholamine-mediated structural myocardial injury, plus acidosis and circulating toxic factors, in metabolic derangement during hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Oxygen Deficit in Irreversible Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Oxygen Deficit in Irreversible Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In hemorrhagic shock, the transition to irreversibility in dogs is better defined by a critical whole-body oxygen deficit—modifiable by cardiac digitalization—than by hypotension duration or pressure…
raw_front_matter.authors: J. W. Crowell and E. E. Smith
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, oxygen deficit, shock irreversibility, cardiac failure, digitalis, ouabain, animal model, canine physiology, tissue hypoxia

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In hemorrhagic shock, the transition to irreversibility in dogs is better defined by a critical whole-body oxygen deficit—modifiable by cardiac digitalization—than by hypotension duration or pressure, underscoring global tissue hypoxia and cardiac performance as central determinants of fatal outcome.
key_points: Irreversible hemorrhagic shock in dogs correlates more consistently with accumulated whole-body oxygen deficit than with duration or level of hypotension.
A critical oxygen deficit threshold (≈120–140 ml O2/kg) predicts fatal, irreversible shock in untreated animals.
Digitalization with ouabain increases the oxygen deficit that animals can tolerate before death, shifting the fatal threshold upward.
Marked inter-animal variability in oxygen consumption during hypotension explains differing survival times at a fixed arterial pressure.
When shock severity is indexed by oxygen deficit rather than time, catecholamines, alpha-blockade, and conditioning to hypotension do not change the lethal oxygen deficit.
The findings support a central role for global tissue hypoxia, modulated by cardiac function, in the pathogenesis of irreversible shock.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock: The Physiology Approach

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock: The Physiology Approach
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhagic shock management should be fundamentally reoriented from volume-based ATLS paradigms to a physiology-driven strategy that uses a therapeutic–physiological classification, early source con…
raw_front_matter.authors: Fabrizio Giuseppe Bonanno
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, shock classification, resuscitation, permissive hypotension, damage control resuscitation, microcirculation, vasopressors, trauma care, cardiovascular physiology
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Emergencies, Trauma, and Shock

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock management should be fundamentally reoriented from volume-based ATLS paradigms to a physiology-driven strategy that uses a therapeutic–physiological classification, early source control, blood-first and titrated hypotensive resuscitation, and selective vasopressor support to preserve microcirculation, limit bleeding, and improve outcomes.
key_points: The ATLS hemorrhagic shock classification, centered on estimated blood loss and large crystalloid boluses, is physiologically unsound and often harmful.
A new therapeutic–physiological classification of hemorrhagic shock is proposed that emphasizes the degree of physiologic compensation and guides timing of source control.
Aggressive early crystalloid resuscitation before hemorrhage control worsens bleeding, coagulopathy, and outcomes; fluids should be secondary to blood and tailored to physiology.
Titrated hypotensive resuscitation (permissive hypotension) is advocated as the default strategy in critical and severe hemorrhagic shock until bleeding is controlled.
Exogenous vasoconstrictors (vasopressin, norepinephrine) can be used to maintain arteriolar tone when endogenous vasoconstriction fails, delaying vasomotor collapse.
Management should prioritize early source control, blood replacement, and microcirculatory optimization within a comprehensive ‘physiology approach’.
The overarching therapeutic goals are to save life in decompensated hypotensive shock (accepting inevitable ischemia–reperfusion injury) and to prevent complications in compensated shock.

docs.title: Hematocrit and Susceptibility to Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Hematocrit and Susceptibility to Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine hemorrhagic shock model, susceptibility to irreversible shock followed a U‑shaped relationship to hematocrit, with maximal resistance at intermediate values (~35%) and rapid deterioration…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jack W. Crowell, Sara H. Bounds, W. W. Johnson
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hematocrit, irreversible shock, oxygen delivery, buffering capacity, canine model, hemodynamics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine hemorrhagic shock model, susceptibility to irreversible shock followed a U‑shaped relationship to hematocrit, with maximal resistance at intermediate values (~35%) and rapid deterioration at both very low and very high hematocrits, likely reflecting an optimal balance between blood flow, oxygen delivery, and buffering against acidosis.
key_points: Dogs with hematocrits ranging from 12–56% were subjected to standardized hemorrhagic shock at 30 mmHg arterial pressure.
Resistance to irreversible shock, indexed by time to need for reinfusion (blood flow reversal), rose sharply as hematocrit increased from 12% to ~35%.
Above ~35% hematocrit, further increases shortened the time to irreversible shock, producing a U‑shaped relationship between hematocrit and shock resistance.
Very low and very high hematocrits were both associated with rapid progression to irreversible shock.
The authors interpret the optimal hematocrit as reflecting a balance between blood flow, oxygen-carrying capacity, and buffering capacity, with buffering likely dominant.
Irreversible shock in this model is hypothesized to result primarily from tissue acidosis.

docs.title: NEJM Correspondence on Hemorrhagic Shock (2018)

raw_front_matter.title: NEJM Correspondence on Hemorrhagic Shock (2018)
raw_front_matter.description: These NEJM correspondence pieces underscore that hemorrhagic shock is biologically heterogeneous in fibrinolysis, immunity, and microcirculatory control, arguing for individualized, blood product–cen…
raw_front_matter.authors: Giuseppe Famularo; Kim Timmermans; Cornelis Slagt; Matthijs Kox; Nicolas Morel; Marie Moisan; Sung W. Lee; Sang W. Shin; Jeremy W. Cannon
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, trauma, fibrinolysis, tranexamic acid, coagulopathy, immune dysfunction, inflammation, microcirculation, nitric oxide, blood transfusion, fluid resuscitation, permissive hypotension, damage control resuscitation
raw_front_matter.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine (Correspondence section)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: These NEJM correspondence pieces underscore that hemorrhagic shock is biologically heterogeneous in fibrinolysis, immunity, and microcirculatory control, arguing for individualized, blood product–centered, and physiologically informed resuscitation strategies rather than empirical tranexamic acid use and large-volume crystalloid infusion.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock encompasses a spectrum of fibrinolytic states—hyperfibrinolysis, physiologic fibrinolysis, and fibrinolysis shutdown—with a U-shaped relationship to mortality.

Empirical early tranexamic acid in all bleeding patients may be inappropriate because it may benefit those with hyperfibrinolysis but be futile or harmful in patients with fibrinolysis shutdown or normal fibrinolysis.
Severe trauma is associated very early with a predominant anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive phenotype, linked to DAMPs, catecholamines, tissue hypoxia, viral reactivation, and secondary infections.

Nitric oxide bioavailability and blood viscosity–dependent wall shear stress are central to microcirculatory perfusion in hemorrhagic shock, with an initial NO-depletion phase followed by NO overproduction and vasoplegia.
Early, warm red blood cell transfusion that avoids hemodilution may help preserve viscosity, shear stress, NO signaling, and microcirculatory flow in hemorrhagic shock.

The optimal prehospital fluid resuscitation strategy (permissive hypotension vs conventional resuscitation) remains debated; current ATLS guidance favors judicious, limited crystalloid with rapid hemostatic resuscitation.
Future management is trending toward individualized tranexamic acid use guided by viscoelastic testing, minimized crystalloid, and blood-based, hemostatic resuscitation products.

docs.title: Endotoxin and TNF Kinetics After Hemorrhagic Shock in Rats

raw_front_matter.title: Endotoxin and TNF Kinetics After Hemorrhagic Shock in Rats
raw_front_matter.description: In a rat model of hemorrhagic shock, early gut bacterial translocation leads to transient portal-vein–mediated endotoxemia that drives TNF release from gut and liver macrophages, contributing to syst…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jianxin Jiang, Soheyl Bahrami, Guenther Leichtfried, Heinz Redl, Wolfgang Ohlinger, Guenther Schlag
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endotoxemia, bacterial translocation, tumor necrosis factor (TNF), lipopolysaccharide (LPS), portal circulation, systemic inflammation, gut-liver axis, rat model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of hemorrhagic shock, early gut bacterial translocation leads to transient portal-vein–mediated endotoxemia that drives TNF release from gut and liver macrophages, contributing to systemic inflammation, organ injury, and mortality.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in rats leads to early gut bacterial translocation and transient endotoxemia.
Portal vein LPS levels rise significantly before systemic LPS, indicating the portal route as the primary entry into circulation.
TNF increases rapidly in both portal and systemic blood, with an earlier and sustained rise in portal circulation.
Systemic TNF peaks later than portal TNF, suggesting sequential contribution from gut-associated macrophages and hepatic Kupffer cells.
Higher systemic LPS and TNF levels after resuscitation are associated with non-survival within 48 hours.
Significant histologic injury develops in small intestine, liver, and lung following hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation.

docs.title: Hypocalcemia in Trauma: Systematic Review

raw_front_matter.title: Hypocalcemia in Trauma: Systematic Review
raw_front_matter.description: In adult trauma patients, admission ionized hypocalcemia before any transfusion is common and consistently associated with higher mortality, greater transfusion requirements, and coagulopathy, but de…
raw_front_matter.authors: Mayank Vasudeva, Joseph K. Mathew, Christopher Groombridge, Jin W. Tee, Cecil S. Johnny, Amit Maini, Mark C. Fitzgerald
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, hemorrhagic shock, hypocalcemia, ionized calcium, coagulopathy, massive transfusion, critical care, mortality
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In adult trauma patients, admission ionized hypocalcemia before any transfusion is common and consistently associated with higher mortality, greater transfusion requirements, and coagulopathy, but definitive evidence that calcium replacement improves outcomes is still lacking.
key_points: Admission ionized hypocalcemia is common in severely injured, shocked trauma patients, affecting roughly one-quarter to over half of patients on arrival.
Pretransfusion hypocalcemia (before any blood products) is consistently associated with higher mortality across the included studies.
Hypocalcemia is linked to greater blood transfusion requirements, including increased likelihood of multiple and massive transfusions.
One study found admission hypocalcemia to be independently associated with traumatic coagulopathy on arrival.
Calcium plays a central role in coagulation and cardiac function, and derangements during hemorrhagic shock may contribute to a self-perpetuating cycle of bleeding and instability.
Existing evidence is observational and moderate in quality; causality and treatment effects of calcium supplementation remain unproven.
Prospective, randomized trials are needed to define optimal calcium monitoring and replacement strategies in hemorrhagic shock resuscitation.

docs.title: Treatment of Hemorrhagic Shock Irreversible to Transfusion

raw_front_matter.title: Treatment of Hemorrhagic Shock Irreversible to Transfusion
raw_front_matter.description: In dogs with advanced hemorrhagic shock already unresponsive to complete blood volume replacement, neither massive fluid/albumin infusions, correction of acidosis, metabolic substrates, nor vasopress…
raw_front_matter.authors: Howard A. Frank, Arnold M. Seligman, Jacob Fine
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, irreversible shock, cardiovascular collapse, resuscitation, transfusion, volume resuscitation, vasopressors, liver function, experimental dog model, albumin infusion

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs with advanced hemorrhagic shock already unresponsive to complete blood volume replacement, neither massive fluid/albumin infusions, correction of acidosis, metabolic substrates, nor vasopressor or neuromodulatory drugs can reverse the progressive circulatory collapse, highlighting that late shock reflects largely irreversible organ and biochemical injury rather than simple volume deficiency.
key_points: In advanced hemorrhagic shock that is already unresponsive to full blood volume replacement, large-volume fluid or drug therapies fail to restore sustained circulatory function.
Massive saline or Ringer’s infusions can transiently improve blood pressure but ultimately lead to severe edema and do not prevent death.
Even extreme expansion of blood volume with 5% bovine albumin rarely rescues animals once shock is irreversible to transfusion and is associated with marked bleeding.
Vasoconstrictors (pitressin, ergotamine, paredrine, tuamine) can raise arterial pressure briefly but do not improve cardiac output or survival.
Correction of metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate, or metabolic support with sodium succinate, does not reverse advanced shock.

The authors argue that late, transfusion‑irreversible hemorrhagic shock reflects fundamental, largely irreversible biochemical and organ injury—likely involving the liver—beyond simple blood volume deficit.
They emphasize that testing anti-shock agents must occur after demonstrating failure of transfusion alone, not concurrently with initial blood replacement.

docs.title: Superoxide and H2O2 in the Vascular Lumen

raw_front_matter.title: Superoxide and H2O2 in the Vascular Lumen
raw_front_matter.description: Superoxide and hydrogen peroxide produced by vascular endothelium exist at low nanomolar levels with millisecond lifetimes in the blood lumen, enabling only highly sensitive, largely short-range redo…
raw_front_matter.authors: Tânia Sousa, Marcos Gouveia, Rui D.M. Travasso, Armindo Salvador
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, vascular biology, redox signaling, superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, endothelium, mathematical modeling, microcirculation, oxidative stress

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Superoxide and hydrogen peroxide produced by vascular endothelium exist at low nanomolar levels with millisecond lifetimes in the blood lumen, enabling only highly sensitive, largely short-range redox signaling, except in arterioles and arteries where O2•−-derived H2O2 can mediate weak, millimeter-scale downstream communication.
key_points: Reaction–diffusion–advection models were used to quantify superoxide (O2•−) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) levels and transport in human capillaries, arterioles, and arteries.
Physiological H2O2 concentrations in the vascular lumen are predicted to be in the low nanomolar range, with half-lives under ~40 ms due to rapid clearance by erythrocytes and endothelial cells.
O2•− has an even shorter half-life (<60 ms) dominated by extracellular SOD3 and NO, so only excess O2•− over NO production is available for H2O2-mediated signaling.
In capillaries, O2•− and H2O2 act as very short-range paracrine signals (<50 µm), essentially diffusion-limited.
In arterioles and arteries, O2•−-derived H2O2 can be advected by flow and support redox signaling over up to millimeter scales, but only at very low (nM) concentrations.
Cytosolic dismutation of O2•− taken up by endothelial cells can be a major source of intracellular H2O2, especially in arterioles.
The feasible redox signaling mechanisms in vivo must be sensitive to nM-scale extracellular H2O2 and rely heavily on peroxiredoxin-based redox relays.

docs.title: Plasma Metabolites in Combat Hemorrhagic Trauma

raw_front_matter.title: Plasma Metabolites in Combat Hemorrhagic Trauma
raw_front_matter.description: In combat casualties with hemorrhagic and traumatic shock, plasma succinate, hypoxanthine, and 5-aminolevulinate define a distinctive metabolic signature that predicts trauma presence, injury severit…
raw_front_matter.authors: Elizabeth R. Lusczek, Sydne L. Muratore, Michael A. Dubick, Greg J. Beilman
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, combat trauma, metabolomics, succinate, hypoxanthine, 5-aminolevulinate, biomarkers, ischemia-reperfusion, triage, cardiovascular failure
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In combat casualties with hemorrhagic and traumatic shock, plasma succinate, hypoxanthine, and 5-aminolevulinate define a distinctive metabolic signature that predicts trauma presence, injury severity, and mortality at least as well as lactate, offering mechanistically grounded biomarkers to improve early triage and management.
key_points: Combat-injured patients show marked and persistent alterations in plasma metabolism compared with healthy controls for at least 24 hours after injury.
Succinate and malonate best discriminated survivors from non-survivors among combat casualties and were associated with mortality.
Succinate and hypoxanthine levels correlated with higher injury severity and outperformed or matched lactate for this purpose.
Hypoxanthine and 5-aminolevulinate (5-ALA) were strong discriminators of the presence of trauma and remained elevated beyond initial presentation.
Metabolic biomarkers tied to TCA cycle flux, oxidative stress/ATP depletion, and heme/iron metabolism may improve early triage in hemorrhagic combat trauma.
Overall, these novel metabolites performed as well as or better than lactate in ROC analyses for trauma presence, injury severity, and mortality prediction.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock, Coronary Flow Reversal, and LV Function

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock, Coronary Flow Reversal, and LV Function
raw_front_matter.description: In a swine model of progressive hemorrhagic shock, increasing shock class is tightly associated with greater diastolic coronary flow reversal, reduced myocardial oxygen delivery, and intrinsic LV con…
raw_front_matter.authors: Elansary NN, Stonko DP, Treffalls RN, Abdou H, Madurska MJ, Morrison JJ
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, exsanguination cardiac arrest, coronary flow, diastolic flow reversal, left ventricular function, pressure-volume loops, swine model, preload recruitable stroke work, systemic vascular resistance, resuscitation physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of progressive hemorrhagic shock, increasing shock class is tightly associated with greater diastolic coronary flow reversal, reduced myocardial oxygen delivery, and intrinsic LV contractile failure, underscoring the need for left-sided, coronary-directed resuscitation strategies in exsanguination cardiac arrest.
key_points: In a swine model exsanguinated through all four classes of hemorrhagic shock, diastolic coronary flow increasingly reversed and left ventricular (LV) function progressively deteriorated.
The proportion of diastole spent in retrograde coronary flow rose from ~6% at baseline to ~64% in class IV hemorrhagic shock.
LV preload (EDV, EDP), stroke volume, and stroke work declined markedly with advancing shock, while systemic vascular resistance increased.
Myocardial oxygen delivery and cardiac output decreased with hemorrhage severity, despite compensatory vasoconstriction.

Preload recruitable stroke work (PRSW), a load-independent inotropy index, fell significantly in class II–IV shock, indicating intrinsic contractile impairment beyond simple changes in preload/afterload.
Coronary vascular resistance increased in intermediate stages of shock, and total diastolic coronary flow became progressively more negative in severe shock.
Findings support targeting left-sided, coronary-directed resuscitation strategies (e.g., REBOA, SAAP, ECMO) to counter diastolic flow reversal and LV failure in exsanguination cardiac arrest.

raw_front_matter.title: Time and Reversibility of Myocardial Metabolic Changes in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of hemorrhagic shock, myocardial abnormalities in lactate, pyruvate, and oxygen handling are reversible with blood transfusion only if shock is relieved within about 1–1.5 hours, wh…
raw_front_matter.authors: Hackel DB, Breitenecker R
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial metabolism, cardiac failure, oxygen extraction, lactate, pyruvate, irreversible shock, canine model
raw_front_matter.journal: Proceedings of the Society for Experimental Biology and Medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of hemorrhagic shock, myocardial abnormalities in lactate, pyruvate, and oxygen handling are reversible with blood transfusion only if shock is relieved within about 1–1.5 hours, whereas longer shock durations produce largely irreversible myocardial metabolic failure that likely underlies irreversible shock.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock induces abnormal myocardial metabolism characterized by reduced or reversed extraction of lactate and pyruvate.
The reversibility of these metabolic abnormalities depends critically on the duration of shock before transfusion.
Transfusion within ~1–1.5 hours of shock onset can normalize myocardial substrate and oxygen extraction.
After ≥3 hours of shock at very low arterial pressures, myocardial metabolic disturbances become largely irreversible to transfusion.
Prolonged shock leads to abnormal myocardial oxygen extraction patterns after transfusion, suggesting intrinsic myocardial damage.
Findings support the concept that irreversible myocardial injury is a key component of irreversible hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Inflammatory Basis of Trauma/Shock-Associated MOF

raw_front_matter.title: Inflammatory Basis of Trauma/Shock-Associated MOF
raw_front_matter.description: Trauma- and hemorrhagic shock–associated multiple organ failure arises from a complex, self-amplifying inflammatory cascade involving complement, neutrophils, endothelial adhesion, cytokines, and oft…
raw_front_matter.authors: Y.-M. Yao, H. Redl, S. Bahrami, G. Schlag
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, multiple organ failure, systemic inflammatory response, sepsis, neutrophils, complement, cytokines, endothelium, adhesion molecules, gut hypothesis, bacterial translocation, endotoxemia

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Trauma- and hemorrhagic shock–associated multiple organ failure arises from a complex, self-amplifying inflammatory cascade involving complement, neutrophils, endothelial adhesion, cytokines, and often gut-derived bacteria/endotoxin, with experimental data supporting multiple potential therapeutic targets whose clinical utility is still being defined.
key_points: Multiple organ failure (MOF) after trauma/hemorrhage is largely driven by an exaggerated and dysregulated inflammatory response rather than the initial insult alone.
Complement activation, neutrophil priming/activation, and endothelial–leukocyte adhesion represent early and central events in post-shock organ injury.
Proinflammatory cytokines (especially TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) contribute to post-traumatic systemic inflammatory response and MOF, often via local rather than easily detectable systemic production.
Neutrophil-derived proteases (e.g., elastase) and reactive oxygen species are strongly linked to lung and other organ damage and correlate with injury severity and MOF.
Endothelial activation and upregulation/shedding of adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, E-selectin, P-selectin) correlate with later development and severity of MOF in trauma patients.

Experimental data support the ‘gut hypothesis’ in which hemorrhagic shock disrupts intestinal barrier function, enabling bacterial/endotoxin translocation that amplifies systemic inflammation and organ failure.

Targeted interventions against TNF, IL-1, endotoxin, and gut-derived mediators improve outcomes in animal models, but clinical translation and the true relevance of bacterial/endotoxin translocation remain incompletely resolved.

raw_front_matter.title: Resuscitation-Associated Endotheliopathy (RAsE)
raw_front_matter.description: This systematic review proposes resuscitation-associated endotheliopathy (RAsE) as a framework for understanding how aggressive resuscitation in shock may worsen endothelial and microvascular injury,…
raw_front_matter.authors: Obonyo NG, Sela DP, Raman S, Rachakonda R, Schneider B, See Hoe LE, Fanning JP, Li Bassi G, Maitland K, Suen JY, Fraser JF
raw_front_matter.tags: resuscitation-associated endotheliopathy, RAsE, shock-induced endotheliopathy, SHINE, endothelial dysfunction, glycocalyx, microcirculation, septic shock, hemorrhagic shock, cardiogenic shock, critical care, biomarkers

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: This systematic review proposes resuscitation-associated endotheliopathy (RAsE) as a framework for understanding how aggressive resuscitation in shock may worsen endothelial and microvascular injury, highlights syndecan-1 and microvascular flow as key but inconsistently used measures, and underscores the urgent need for standardized endothelial-focused assessment in shock resuscitation research.
key_points: The authors introduce and define resuscitation-associated endotheliopathy (RAsE) as worsening endothelial dysfunction caused by acute resuscitation therapies given for shock.

A systematic review of 32 human studies (2011–2023) shows heterogeneous and non-standardized assessment of endothelial injury after resuscitation across septic, hemorrhagic/trauma, and cardiogenic shock.

Syndecan-1 was the most frequently measured glycocalyx biomarker post-resuscitation, and meta-analysis suggests resuscitation is associated with increased shedding, though with substantial heterogeneity.
Only a minority of studies directly assessed microcirculatory flow, and very few yielded comparable data suitable for quantitative synthesis.
Meta-analysis of microvascular flow index (MFI) from two studies suggested resuscitation was associated with significantly reduced microvascular flow.
Overall evidence is limited and inconsistent, underscoring major gaps in understanding how resuscitation strategies contribute to endothelial and microvascular injury.
The paper calls for standardized biomarker panels, timing, and reporting frameworks to study RAsE and guide endothelial-protective resuscitation strategies.

docs.title: Modelling Myocardial Ischaemia and Reperfusion

raw_front_matter.title: Modelling Myocardial Ischaemia and Reperfusion
raw_front_matter.description: By integrating experimentally constrained models of cardiac pH regulation and bioenergetics into detailed electrophysiological cell models, this work shows how metabolite and pH changes during myocar…
raw_front_matter.authors: F.F.-T. Ch’en, R.D. Vaughan-Jones, K. Clarke, D. Noble
raw_front_matter.tags: computational model, myocardial ischaemia, reperfusion, cardiac metabolism, pH regulation, electrophysiology, calcium overload, arrhythmias, bioenergetics, Na+/H+ exchange, Na+/Ca2+ exchange

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: By integrating experimentally constrained models of cardiac pH regulation and bioenergetics into detailed electrophysiological cell models, this work shows how metabolite and pH changes during myocardial ischaemia and reperfusion drive Na+ and Ca2+ overload arrhythmias and yields counterintuitive therapeutic predictions about Na+/H+ and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger modulation.
key_points: The authors extend existing biophysical cardiac cell models to incorporate detailed descriptions of bioenergetics and pH regulation during myocardial ischaemia and reperfusion.
Intracellular acidosis, substrate depletion, and inorganic phosphate accumulation are quantitatively modelled and linked to changes in contractility, ion homeostasis, and arrhythmogenesis.
pHi regulation is described via four sarcolemmal transport systems (Na+/H+ exchange, Na+-HCO3− symport, Cl−-HCO3− exchange, and a novel Cl−-OH− exchanger) constrained by single-cell experiments.
Bioenergetic changes in ATP, creatine phosphate, ADP, AMP, Pi, glycogen, and lactate are modelled based on and validated against whole-heart 31P NMR data.
The integrated model reproduces calcium-overload arrhythmias during ischaemia and shows even more severe arrhythmias during reperfusion, aligning with experimental and clinical observations.
Simulations predict that Na+/H+ exchange inhibition is anti-arrhythmic in acidosis, whereas chronic inhibition of Na+/Ca2+ exchange can worsen calcium overload and arrhythmias.
The work illustrates how multiscale, integrative modelling can generate non-obvious therapeutic predictions for controlling arrhythmias in ischaemic and reperfused myocardium.

raw_front_matter.title: Cineangiocardiography in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.authors: A. M. Martin Jr., D. B. Hackel, Madison S. Spach, M. P. Capp, E. Mikat
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, left ventricular function, cineangiocardiography, intraventricular pressure gradients, subendocardial injury, experimental cardiology, canine model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, biplane cineangiocardiography reveals dynamic systolic obliteration of the left ventricular apex that creates a high-pressure distal chamber, explaining large apical pressure gradients and likely contributing mechanically to subendocardial myocardial injury, with important implications for interpreting hemodynamics and for the harmful effects of inotropic therapy such as noradrenalin.
key_points: In hemorrhagic shock, large systolic pressure gradients develop within the left ventricle between the apex and the body of the cavity, without fixed anatomic obstruction.
Biplane cineangiocardiography in dogs shows marked reduction of left ventricular volumes and systolic obliteration of the apical cavity during shock.
Apical systolic obliteration creates a closed high-pressure distal chamber that explains unusually high apical pressure recordings.
The intraventricular pressure gradient evolves from a terminal systolic spike to occupying the entire systolic period as shock progresses.
Prolonged contact between opposing myocardial surfaces during apical obliteration may contribute to subendocardial lesions seen in hemorrhagic shock.
Positive inotropic therapy with noradrenalin (norepinephrine) likely worsens this mechanical insult and has been shown to be deleterious in this model.

docs.title: Microcirculation in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Microcirculation in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhagic shock in skeletal muscle is dominated by leukocyte-driven, highly heterogeneous capillary perfusion and impaired interstitial transport that conceal profound local metabolic failure from…
raw_front_matter.authors: Hengo Haljamae
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, microcirculation, skeletal muscle, microvascular perfusion, leukocyte plugging, blood-tissue exchange, interstitial fluid shifts, tissue oxygenation, cell membrane potential, shock resuscitation, hypertonic therapy, ATP-MgCl2, steroids, critical care monitoring

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock in skeletal muscle is dominated by leukocyte-driven, highly heterogeneous capillary perfusion and impaired interstitial transport that conceal profound local metabolic failure from systemic measurements, so successful therapy must directly address microcirculatory dysfunction and be guided by tissue-level monitoring.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock produces profound microcirculatory derangements in skeletal muscle, with highly heterogeneous capillary perfusion and large areas of no-flow.
Leukocyte trapping and plugging of capillaries, not red-cell aggregation, are key determinants of maldistributed capillary flow in shock.
Reduced capillary surface area and increased interstitial colloid density markedly impair blood–tissue exchange, so major metabolic disturbances remain “hidden” from central blood measurements.
Local tissue hypoxia in skeletal muscle leads to anaerobiosis, acidosis, high-energy phosphate depletion, and loss of normal transmembrane ion gradients.
After fluid resuscitation, global hemodynamics may normalize but capillary maldistribution and leukocyte plugging often persist, limiting effective nutritive reperfusion.
Hypertonic solutions, ATP-MgCl2, and steroids may improve microvascular reperfusion by reducing cellular/interstitial swelling and enhancing mobilization of trapped leukocytes.
Direct monitoring of skeletal muscle tissue gases, pH, and potassium with microelectrodes offers a practical way to track microcirculatory failure and guide shock management in the ICU.

docs.title: Resuscitation from Severe Hemorrhage

raw_front_matter.title: Resuscitation from Severe Hemorrhage
raw_front_matter.description: Across epidemiologic, experimental, and early clinical data, this symposium argues that survival from severe hemorrhage hinges on preventing exsanguination-induced cardiac arrest and carefully titrat…
raw_front_matter.authors: Shoemaker WC, Peitzman AB, Bellamy R, Bellomo R, Bruttig SP, Capone A, Dubick M, Kramer GC, McKenzie JE, Pepe PE, Safar P, Schlichtig R, Severinghaus JW, Tisherman SA, Wiklund L
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, uncontrolled hemorrhage, trauma, combat casualty care, resuscitation strategies, hypotensive resuscitation, fluid therapy, blood substitutes, hypertonic saline, stroma-free hemoglobin, perfluorocarbons, monitoring, lactate, hypothermia

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Across epidemiologic, experimental, and early clinical data, this symposium argues that survival from severe hemorrhage hinges on preventing exsanguination-induced cardiac arrest and carefully titrating limited, often hypotensive and small-volume resuscitation—potentially combined with hypothermia and advanced monitoring—rather than aggressively normalizing blood pressure with large-volume crystalloids before bleeding is controlled.
key_points: Early death after trauma is dominated by exsanguination within minutes, shifting focus from the traditional "golden hour" to the first 5–10 minutes and the pre-arrest phase.
In uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock, aggressive normotensive crystalloid resuscitation can worsen bleeding, hemodilution, and outcome; limited (hypotensive) resuscitation is often superior.

The traditional reliance on blood lactate as a direct marker of tissue hypoxia or “oxygen debt” is overly simplistic; lactate kinetics in sepsis and shock are organ-specific and mechanistically complex.
Noninvasive hemodynamic monitoring and advanced decision-support/information systems are envisioned as key tools for early recognition and goal-directed resuscitation in shock.

Animal models are moving from controlled hemorrhage to more realistic uncontrolled hemorrhagic shock and combined trauma–shock outcome models, including long-term survival and organ failure endpoints.
Moderate hypothermia combined with hypotensive fluid resuscitation in uncontrolled hemorrhage prolongs the tolerable shock period and improves survival in animal models.

Small-volume, high-efficiency resuscitation strategies using hypertonic solutions, stroma-free hemoglobin, and perfluorocarbon emulsions show promise but require further investigation, especially in uncontrolled hemorrhage.

docs.title: Experimental Models of Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Experimental Models of Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: This review outlines the spectrum of experimental hemorrhagic shock models, emphasizing that while fixed-volume and fixed-pressure systems offer control and reproducibility, clinically relevant insig…
raw_front_matter.authors: A. Fülöp, Z. Turóczi, D. Garbaisz, L. Harsányi, A. Szijártó
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, animal models, fixed-volume hemorrhage, fixed-pressure hemorrhage, uncontrolled hemorrhage, oxygen debt, trauma, ischemia-reperfusion

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: This review outlines the spectrum of experimental hemorrhagic shock models, emphasizing that while fixed-volume and fixed-pressure systems offer control and reproducibility, clinically relevant insights and therapy evaluation increasingly depend on oxygen-debt–based and uncontrolled, combined-trauma models designed with careful attention to species and confounding variables.
key_points: Animal models are essential for studying hemorrhagic shock pathophysiology and testing therapies, but no single model accurately reproduces the human clinical situation.
Three major controlled model types are used: fixed-volume, fixed-pressure, and uncontrolled hemorrhage, each with distinct strengths and limitations.
Species choice (mouse, rat, pig, dog, primate) must balance cost, ethics, technical feasibility, and physiological similarity to humans.

Fixed-volume and fixed-pressure models offer superior standardization and mechanistic insight, whereas uncontrolled models (often with added trauma) are more clinically relevant for preclinical therapeutic testing.
Models based on oxygen debt and metabolic markers (lactate, base deficit) better quantify shock severity and organ injury than blood pressure or shed volume alone.
Key confounders include sex, age, anesthesia, heparinization, and concomitant tissue trauma, all of which can substantially alter cardiovascular, immune, and inflammatory responses.
Complex models combining hemorrhage with trauma, extremity ischemia-reperfusion, or ruptured aortic aneurysm better mirror real-world scenarios but are technically demanding and less reproducible.

docs.title: Isoproterenol in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Isoproterenol in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of severe hemorrhagic shock, isoproterenol markedly improved cardiac output, oxygen utilization, and mesenteric perfusion without worsening—and possibly improving—survival, shifting…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur E. Baue, Earl F. Jones, William M. Parkins
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, beta-adrenergic agonists, isoproterenol, cardiac output, mesenteric perfusion, oxygen consumption, animal model, dog

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of severe hemorrhagic shock, isoproterenol markedly improved cardiac output, oxygen utilization, and mesenteric perfusion without worsening—and possibly improving—survival, shifting the principal risk from gut ischemic injury to preventable pulmonary complications related to airway secretions.
key_points: Isoproterenol, a beta-adrenergic agonist with inotropic, chronotropic, and vasodilatory effects, was tested in severe hemorrhagic shock in dogs.
During fixed-pressure hemorrhagic shock (mean arterial pressure 30 mm Hg, ~68% blood volume removed), isoproterenol substantially increased cardiac output and oxygen consumption.
Large doses of isoproterenol increased mesenteric blood flow and prevented typical gastrointestinal lesions of irreversible hemorrhagic shock.
Across multiple dosing regimens (1–3 µg/kg/min), isoproterenol did not worsen survival and tended to improve it compared with saline controls.
Non-survivors at higher doses frequently died later from respiratory failure associated with obstructive tracheobronchial casts and pulmonary consolidation, not from classic shock gut injury.
Driving a markedly hypovolemic circulation with an inotropic vasodilator was not intrinsically lethal in this model, but respiratory complications emerged as a key hazard.
Findings contrast with vasoconstrictor drugs, which often reduce organ blood flow, increase metabolic debt, and worsen survival in hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: AF in Trauma Patients Requiring ICU Care

raw_front_matter.title: AF in Trauma Patients Requiring ICU Care
raw_front_matter.description: In trauma patients requiring intensive care, new‑onset atrial fibrillation is an early, transient arrhythmia that strongly signals high inflammatory and injury severity but, after adjustment for base…

raw_front_matter.tags: atrial fibrillation, trauma, intensive care, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, catecholamines, shock, cardiac arrhythmia, critical care outcomes

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In trauma patients requiring intensive care, new‑onset atrial fibrillation is an early, transient arrhythmia that strongly signals high inflammatory and injury severity but, after adjustment for baseline risk, does not independently worsen mortality.
key_points: Atrial fibrillation (AF) occurred in 5.5% of trauma patients admitted to a surgical ICU who had sinus rhythm on admission.
Patients who developed AF were older, more severely injured, and had more body regions traumatized.
AF was independently associated with catecholamine use, higher SAPS II, SIRS, multiple trauma regions, and age ≥40 years.
AF episodes occurred early (median day 3), were generally short, and resolved in all cases, often with cardioversion and/or amiodarone.
AF was associated with higher ICU resource use and longer ICU stay, but did not increase standardized mortality ratio after adjustment for severity.
Findings support AF as a marker of systemic inflammation and trauma severity rather than a direct cause of excess mortality.

docs.title: Circulatory Responses to Hemorrhage in the Dog

raw_front_matter.title: Circulatory Responses to Hemorrhage in the Dog
raw_front_matter.description: In dogs subjected to progressive hemorrhage, circulatory failure emerges through a three-phase sequence in which modest, regionally redistributed vasoconstriction and tachycardia initially preserve f…
raw_front_matter.authors: J. W. Remington, W. F. Hamilton, H. M. Caddell, G. H. Boyd Jr., W. F. Hamilton Jr.
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac output, systemic vascular resistance, canine model, hemodynamics, oxygen transport, venous return

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs subjected to progressive hemorrhage, circulatory failure emerges through a three-phase sequence in which modest, regionally redistributed vasoconstriction and tachycardia initially preserve flow, but ultimately give way to central volume depletion, loss of effective vascular resistance, and impaired cardiac filling and oxygen transport, rather than to uniformly overwhelming vasoconstriction alone.
key_points: Serial controlled hemorrhage in anesthetized dogs revealed three distinct hemodynamic phases culminating in circulatory collapse.
Early hemorrhage produced modest falls in blood pressure and cardiac output with slight increases in calculated systemic resistance but no tachycardia.
Mid-phase tachycardia transiently restored or augmented cardiac output without large, sustained rises in total peripheral resistance.
Late hemorrhage was characterized by concurrent falls in arterial pressure, cardiac output, and systemic resistance, with severe impairment of oxygen transport.
Calculated whole-body resistance changes were small compared with those produced by pharmacologic vasoconstrictors, implying marked regional redistribution rather than uniform vasoconstriction.
Venous pressure did not reliably track venous return or cardiac output, and heart volume remained small until terminal dilation shortly before death.

The authors argue that late circulatory failure reflects both peripheral vascular changes (increased bed capacity, local dilation) and limitations of cardiac filling, rather than simply overwhelming vasoconstriction.

docs.title: Metabolism of Cardiac Muscle in Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Metabolism of Cardiac Muscle in Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In rat models of traumatic and hemorrhagic shock, the myocardium undergoes a late decline in oxygen consumption accompanied by glycogen depletion and accumulation of lactate and pyruvate that are not…

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, traumatic shock, cardiac metabolism, myocardial energetics, oxygen consumption, glycogen, lactate, pyruvate, potassium, iodoacetate

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In rat models of traumatic and hemorrhagic shock, the myocardium undergoes a late decline in oxygen consumption accompanied by glycogen depletion and accumulation of lactate and pyruvate that are not corrected by lowering extracellular potassium, indicating a primarily anoxic impairment of cardiac energy metabolism rather than a simple ionic effect.
key_points: Cardiac muscle in traumatic and hemorrhagic shock shows time‑dependent alterations in oxygen consumption, glycogen, lactate, and pyruvate content.
Myocardial glycogen stores fall significantly in traumatic shock, especially several hours after release of limb tourniquets.
Both lactate and pyruvate accumulate in shocked hearts, suggesting impaired oxidative carbohydrate metabolism and relative anoxia.
Reducing extracellular potassium in vitro does not reverse the depressed oxygen consumption of cardiac muscle from shocked animals.
Sodium iodoacetate further suppresses myocardial oxygen consumption in both control and shocked tissue, indicating glycolytic pathways remain functionally important.
Respiratory quotient values <1.0 in both groups imply substantial non‑carbohydrate fuel utilization by the heart during shock.

raw_front_matter.authors: Norman B. Ratliff, Donald B. Hackel, Eileen Mikat
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial blood flow, myocardial oxygen consumption, hyperbaric oxygen, xenon-133 washout, coronary circulation, canine model, cardiovascular physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs with hemorrhagic shock, hyperbaric oxygen increases myocardial oxygen consumption without further lowering an already minimized myocardial blood flow, and upon return to normobaric air it elicits a consistent rise in coronary flow, indicating that myocardial perfusion in shock is actively regulated and can be favorably modulated by oxygen therapy.
key_points: In normal anesthetized dogs, breathing oxygen at high pressure markedly reduced myocardial blood flow and proportionally reduced myocardial oxygen consumption.
In dogs in controlled hemorrhagic shock, hyperbaric oxygen did not further reduce myocardial blood flow but significantly increased myocardial oxygen consumption and coronary sinus oxygen content.
After withdrawal of hyperbaric oxygen during shock, myocardial blood flow rose above pre-hyperbaric shock levels while myocardial oxygen consumption remained elevated.
Data support the existence of a baseline (minimal) myocardial blood flow below which flow no longer decreases in response to hyperoxia.
Myocardial blood flow regulation in hemorrhagic shock is not a purely passive maximal vasodilatation but reflects active, modifiable control mechanisms.
Hyperbaric oxygen appears to alter coronary control during shock, making flow more responsive to myocardial oxygen demands when normobaric air is resumed.

docs.title: Mechanisms of Secondary Cardiac Dysfunction in Trauma/Hemorrhage

raw_front_matter.title: Mechanisms of Secondary Cardiac Dysfunction in Trauma/Hemorrhage
raw_front_matter.description: Trauma-induced secondary cardiac dysfunction arises from TLR-driven sterile inflammation, oxidative/nitrative stress, and cardiomyocyte apoptosis that overwhelm endogenous protective pathways, and ex…
raw_front_matter.authors: Nick M. Wilson, Johanna Wall, Veena Naganathar, Karim Brohi, Henry D. De’Ath
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma-induced secondary cardiac injury, hemorrhagic shock, cardiac dysfunction, innate immunity, sterile inflammation, animal models, myocardial apoptosis, hemodynamic dysfunction

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Trauma-induced secondary cardiac dysfunction arises from TLR-driven sterile inflammation, oxidative/nitrative stress, and cardiomyocyte apoptosis that overwhelm endogenous protective pathways, and experimental modulation of these mechanisms markedly improves post-traumatic myocardial function in animal models.
key_points: Trauma-induced secondary cardiac injury (TISCI) occurs without direct cardiac trauma and is associated with increased mortality and adverse cardiac events in patients.
Animal models of trauma and hemorrhagic shock consistently demonstrate myocardial inflammation, contractile dysfunction, and biomarker evidence of cardiac injury.
Innate immune activation via Toll-like receptors (especially TLR4, and modulated by TLR9) in cardiomyocytes is central to sensing tissue damage and initiating myocardial inflammation.
Cardiomyocytes themselves amplify inflammation by producing TNF-α, IL-6, adhesion molecules, and chemokines that drive neutrophil infiltration and oxidative/nitrative stress.

Excess oxidative and nitrative stress (MPO, NADPH oxidase, iNOS, peroxynitrite) promotes protein damage, mitochondrial injury, and caspase-dependent cardiomyocyte apoptosis, leading to reduced contractility.

Cardioprotective pathways (Akt, p38 MAPK, heat shock proteins, estrogen signaling) are downregulated after trauma-hemorrhage, and their pharmacologic preservation improves cardiac function in animal studies.

The balance between damaging inflammatory/oxidative mediators and depleted protective mechanisms appears to determine the extent of post-traumatic cardiac dysfunction and represents a key therapeutic target.
