raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endotoxemia, tumor necrosis factor, bacterial translocation, gut-liver axis, portal circulation, systemic inflammation, rat model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of hemorrhagic shock, early gut bacterial translocation causes portal endotoxemia that spills into the systemic circulation, driving a surge in TNF—initially from gut macrophages and later from Kupffer cells—which correlates with organ damage and mortality.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in rats rapidly induces gut bacterial translocation and portal endotoxemia, followed by systemic endotoxemia.
Portal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels rise earlier and remain higher than systemic levels, implicating the portal vein as the main route of systemic exposure.
Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) increases early in both portal and systemic blood, with an earlier portal rise and a later, higher systemic peak.
Histologic injury is prominent in jejunum/ileum, liver, and lung, while the colon remains relatively spared.
Higher systemic LPS and TNF concentrations are associated with non-survival after hemorrhagic shock.
Findings support gut-derived LPS and LPS-induced TNF as mediators of post-hemorrhagic organ injury and mortality.

docs.title: Combined Adrenergic Blockade in Hemorrhagic Hypotension

raw_front_matter.title: Combined Adrenergic Blockade in Hemorrhagic Hypotension
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of fixed-pressure hemorrhagic hypotension, a carefully balanced combined alpha–beta adrenergic blockade offers superior protection against metabolic acidosis and supports plasma ref…
raw_front_matter.authors: G. Zierott, E. Pappova, P. Lundsgaard-Hansen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hemorrhagic hypotension, adrenergic blockade, alpha-blockade, beta-blockade, combined alpha-beta blockade, dog model, metabolic acidosis, plasma volume, microcirculation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of fixed-pressure hemorrhagic hypotension, a carefully balanced combined alpha–beta adrenergic blockade offers superior protection against metabolic acidosis and supports plasma refill while maintaining near-normal tolerance to blood loss, whereas isolated beta-blockade aggravates shock and isolated alpha-blockade improves tolerance at the cost of reduced blood loss requirements.
key_points: In dogs subjected to fixed-pressure hemorrhagic hypotension at 40 mmHg, alpha- and beta-adrenergic blockade have opposite effects on tolerance and metabolism.
Pure alpha-receptor blockade reduces required blood loss, prolongs tolerance to hypotension, and attenuates metabolic acidosis.
Pure beta-receptor blockade leaves initial blood loss unchanged but shortens tolerated hypotension and worsens metabolic disturbances.
A tailored combined alpha–beta blockade yields near-control levels of tolerated blood loss while providing maximal protection against metabolic sequelae.
During prolonged hypotension, untreated animals lose plasma from the circulation whereas adrenergically blocked animals exhibit plasma refill, increasing circulating blood volume.
A modest (~15%) difference in circulating blood volume is associated with a large (~100%) difference in base excess, underscoring the importance of volume preservation.
Future shock studies should use drug combinations that minimally reduce tolerated blood loss while maximally limiting metabolic consequences.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Disturbances in extracellular potassium—whether systemic or ischemia-induced—profoundly reshape cardiac ion fluxes, repolarization reserve, and conduction to promote distinct but mechanistically linked pathways to ventricular arrhythmias, many of which may be preventable by stabilizing K+ balance and interrupting CaMK/late Na+-dependent feedback loops.
key_points: Both low and high extracellular potassium strongly modulate cardiac excitability and arrhythmia risk through tightly coupled changes in K+, Na+, and Ca2+ handling.

Hypokalemia reduces repolarization reserve via direct K+ current suppression and Na+-K+ ATPase inhibition, leading to intracellular Na+/Ca2+ overload, CaMK activation, and EAD/DAD-mediated arrhythmias.
Even moderate hypokalemia (≈2.5–3.0 mmol/L) can be highly arrhythmogenic in structurally normal hearts, especially in the presence of K+ channel–blocking drugs.
Systemic hyperkalemia depolarizes resting membrane potential, shortens action potential duration, alters conduction velocity, and can induce conduction block, reentry, and VT/VF at higher levels.
Interstitial hyperkalemia during acute regional myocardial ischemia produces injury currents that underlie ST elevation/TQ depression and provide both triggers and substrate for reentrant VT/VF.
Purkinje and epicardial tissues show distinct sensitivities to potassium disturbances, shaping where and how arrhythmias arise in hypokalemia and ischemia.
Targeting late Na+ current and CaMK-dependent signaling may be effective strategies to prevent hypokalemia- and drug-induced afterdepolarization-mediated arrhythmias.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In cats, late postoligemic shock and spontaneous circulatory collapse are associated with intrinsic depression of papillary muscle excitability and contractility and reduced responsiveness to angiotensin II and norepinephrine, while ouabain responses and muscle histology remain largely preserved, making this an informative in vitro model of shock-induced myocardial failure.
key_points: Papillary muscles from cats in late postoligemic shock and spontaneous circulatory collapse show depressed excitability and contractility in vitro.
Early postoligemic shock and acute anoxia do not measurably impair papillary muscle function compared with controls.
In late shock and failing hearts, inotropic responses to angiotensin II and low-dose norepinephrine are significantly blunted, whereas responses to ouabain are preserved.
The myocardial depression persists in isolated muscle bathed in artificial solution, arguing against a purely circulating, freely diffusible depressant factor.
No major histologic or glycogen depletion changes are detectable in papillary muscles despite functional impairment.
The isolated cat papillary muscle is a practical in vitro model for studying myocardial depression in late hemorrhagic/postoligemic shock.

raw_front_matter.authors: Joseph Edwards, Hossam Abdou, Marta J. Madurska, Neerav Patel, Michael J. Richmond, David Poliner, Joseph M. White, Todd E. Rasmussen, Thomas M. Scalea, Jonathan J. Morrison
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, exsanguination cardiac arrest, selective aortic arch perfusion, open cardiac massage, resuscitative thoracotomy, coronary perfusion pressure, porcine model, endovascular resuscitation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a hypovolemic swine model of exsanguination cardiac arrest, selective aortic arch perfusion produced substantially higher and more efficient coronary perfusion pressures than open cardiac massage, suggesting it may be a superior strategy to support the heart and brain during resuscitation from noncompressible torso hemorrhage.
key_points: In hypovolemic swine after exsanguination cardiac arrest, selective aortic arch perfusion (SAAP) generated substantially higher coronary perfusion pressures (CPP) and aortic–right atrial (AoP–RAP) gradients than open cardiac massage (OCM).
CPP during SAAP closely approximated the AoP–RAP gradient, indicating more efficient conversion of proximal aortic pressure into coronary perfusion than with OCM.
Using a CPP threshold of 15 mmHg (associated with return of spontaneous circulation in cardiac arrest), SAAP segments met or exceeded this level 97% of the time versus 17% with OCM.
OCM increased right atrial pressures during compression, limiting effective coronary driving pressure despite a measurable AoP–RAP gradient.
SAAP uses balloon occlusion of the descending thoracic aorta and retrograde aortic infusion to preferentially perfuse the heart and brain without large rises in right atrial pressure.

The study focused on hemodynamic surrogates and did not measure actual return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), but supports SAAP as a promising adjunct in exsanguination cardiac arrest from noncompressible torso hemorrhage.

raw_front_matter.authors: Shunichi Miyazaki, Hisayoshi Fujiwara, Tomoya Onodera, Yasuki Kihara, Mitsuo Matsuda, Der-Jinn Wu, Yasuyuki Nakamura, Toshiaki Kumada, Shigetake Sasayama, Chuichi Kawai, Yoshihiro Hamashima

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In porcine hearts without collateral circulation, LAD reperfusion after 60 minutes of ischemia produces a nearly transmural infarct dominated by contraction band necrosis, indicating that early microvascular and myocyte injury severely limits myocardial salvage unless reperfusion occurs within about 1 hour or is specifically modified to prevent contraction band damage.
key_points: In pig hearts lacking collateral circulation, 60 minutes of LAD occlusion followed by reperfusion produces a nearly transmural infarct, two-thirds of which is contraction band necrosis (CBN).
Infarct size (CBN + coagulation necrosis, CN) increases steeply with ischemia duration; after 120 minutes of occlusion, reperfusion does not reduce infarct size compared with permanent occlusion.
CBN dominates after shorter ischemia (30–60 min), while CN dominates after prolonged ischemia (≥120 min) or permanent occlusion.
Transmural progression of necrosis occurs from endocardium to epicardium despite uniformly near-zero flow during occlusion, indicating determinants beyond collateral flow.
Reperfusion after prolonged ischemia causes marked intramyocardial hemorrhage confined to the infarct zone, associated with severe microvascular damage and no-reflow.
Protection against CBN may be essential to truly reduce infarct size when reperfusion is achieved around 1 hour after coronary occlusion.
These results model patients with poor or absent collaterals and suggest that thrombolysis beyond 1 hour may often yield transmural, largely irreversible injury despite vessel reopening.

raw_front_matter.authors: Lorne H. Blackbourne, David G. Baer, Ramon F. Cestero, Kenji Inaba, Todd E. Rasmussen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, exsanguination shock, battlefield trauma, combat casualty care, cardiovascular collapse, resuscitation failure, trauma systems
raw_front_matter.journal: The Journal of Trauma: Injury, Infection, and Critical Care

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: The authors argue that many combat casualties now die not from uncontrolled bleeding but from a distinct, poorly understood post-resuscitation state they term "exsanguination shock," and they call for targeted research and therapies to address this next frontier in preventing battlefield mortality.
key_points: The commentary reintroduces and defines "exsanguination shock" as a distinct clinical entity in combat trauma.
A subset of severely hemorrhaging patients reach surgical care, achieve apparent hemostasis and volume restoration, yet still progress to cardiovascular collapse and death.
Hemorrhage remains the leading cause of potentially survivable death on the battlefield despite major advances in prehospital care, evacuation, and damage control resuscitation.
The pathophysiology of death after successful hemorrhage control and volume replacement is poorly understood and likely multifactorial.
Animal models suggest that organ failure (particularly of heart, lungs, and small intestine) and mechanisms such as inflammatory dysregulation, endothelial injury, and coagulopathy may be central.
Improved understanding of exsanguination shock is needed to guide new therapies beyond hemorrhage control and blood product resuscitation.
The authors advocate replacing the term "irreversible shock" with "exsanguination shock" to focus research and clinical efforts on this problem.

raw_front_matter.authors: Péter Jávor, Lilla Hanák, Péter Hegyi, Endre Csonka, Edina Butt, Tamara Horváth, István Góg, Anita Lukacs, Alexandra Soós, Zoltán Rumbus, Eszter Pákai, János Toldi, Petra Hartmann

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In contemporary trauma-related hemorrhagic shock, early tachycardia does not show a simple linear relationship with mortality, challenging its central role in ATLS shock classification and calling for revised, more physiologically accurate use of heart rate in early trauma assessment.
key_points: Across 19 contemporary trauma studies (2010–2020), early heart rate showed no linear association with mortality in patients with hemorrhagic shock.
Subgroup analysis limited to patients receiving blood products also failed to demonstrate a linear heart rate–mortality relationship.
The physiological heart rate response to hemorrhage is multiphasic (biphasic/triphasic), not the simple monotonic increase assumed in ATLS shock classes.
Relying on absence of tachycardia as reassurance can be dangerous, as normal or low heart rates can occur in profound hypovolemia and are associated with poor prognosis.
Heart rate appears inferior to other markers (e.g., base deficit, systolic blood pressure, Glasgow Coma Scale) for grading shock severity and predicting outcome.
The authors propose modifying the ATLS hypovolemic shock classification to reflect possible heart rate stagnation around 30% blood loss and bradycardia in class IV shock.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac function, sympathetic nervous system, stellate ganglion, myocardial catecholamines, norepinephrine, dog model, vagus nerve

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs subjected to prolonged hemorrhagic shock, the heart becomes almost completely unresponsive to stellate (sympathetic) stimulation despite normal myocardial catecholamine levels and preserved vagal reactivity, indicating a functional breakdown of cardiac sympathetic transmission that limits myocardial participation in circulatory compensation.
key_points: In open-chest anesthetized dogs, the cardiac response to stellate ganglion stimulation progressively diminishes during prolonged hemorrhagic shock, approaching complete refractoriness.
Despite this functional sympathetic failure, myocardial norepinephrine and epinephrine concentrations remain similar to those of control dogs.
Exogenous norepinephrine restores contractility and heart rate but does not restore the cardiac response to stellate stimulation.
In contrast to sympathetic failure, vagal stimulation in late hemorrhagic shock still produces marked bradycardia and even cardiac arrest.
The loss of response to stellate stimulation may reflect impaired norepinephrine storage/release at nerve endings rather than depletion of bulk myocardial catecholamine content.
These changes suggest that in late hemorrhagic shock the myocardium may no longer participate effectively in baroreflex-mediated pressor responses.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A three-variable mechanistic ODE model capturing interactions among arterial pressure, neurologic function, and systemic acidosis can reproduce key features of hemorrhagic shock and offers a foundation for computerized triage tools that predict survival and survival time after traumatic blood loss.
key_points: The paper presents a three-variable ordinary differential equation (ODE) model of hemorrhagic shock using mean arterial pressure, neurologic function, and systemic acidosis/base deficit.
The model is designed to approximate the dynamic pathophysiology after a traumatic hemorrhagic insult and to predict short‑term survival and survival time without resuscitation.

Validation against classic canine (Guyton & Crowell) and primate (Bar‑Joseph et al.) hemorrhage data showed the model reproduces critical pressure thresholds, neurologic decline, and acidosis accumulation.
The model identifies a pressure threshold below which death is inevitable within hours, consistent with prior animal data on shock physiology.
Survivors and nonsurvivors cluster into distinct regions in model state-space plots, allowing prediction of both outcome and approximate time to death.
The approach is proposed as a basis for computerized decision support tools for trauma triage, especially in mass-casualty or resource-limited settings.

raw_front_matter.description: In swine hemorrhagic shock, full REBOA delivers strong hemodynamic rescue at the cost of extreme afterload and supraphysiologic coronary flows, whereas partial REBOA provides sufficient resuscitative…
raw_front_matter.authors: Stonko DP, Edwards J, Abdou H, Elansary NN, Lang E, Savidge SG, Hicks CW, Morrison JJ
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta, REBOA, partial REBOA, pressure-volume loops, coronary blood flow, afterload, cardiac injury, swine model, non-compressible torso hemorrhage

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In swine hemorrhagic shock, full REBOA delivers strong hemodynamic rescue at the cost of extreme afterload and supraphysiologic coronary flows, whereas partial REBOA provides sufficient resuscitative support with substantially less cardiac stress, supporting early transition from full to partial occlusion in clinical practice.
key_points: In a swine hemorrhagic shock model, full REBOA produces marked afterload augmentation with large increases in end-systolic pressure and contractility, while partial REBOA produces intermediate effects.
Hemorrhagic shock reduced stroke work and end-systolic pressure, confirming a profound depression of left ventricular performance before REBOA deployment.
Full REBOA generated supraphysiologic coronary peak and total flows and reversed shock-induced retrograde coronary flow, but at the cost of markedly increased left ventricular elastance (Ees).
Partial REBOA preserved preload (EDPVR) and restored forward coronary flow while limiting the magnitude of afterload and contractility changes compared with full REBOA.
Transition from full to partial REBOA rapidly normalized many hemodynamic parameters without evidence of acute myocardial necrosis on histology or troponin at 1 hour.
Findings support a dose–response relationship between degree of aortic occlusion, afterload, coronary flow, and LV contractility.
Data mechanistically support clinical strategies that minimize duration of full REBOA and transition early to partial REBOA once proximal perfusion is restored.

raw_front_matter.description: In an acute canine coronary ligation model, propranolol markedly suppresses beta-adrenergic-driven activation of myocardial glycogenolysis in both endocardial and epicardial layers, yet only partiall…
raw_front_matter.authors: Kazuo Ichihara, Yasushi Abiko

raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology: Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In an acute canine coronary ligation model, propranolol markedly suppresses beta-adrenergic-driven activation of myocardial glycogenolysis in both endocardial and epicardial layers, yet only partially attenuates downstream ischemia-induced disturbances in glycolytic intermediates and phosphocreatine.
key_points: Coronary artery ligation in dogs normally activates myocardial glycogen phosphorylase and depletes glycogen in both endocardial and epicardial layers.
Intravenous propranolol (1 mg/kg) before ligation prevents the ischemia-induced activation of phosphorylase a and the associated glycogen breakdown.
Despite blocking glycogenolysis, propranolol does not fully prevent increases in glucose 6-phosphate and lactate or the fall in phosphocreatine following ischemia, especially in the endocardium.
Baseline phosphorylase a activity, glucose 6-phosphate, and lactate levels are substantially lower in propranolol-pretreated hearts than in saline controls.
ATP levels remain relatively stable after coronary artery ligation in both treatment groups, consistent with a relatively small ischemic territory.
Findings support a major role for catecholamine-mediated beta-adrenergic signaling in driving early glycogenolytic responses to acute regional ischemia.

docs.title: Transport Time & Pre-OR Hemostatic Interventions in Truncal Injury

raw_front_matter.title: Transport Time & Pre-OR Hemostatic Interventions in Truncal Injury
raw_front_matter.description: Because patients with severe truncal hemorrhage often die within the first 30–120 minutes after injury while current systems take about 2.1 hours to achieve definitive hemostasis, trauma care must sh…
raw_front_matter.authors: John B. Holcomb
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, truncal hemorrhage, prehospital care, trauma systems, resuscitation, whole blood, REBOA, damage control resuscitation, military trauma, civilian trauma

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Because patients with severe truncal hemorrhage often die within the first 30–120 minutes after injury while current systems take about 2.1 hours to achieve definitive hemostasis, trauma care must shift temporary truncal hemorrhage control and whole blood resuscitation out of the operating room and as close as possible to the point of injury to meaningfully reduce preventable deaths.
key_points: Mortality from severe truncal hemorrhage peaks within 30 minutes of injury, yet definitive hemorrhage control currently occurs a median of ~2.1 hours after injury.
Emergent trauma laparotomy mortality in hypotensive patients (~46%) has remained essentially unchanged for over 20 years, despite mature trauma systems.
Prehospital and early in-hospital blood product resuscitation, especially with whole blood, is associated with improved survival in both military and civilian settings.
Temporary truncal hemorrhage control technologies (e.g., REBOA, intra-abdominal foam) are now feasible outside the operating room and are entering prospective evaluation.
Moving hemorrhage control and balanced/whole blood resuscitation closer to the point of injury is likely the most effective strategy to reduce preventable deaths from truncal bleeding.
Tourniquet experience in extremity hemorrhage demonstrates that shifting hemorrhage control from OR/hospital to prehospital settings can dramatically reduce preventable deaths.
Achieving “zero preventable trauma deaths” will require system-wide changes emphasizing rapid transport plus early, pre-OR truncal hemorrhage control and whole blood resuscitation.

raw_front_matter.title: Mechanisms of Secondary Cardiac Dysfunction in Trauma
raw_front_matter.description: Secondary cardiac dysfunction after trauma and hemorrhagic shock is driven by sterile, TLR-mediated myocardial inflammation and oxidative/nitrative stress that overwhelm endogenous protective pathway…
raw_front_matter.authors: Nick M. Wilson, Johanna Wall, Veena Naganathar, Karim Brohi, Henry D. De’Ath
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma-induced secondary cardiac injury, hemorrhagic shock, cardiac dysfunction, sterile inflammation, innate immunity, Toll-like receptors, NF-κB, TNF-α, IL-6, nitrosative and oxidative stress, apoptosis, sex hormones, heat shock proteins, animal models, translational research
raw_front_matter.journal: Narrative review (Centre for Trauma Sciences, Queen Mary University of London)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Secondary cardiac dysfunction after trauma and hemorrhagic shock is driven by sterile, TLR-mediated myocardial inflammation and oxidative/nitrative stress that overwhelm endogenous protective pathways, but animal data suggest that targeted modulation of these immune and stress responses can preserve cardiac function and may be translatable to human trauma care.
key_points: Trauma-induced secondary cardiac injury (TISCI) occurs in patients without direct cardiac trauma and is associated with arrhythmias, heart failure, adverse cardiac events, and increased mortality.
Animal models of trauma, hemorrhage, and combined trauma–hemorrhage consistently demonstrate intrinsic myocardial depression that is not reversed by simple volume resuscitation.
Cardiac dysfunction after trauma–hemorrhage is driven by sterile inflammation initiated by damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) via Toll-like receptors (especially TLR4) on cardiomyocytes.
Cardiomyocytes actively amplify inflammation, producing NF-κB–dependent cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6), adhesion molecules, and chemokines that recruit neutrophils and increase oxidative/nitrative stress.
Excess production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, largely via MPO, NADPH oxidase and iNOS, leads to protein misfolding, mitochondrial injury, and caspase-dependent cardiomyocyte apoptosis.

Protective pathways (Akt, p38 MAPK, heat shock proteins, estrogen signaling) are downregulated after trauma–hemorrhage, and pharmacologic preservation of these pathways improves cardiac function in animals.
Current preclinical data identify multiple promising cardio-protective interventions, but translation to heterogeneous human trauma populations remains limited and requires focused clinical studies.

docs.title: Calcium-Mediated Cell Death in Myocardial Reperfusion

raw_front_matter.title: Calcium-Mediated Cell Death in Myocardial Reperfusion
raw_front_matter.description: Calcium overload and dysregulated Ca2+ handling during the first minutes of myocardial reperfusion—driving hypercontracture, calpain activation, and mitochondria–SR–coupled permeability transition—ar…
raw_front_matter.authors: David Garcia-Dorado, Marisol Ruiz-Meana, Javier Inserte, Antonio Rodriguez-Sinovas, Hans Michael Piper
raw_front_matter.tags: myocardial infarction, reperfusion injury, calcium handling, calpain, mitochondrial permeability transition, hypercontracture, ischemia-reperfusion, cardiomyocyte death

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Calcium overload and dysregulated Ca2+ handling during the first minutes of myocardial reperfusion—driving hypercontracture, calpain activation, and mitochondria–SR–coupled permeability transition—are central, time-dependent determinants of cardiomyocyte death and remain high-value but underexploited therapeutic targets in acute myocardial infarction.
key_points: Reperfusion after myocardial ischemia induces additional, preventable cardiomyocyte death that is strongly modulated by intracellular Ca2+ handling.
Ca2+-dependent mechanisms (hypercontracture, calpain activation, Ca2+-driven MPT) operate alongside Ca2+-independent triggers such as reactive oxygen species.
During ischemia, Na+ and Ca2+ overload develop via Na+/H+ exchange, persistent Na+ channels, Na+/Ca2+ exchange, and impaired SERCA and Na+/K+-ATPase activity.
Early reperfusion is characterized by intense Ca2+ influx (notably via reverse-mode Na+/Ca2+ exchange), rapid pH normalization, SR-driven Ca2+ oscillations, and high risk of hypercontracture.
Tight structural and functional coupling between sarcoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria creates local Ca2+ microdomains that promote mitochondrial permeability transition and energetic collapse.
The relative contribution of Ca2+-driven hypercontracture versus MPT to cell death depends on ischemia duration: hypercontracture dominates after brief ischemia, MPT after prolonged ischemia.

Clinically effective cardioprotective strategies (e.g., natriuretic peptides, postconditioning, cyclosporin A) likely confer benefit in part by improving Ca2+ handling or blunting Ca2+-mediated injury.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock at systolic pressures ~30 mmHg, the major oxygen deficit and anaerobic metabolism occur in peripheral tissues rather than in the myocardium, which remains predominantly aerobic at the coronary venous O₂ levels observed.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock causes substantial systemic oxygen deficit, but its regional distribution between peripheral tissues and heart is unclear.
In a canine hemorrhagic shock model (systolic BP ~32 mmHg up to 90 min), peripheral tissues showed clear evidence of anaerobic metabolism.
Under the same conditions, no significant increase in anaerobic myocardial metabolism could be demonstrated.
Coronary oxygen extraction rose and coronary sinus O₂ saturation and pO₂ fell in shock, but not below critical thresholds for anaerobic myocardial metabolism.
Global excess lactate and base deficit reflect peripheral, not myocardial, anaerobiosis in this model.
These data support the view that early and mid‑stage hemorrhagic shock is predominantly a peripheral circulatory failure rather than primary cardiac failure.

raw_front_matter.description: In canine hemorrhagic shock, irreversible hypotension is driven by progressive cardiac pump failure with central blood pooling, rather than by peripheral vascular failure or uncorrected volume loss,…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jack W. Crowell, Arthur C. Guyton
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, irreversible shock, cardiac failure, cardiac output curves, atrial pressure, dog model, hemodynamics, digitalis

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, irreversible hypotension is driven by progressive cardiac pump failure with central blood pooling, rather than by peripheral vascular failure or uncorrected volume loss, and once this myocardial dysfunction is advanced, it cannot be reversed by volume replacement alone.
key_points: In irreversible hemorrhagic shock, the primary failure is cardiac, not peripheral vascular.
Serial cardiac output curves in dogs shift progressively to indicate worsening myocardial pump failure.
As shock becomes irreversible, very high atrial pressures are required to maintain any given cardiac output.
Central blood volume and atrial pressures rise, indicating central pooling of blood rather than peripheral sequestration.
Even with restored or increased blood volume, cardiac output cannot be normalized once severe cardiac failure has developed.
Digitalization (ouabain) temporarily improves cardiac performance but does not prevent progressive failure in advanced shock.
The heart becomes trapped between a need for high filling pressures and compensatory mechanisms that tend to lower venous pressure.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Over the last decade, research on trauma-related hemorrhagic shock has expanded globally and shifted toward clinical interventions and endothelial-targeted strategies, with REBOA, whole blood transfusion, exosome-based therapies, and outcome predictors emerging as key frontiers that will shape future management paradigms.
key_points: The study maps global research output on trauma-related hemorrhagic shock between 2012 and 2022 using bibliometric tools.
A total of 3116 English-language articles and reviews from 200 journals, 441 institutions, and 80 countries were analyzed.
The United States dominates the field in publication volume, institutional output, and network centrality, with China and Germany following.
Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA) and whole blood transfusion have emerged as leading research frontiers.
Emerging mechanistic and translational themes include exosomes, endothelial glycocalyx damage, endotheliopathy, and outcome predictors.
Research focus has shifted from primarily mechanistic/basic work (2012–2015) toward clinical interventions and outcome improvement (2016–2022).
The analysis highlights key authors, institutions, journals, and reference clusters that structure the current knowledge domain.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A physiologically interpretable arterial blood pressure waveform feature—the half-rise to dicrotic notch (HRDN)—can, via a simple gradient-boosted model, noninvasively and accurately track compensatory reserve during both simulated hemorrhage and whole blood resuscitation, matching the performance of complex black-box algorithms without requiring individual baseline data.
key_points: Traditional vital signs are insensitive for early detection of hemorrhage and assessment of resuscitation status due to physiological compensation.
ABP waveform–derived features, especially the half-rise to dicrotic notch (HRDN), can noninvasively track compensatory reserve during both simulated hemorrhage and resuscitation.
A gradient-boosted regression tree model using only HRDN predicts compensatory reserve with error comparable to more complex black-box ML approaches.
The same ABP-based algorithm performs similarly across both progressive blood volume loss and restoration, and across multiple hemorrhage/resuscitation rates.
HRDN is physiologically interpretable as a surrogate for timing between ejected and reflected arterial waves and thus for systemic vascular resistance and cardiac output.
Vital-sign-only models perform substantially worse than waveform-feature models, even when baseline-normalized.
The HRDN approach does not require subject-specific baseline normalization, making it more practical for field and pre-hospital use.

docs.title: Myocardial Pyruvate Metabolism in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Pyruvate Metabolism in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of hemorrhagic shock, the heart rapidly shifts from net pyruvate uptake to pyruvate release due to a primary depression of myocardial pyruvate dehydrogenase activity that is not cor…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jerry Nagler
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial metabolism, pyruvate dehydrogenase, cardiac failure, ischemia, metabolic regulation, animal model, catecholamines, acidosis, oxygen debt
raw_front_matter.journal: MD Thesis, Yale University School of Medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of hemorrhagic shock, the heart rapidly shifts from net pyruvate uptake to pyruvate release due to a primary depression of myocardial pyruvate dehydrogenase activity that is not corrected by thiamine but is partially reversible with restored systemic perfusion, suggesting an early, flow-dependent metabolic injury that may contribute to later cardiac failure.
key_points: Early hemorrhagic shock in dogs consistently produces a negative myocardial pyruvate arteriovenous (A–V) difference, while lactate uptake is maintained.

This metabolic signature is associated with a significant decrease in myocardial pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex activity, indicating a block at pyruvate oxidation rather than upstream glycolysis.
Exogenous thiamine or cocarboxylase administration does not correct the abnormal myocardial pyruvate extraction nor restore PDH activity in vitro, arguing against isolated cocarboxylase deficiency.
Restoration of systemic arterial pressure and flow with dextran (volume expansion) can normalize myocardial pyruvate extraction transiently, despite hemodilution and unchanged acidosis.
The PDH defect appears during a phase when myocardial oxygen consumption is still maintained via increased extraction, i.e., before overt myocardial anaerobic glycolysis and lactate production.

The author proposes that decreased PDH activity represents an early, potentially pathogenic myocardial lesion in hemorrhagic shock, possibly driven by hypoxia, acidosis, catecholamines, or circulating toxins rather than coronary flow alone.
Metabolic derangements in the myocardium may precede, and possibly contribute to, the later hemodynamic and contractile failure that characterizes irreversible hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Myocardial Metabolism and Coronary Flow in Endotoxemia

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Metabolism and Coronary Flow in Endotoxemia
raw_front_matter.description: Sublethal endotoxemia renders the rat heart hypermetabolic and hypercontractile while uncoupling coronary flow from myocardial metabolic demand, leading to excessive basal vasodilation but impaired v…
raw_front_matter.authors: William L. Rumsey, Laurie Kilpatrick, David F. Wilson, Maria Erecinska
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, sepsis, endotoxemia, cardiac metabolism, coronary flow regulation, rat heart, calcium signaling, pyruvate dehydrogenase, myocardial oxygen consumption, vasodilation, microcirculation
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Sublethal endotoxemia renders the rat heart hypermetabolic and hypercontractile while uncoupling coronary flow from myocardial metabolic demand, leading to excessive basal vasodilation but impaired vasodilatory responsiveness, a defect that may predispose to cardiac ischemia as systemic pressure falls in sepsis.
key_points: Sublethal endotoxemia produces a hypermetabolic, hyperdynamic state in isolated rat hearts, with increased myocardial oxygen consumption and markedly increased coronary flow.
Despite elevated basal coronary flow, the normal coupling between myocardial metabolism and coronary vasomotor tone is disrupted after endotoxin exposure.

Endotoxemia is associated with evidence of increased intracellular calcium in cardiomyocytes, including lowered mitochondrial [NAD+]/[NADH], increased active pyruvate dehydrogenase, and enhanced contractility.
Coronary vessels from endotoxemic hearts fail to sustain vasodilation when metabolism is stimulated or inhibited, in contrast to hearts from control animals.

Adenosine, a potent coronary vasodilator, markedly increases flow in control hearts but has little or no effect in endotoxemic hearts, suggesting near-maximal vasodilation at baseline and impaired vasodilatory reserve.

Calcium channel blockade with verapamil normalizes oxygen consumption between groups but does not correct the excessive coronary flow in endotoxemic hearts, implying distinct myocardial and vascular mechanisms.
The uncoupling of flow from metabolic demand in endotoxemia may predispose the heart to ischemia when systemic pressure falls, as occurs in late septic shock.

docs.title: Interstitial Fluid Pressure and Tissue Fluid Mobility

raw_front_matter.title: Interstitial Fluid Pressure and Tissue Fluid Mobility
raw_front_matter.description: As interstitial fluid pressure rises from its normal subatmospheric level to slightly above atmospheric, the resistance to tissue fluid movement collapses by several orders of magnitude, revealing a…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur C. Guyton, Konrad Scheel, Dennis Murphree
raw_front_matter.tags: interstitial fluid pressure, edema, tissue mechanics, microcirculation, extracellular matrix, fluid resistance, collapsible tubes

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: As interstitial fluid pressure rises from its normal subatmospheric level to slightly above atmospheric, the resistance to tissue fluid movement collapses by several orders of magnitude, revealing a transition from predominantly immobilized gel-bound fluid to highly mobile edema fluid within expanded, collapsible interstitial channels.
key_points: Resistance to interstitial fluid movement is extremely high when interstitial pressure is subatmospheric and collapses when pressure rises to around atmospheric levels.
Transition from negative to slightly positive interstitial pressure increases interstitial fluid conductance by roughly 10^4–10^5-fold.
The pressure–volume behavior of mobile interstitial fluid differs markedly from that of total interstitial fluid volume.
Most interstitial water at normal negative pressures is presumed to be immobilized within a gelatinous ground substance matrix.
In edema, tissue spaces suddenly expand and support large volumes of freely mobile fluid.
Interstitial spaces behave mechanically like collapsible tubes with a small amount of resilient filling material.

docs.title: Transfusion, Hemorrhage, and Venous Return Curves

raw_front_matter.title: Transfusion, Hemorrhage, and Venous Return Curves
raw_front_matter.description: In anesthetized dogs, blood volume changes shift the venous return curve—raising mean circulatory pressure and lowering resistance with transfusion, or the reverse with hemorrhage—thereby quantitativ…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur C. Guyton, Arthur W. Lindsey, Berwind N. Kaufmann, Joseph B. Abernathy
raw_front_matter.tags: venous return, cardiac output, hemorrhage, blood transfusion, mean circulatory pressure, resistance to venous return, canine model, shock, high-output heart failure, volume loading

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized dogs, blood volume changes shift the venous return curve—raising mean circulatory pressure and lowering resistance with transfusion, or the reverse with hemorrhage—thereby quantitatively determining cardiac output and right atrial pressure independent of intrinsic cardiac contractility, and providing a mechanistic basis for both hypovolemic shock and high-output failure in hypervolemia.
key_points: Transfusion shifts the venous return curve upward and hemorrhage shifts it downward across the entire range of right atrial pressures, in both reflex-intact and areflex dogs.
Increased blood volume from transfusion both raises mean circulatory pressure and decreases resistance to venous return via vascular distension.
The increase in venous return after transfusion is transient due to rapid redistribution and loss of the excess volume, whereas the depression after hemorrhage is prolonged.
Cardiac output changes after hemorrhage or transfusion can be quantitatively predicted by intersecting venous return curves with the cardiac function curve.
Infusion of crystalloid (Tyrode’s solution) produces qualitatively similar venous return changes to blood transfusion, indicating a volume effect rather than a blood-specific effect.
A depressed venous return curve after blood loss explains low-output circulatory shock even when cardiac contractile function is normal.
Marked upward shifts of the venous return curve with hypervolemia can produce high-output states with elevated right atrial pressure, contributing to high-output cardiac failure.

docs.title: Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion Pathophysiology

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Ischemia/Reperfusion Pathophysiology
raw_front_matter.description: Ischemic heart disease is fundamentally a coronary vascular and myocardial ischemia/reperfusion disorder in which dynamic epicardial and microvascular pathology, diverse regulated cell death programs…
raw_front_matter.authors: Gerd Heusch
raw_front_matter.tags: ischemic heart disease, myocardial ischemia, reperfusion injury, coronary microcirculation, myocardial infarction, cardiogenic shock and heart failure, cell death pathways, microvascular obstruction, immune response and remodeling, cardioprotection, sex differences

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Ischemic heart disease is fundamentally a coronary vascular and myocardial ischemia/reperfusion disorder in which dynamic epicardial and microvascular pathology, diverse regulated cell death programs, and immune-driven healing/remodeling govern infarct size and outcomes, and a more mechanistic, personalized approach is needed to achieve effective cardioprotection and prevent post-infarct heart failure.
key_points: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) remains the leading global cause of death; progress in reducing mortality has stalled and the clinical phenotype is shifting (more NSTEMI, more MINOCA/INOCA).

Myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury is driven by both coronary vascular pathology (epicardial atherosclerosis, spasm, microembolization, microvascular dysfunction) and myocardial vulnerability (energy failure, Ca2+ overload, ROS, regulated cell death).

Active coronary vasomotion and microvascular dysfunction, including in patients without obstructive epicardial disease, play a central but often under-recognized role in angina, AMI, and subsequent heart failure.

Myocardial cell death after ischemia/reperfusion is heterogeneous, involving necrosis, apoptosis, necroptosis, pyroptosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy/mitophagy, which together determine infarct size and quality.
Coronary microvascular obstruction and intramyocardial hemorrhage are key determinants of prognosis after reperfused AMI, beyond infarct size alone.
Post-infarct healing and remodeling are immune- and fibroblast-driven processes that can yield either stable scar with preserved function or adverse remodeling with heart failure and arrhythmias.

Despite strong preclinical data (e.g., ischemic conditioning, mitoprotective drugs), translation of cardioprotective strategies into clinical benefit has largely failed, highlighting the need for more rigorous, personalized, and mechanistically grounded approaches.

docs.title: Blood Viscosity and Recovery from Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Blood Viscosity and Recovery from Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In experimental hemorrhagic shock in rabbits, recovery is driven primarily by volume replacement, with only very high–molecular-weight dextran at substantial doses causing enough viscosity and erythr…
raw_front_matter.authors: P. Lundsgaard-Hansen, B. Marti
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, blood viscosity, erythrocyte aggregation, dextran, gelatin plasma substitutes, microcirculation, rabbit model, acid-base balance, resuscitation fluids

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In experimental hemorrhagic shock in rabbits, recovery is driven primarily by volume replacement, with only very high–molecular-weight dextran at substantial doses causing enough viscosity and erythrocyte aggregation change to modestly delay metabolic normalization, implying that standard dextran and gelatin plasma substitutes are rheologically safe within usual clinical use.
key_points: In a rabbit model of standardized hemorrhagic shock, various dextran and gelatin solutions used to resuspend autologous erythrocytes were compared for effects on rheology and metabolic recovery.
Commercially available dextran and gelatin plasma substitutes with moderate rheological effects did not meaningfully impair recovery from shock.
Only high–molecular-weight dextran 500,000 at ~0.64 g/kg, which markedly increased blood viscosity and ESR, produced a modest but measurable delay in arterial pH recovery.
The maximal viscosity changes observed with dextran 500,000 corresponded to an effective hematocrit of ~78% in an otherwise normal animal.
Erythrocyte aggregation (ESR) and viscosity were positively correlated when markedly altered, yet still had limited impact on post-shock recovery compared with volume replacement.
The extreme rheological derangements reported with 1.0 g/kg dextran 1,000,000 in prior studies likely exceed physiologically and clinically relevant conditions.

raw_front_matter.title: Negative Interstitial Pressure via Implanted Capsules
raw_front_matter.description: Using implanted perforated capsules in dogs, Guyton demonstrated that interstitial pressure in many normal tissues is distinctly negative and becomes positive only with edema, fundamentally revising…
raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur C. Guyton, with Malcolm Franklin and Berry Abernathy
raw_front_matter.tags: interstitial pressure, microcirculation, Starling forces, edema, lymphatics, tissue biomechanics, measurement methods, animal model, shock and fluid balance

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Using implanted perforated capsules in dogs, Guyton demonstrated that interstitial pressure in many normal tissues is distinctly negative and becomes positive only with edema, fundamentally revising how tissue fluid dynamics and Starling forces should be understood.
key_points: Implanted perforated capsules in dog tissues recorded consistently negative pressures (~−6 mm Hg) in non-edematous states after healing.
In all forms of edema (local, generalized, inflammatory), intracapsular pressures became positive and rose with edema severity.
Capsular pressures, but not standard needle-based tissue pressures, behaved in accordance with Starling’s law of the capillaries.
Experiments indicate that capsule pressure closely reflects surrounding interstitial fluid pressure rather than a local artifact.
Traditional needle methods likely distort tissue architecture and overestimate interstitial pressure in non-edematous tissues.
Interstitial pressure–volume relations are highly nonlinear: very stiff (large pressure changes) when negative and compliant when positive/edematous.
A mechanistic hypothesis links negative interstitial pressure to low mean capillary pressure and lymphatic “pumping” driven by tissue movement.

docs.title: β3-Blockade in Endotoxin-Induced Heart Failure

raw_front_matter.title: β3-Blockade in Endotoxin-Induced Heart Failure
raw_front_matter.description: In a murine model of endotoxin-induced septic cardiomyopathy, β3-adrenergic receptor blockade—not stimulation—improves survival and cardiac function by suppressing iNOS-derived NO and preserving mito…
raw_front_matter.authors: Kawaguchi S, Okada M, Ijiri E, Koga D, Watanabe T, Hayashi K, Kashiwagi Y, Fujita S, Hasebe N
raw_front_matter.tags: sepsis, endotoxemia, hemorrhagic and septic shock, sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy, heart failure, β3-adrenergic receptor, nitric oxide, iNOS, mitochondria, fatty acid oxidation, cardiac metabolism, mouse model
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology - Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a murine model of endotoxin-induced septic cardiomyopathy, β3-adrenergic receptor blockade—not stimulation—improves survival and cardiac function by suppressing iNOS-derived NO and preserving mitochondrial and substrate metabolism, highlighting β3AR as a promising metabolic target in sepsis-related heart failure.
key_points: In a murine lipopolysaccharide (LPS) model of endotoxin-induced heart failure, pharmacologic β3-adrenergic receptor (β3AR) blockade markedly improved survival, while β3AR stimulation worsened mortality.
β3AR antagonism preserved left ventricular systolic function (LVFS, LVEF) during the acute phase of septic cardiomyopathy, whereas β3AR agonism exacerbated cardiac dysfunction and delayed recovery.
Myocardial ATP content and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS complex proteins and COX-1 signal) were maintained with β3AR blockade but were reduced with β3AR stimulation.
β3AR antagonism suppressed inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression and nitric oxide (NO) production in the heart, without altering eNOS, NF-κB p65, or major pro-inflammatory cytokines.

Genes regulating fatty acid oxidation (PPARα, CPT1), mitochondrial biogenesis (PGC-1α, ERRα), and glucose utilization (GLUT4, reduced PDK4) were upregulated by β3AR blockade, consistent with preserved energy metabolism.
β3AR agonism was associated with systemic hyperlipidemia and prominent accumulation of myocardial lipid droplets, indicating lipid handling/oxidation failure and lipotoxicity.

The data support β3AR as a mechanistic link between inflammatory signaling, NO overproduction, metabolic failure, and acute septic cardiodepression, and suggest β3AR antagonism as a potential therapeutic strategy in sepsis-related heart failure.

docs.title: Subendocardial Hemorrhages (SEH)

raw_front_matter.title: Subendocardial Hemorrhages (SEH)
raw_front_matter.description: Subendocardial hemorrhages are characteristic left-ventricular lesions arising rapidly in severe stress states—especially catecholamine-driven shock and intracranial catastrophe—that target the vulne…
raw_front_matter.authors: Stephan Seidl
raw_front_matter.tags: subendocardial hemorrhage, hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, forensic pathology, catecholamines, head injury, intracranial lesions, myocardial ischemia, resuscitation injury

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Subendocardial hemorrhages are characteristic left-ventricular lesions arising rapidly in severe stress states—especially catecholamine-driven shock and intracranial catastrophe—that target the vulnerable subendocardial conduction and papillary muscle zones, thereby predisposing to lethal arrhythmias and heart failure and carrying major forensic and clinical implications.
key_points: Subendocardial hemorrhages (SEH) are frequent autopsy findings in shock states, head injury, intoxications, and after cardiac trauma or resuscitation.
SEH predominantly involve the subendocardium of the left ventricle, especially the upper interventricular septum and papillary muscles, regions rich in conduction tissue.
Most evidence supports massive sympathetic discharge and catecholamine excess as central mechanisms, often combined with hypotension and subendocardial ischemia.
SEH and associated subendocardial necrosis can cause conduction disturbances, ventricular arrhythmias, papillary muscle dysfunction, and contribute to sudden death or heart failure.
Experimental data from animals (dogs, rats, miniature swine) and clinical observations link SEH to both endogenous and exogenous catecholamine surges.
SEH may appear within a few heartbeats and can occur even when coronary arteries are unobstructed, highlighting the vulnerability of the subendocardial zone.
Presence and severity of SEH may have implications for interpreting cause of death and for assessing suitability of trauma victims with head injury as heart donors.

raw_front_matter.title: Key Plasma Metabolites in Combat Casualties
raw_front_matter.description: In combat casualties with hemorrhagic traumatic injury, plasma succinate, malonate, hypoxanthine, and 5-aminolevulinate provide mechanistically meaningful biomarkers that equal or surpass lactate for…
raw_front_matter.authors: Elizabeth R. Lusczek, Sydne L. Muratore, Michael A. Dubick, Greg J. Beilman

raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In combat casualties with hemorrhagic traumatic injury, plasma succinate, malonate, hypoxanthine, and 5-aminolevulinate provide mechanistically meaningful biomarkers that equal or surpass lactate for early detection of trauma, injury severity, and mortality risk, offering a basis for improved triage and therapeutic targeting.
key_points: Plasma metabolomic profiles of combat-injured patients differ markedly from healthy controls and remain altered for at least 24 hours after injury.
Hypoxanthine and 5-aminolevulinate (5-ALA) discriminate injured from non-injured subjects and perform as well as or better than lactate for detecting trauma.
Succinate and malonate are the strongest metabolic discriminators of mortality among combat casualties.
Higher plasma succinate and hypoxanthine levels correlate with greater injury severity.
Identified metabolic biomarkers are mechanistically linked to the TCA cycle, oxidative stress/ATP depletion, and heme/iron metabolism.
These novel metabolites have equivalent or superior prognostic performance compared with lactate for trauma presence, severity, and mortality.
Findings support the feasibility of metabolomics-based tools to improve early triage and management of hemorrhagic combat casualties.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock (Cannon 2018)

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock (Cannon 2018)
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhagic shock is a globally important, rapidly lethal condition in which improved understanding of its complex pathobiology and aggressive, time-sensitive implementation of damage-control resusci…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jeremy W. Cannon
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hypovolemic shock, trauma, coagulopathy, damage-control resuscitation, massive transfusion, resuscitation, REBOA, critical care, cardiovascular failure
raw_front_matter.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock is a globally important, rapidly lethal condition in which improved understanding of its complex pathobiology and aggressive, time-sensitive implementation of damage-control resuscitation and definitive hemostasis—from prehospital care through the ICU—can substantially reduce preventable deaths.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock is a hypovolemic state driven by severe blood loss causing inadequate cellular oxygen delivery, rapid oxygen debt accumulation, and high early mortality if not quickly reversed.
Pathobiology involves cellular hypoxia and anaerobic metabolism, systemic inflammatory activation via DAMPs, endothelial glycocalyx shedding, and complex disturbances in coagulation and fibrinolysis.
Clinical coagulopathy in hemorrhagic shock reflects both trauma- and shock-induced mechanisms, along with iatrogenic contributors such as crystalloid over-resuscitation, hypothermia, and acidosis.

Prehospital priorities are early hemorrhage control (tourniquets, hemostatic dressings, pelvic binders), limited fluid resuscitation, hypothermia prevention, and rapid transport to a definitive care facility.

In-hospital management centers on rapid identification of bleeding sources, early activation of massive-transfusion protocols, plasma/platelet/RBC resuscitation in balanced ratios, and prompt definitive hemostasis.
Damage-control surgery and damage-control resuscitation, including minimized crystalloid use and goal-directed correction of coagulopathy, improve survival in severe hemorrhage.
Emerging technologies such as REBOA, viscoelastic testing, whole blood, and freeze-dried plasma aim to shorten time to hemostasis and improve outcomes in hemorrhagic shock.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock in the Dog II: Hemodynamics & Regional Flow

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock in the Dog II: Hemodynamics & Regional Flow
raw_front_matter.description: In a standardized canine hemorrhagic shock model, survival is determined less by regional blood flow during hypotension than by reperfusion responses of kidney, pancreas, and gut—particularly pancrea…
raw_front_matter.authors: M. H. Schoenberg, C. Lundberg, B. Gerdin, G. Smedegård, K. Messmer, K.-E. Arfors
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, dog model, central hemodynamics, regional blood flow, microspheres, microcirculation, intestinal ischemia, pancreatic ischemia, irreversible shock

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a standardized canine hemorrhagic shock model, survival is determined less by regional blood flow during hypotension than by reperfusion responses of kidney, pancreas, and gut—particularly pancreatic ischemia and intestinal ischemia–reperfusion injury that promote persistent acidosis, myocardial depression, and progressive circulatory collapse.
key_points: A standardized dog model of hemorrhagic shock (MAP 40 mmHg, 15% blood uptake before retransfusion) yields ~50% survival despite identical shock severity.
During hypotension, global and regional blood flows were largely similar in survivors and nonsurvivors, indicating that early flow patterns alone do not predict outcome.
Cerebral blood flow was relatively preserved, while myocardial, renal, pancreatic, and intestinal flows showed distinct adaptive or maladaptive patterns.
After retransfusion, nonsurvivors exhibited persistent metabolic and respiratory acidosis, lower arterial pressure and cardiac output, and abnormal regional reperfusion patterns.
Renal blood flow normalized in survivors but remained depressed in nonsurvivors after resuscitation.
Pancreatic flow was lower already before shock in nonsurvivors, suggesting pre-existing higher sympathetic tone and longer effective pancreatic ischemic exposure.
Reactive hyperemia and mucosal injury in ileum and colon, together with pancreatic and intestinal-derived factors, are implicated in progression to irreversible shock.

docs.title: Herzstoffwechsel im hämorrhagischen Schock

raw_front_matter.title: Herzstoffwechsel im hämorrhagischen Schock
raw_front_matter.description: In experimental dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock does not primarily impair the heart through a global or selectively subendocardial oxygen deficit but instead induces a distinctive transmural reorga…
raw_front_matter.authors: G. Zierott, P. Lundsgaard-Hansen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial metabolism, coronary oxygen supply, lactate-pyruvate ratio, glycolytic enzymes, transmural gradients, experimental dog model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In experimental dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock does not primarily impair the heart through a global or selectively subendocardial oxygen deficit but instead induces a distinctive transmural reorganization of myocardial enzyme activities consistent with functional disorganization, while additional insults such as hypoxemia, coronary disease, or severe hemodilution may still precipitate critical myocardial under-oxygenation.
key_points: In prolonged experimental hemorrhagic shock, a global myocardial oxygen deficit is unlikely to be the primary cause of cardiac dysfunction.
Coronary sinus oxygen saturation in shocked dogs generally remains above the critical level associated with anaerobic myocardial metabolism.
Myocardial lactate and lactate/pyruvate balance do not indicate a global or regionally confined oxygen deficit under the studied conditions.
Prolonged hemorrhagic shock produces characteristic transmural gradients in glycolytic enzyme activities within the left ventricle.
The enzymatic pattern is interpreted as a functional disorganization of the myocardium rather than straightforward hypoxic damage.
Additional risk factors such as arterial hypoxemia, coronary artery disease, or extreme hemodilution may render the myocardium vulnerable to critical under-oxygenation during shock.

raw_front_matter.title: Mortality After Emergent Trauma Laparotomy
raw_front_matter.description: In modern Level I trauma centers, hypotensive patients undergoing emergent trauma laparotomy still experience nearly 50% mortality driven largely by early hemorrhage, with little improvement compared…
raw_front_matter.authors: Harvin JA, Maxim T, Inaba K, Martinez-Aguilar MA, King DR, Choudhry AJ, Zielinski MD, Akinyeye S, Todd SR, Griffin RL, Kerby JD, Bailey JA, Livingston DH, Cunningham K, Stein DM, Cattin L, Bulger EM, Wilson A, Undurraga Perl VJ, Schreiber MA, Cherry-Bukowiec JR, Alam HB, Holcomb JB

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In modern Level I trauma centers, hypotensive patients undergoing emergent trauma laparotomy still experience nearly 50% mortality driven largely by early hemorrhage, with little improvement compared to two decades ago despite widespread adoption of contemporary damage control and resuscitation strategies.
key_points: Among 1,706 emergent trauma laparotomies at 12 US Level I centers (2012–2013), overall in-hospital mortality was 21%, and 46% for patients presenting hypotensive (SBP ≤90 mmHg).
Hemorrhage accounted for 60% of deaths overall and 65% of deaths in hypotensive patients, with most deaths occurring within the first 24 hours, frequently within 2 hours of arrival.
Despite widespread adoption of damage control strategies and modern resuscitation, mortality for hypotensive patients appears unchanged from the 40% reported in 1986–1999.
Damage control laparotomy was used in 38% of all patients and 62% of hypotensive patients, most commonly for intra-abdominal packing, planned second look, and hemodynamic instability.
Hypotensive patients had higher Injury Severity Scores, more severe chest and abdominal injuries, and more frequent need for major hemorrhage-control procedures.
Substantial inter-institutional variability in mortality was observed, both overall and in the hypotensive subgroup.
The findings highlight a persistent early hemorrhage-driven mortality burden in emergent trauma laparotomy despite contemporary trauma system advances.

docs.title: Myocardial Performance in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog & Primate)

raw_front_matter.title: Myocardial Performance in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog & Primate)
raw_front_matter.description: Under conditions of constant afterload, both dogs and primates exhibit an initial catecholamine-driven augmentation of myocardial performance after hemorrhagic shock that rapidly transitions to intri…
raw_front_matter.authors: Francis L. Abel, David P. Kessler
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial depression, cardiac failure, ventricular function, catecholamines, dog model, primate model, constant afterload

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Under conditions of constant afterload, both dogs and primates exhibit an initial catecholamine-driven augmentation of myocardial performance after hemorrhagic shock that rapidly transitions to intrinsic ventricular depression and high-filling-pressure cardiac failure, implicating shock-induced myocardial depressant factors rather than simple hypovolemia or catecholamine depletion.
key_points: In both dogs and monkeys, hemorrhagic shock followed by reinfusion produced an initial enhancement of myocardial performance under constant afterload, followed by a marked decline leading to cardiac failure.
Maintaining arterial pressure constant (80–100 mm Hg) allowed direct assessment of ventricular performance independent of afterload changes.
Dogs showed significantly elevated ventricular function 0–2 hours after reinfusion, then a progressive deterioration by 2–4 hours despite comparable or higher filling pressures.
Monkeys tolerated the procedure poorly, with survival limited to ~2 hours post-reinfusion and frequent development of frank cardiac failure.
Terminal plasma catecholamine levels in monkeys did not fall below or were only slightly below normal, arguing against simple catecholamine depletion as the mechanism of myocardial depression.
Control dogs exposed to the full surgical and pump protocol without hypotension showed no deterioration in ventricular function over 10 hours, implicating the hypotensive episode itself.

Findings support the presence of circulating myocardial depressant factor(s) contributing to late post-shock myocardial failure despite preserved coronary driving pressure and arterial oxygen content.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock in Dogs and Myocardial Lesions

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock in Dogs and Myocardial Lesions
raw_front_matter.description: In canine hemorrhagic shock, abnormal myocardial metabolism alone is insufficient to cause structural heart damage; instead, high heart rates during shock are essential for the development of charact…
raw_front_matter.authors: Hackel DB, Martin AM Jr, Spach MS, Sieker HO
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, myocardial lesions, cardiac failure, zonal lesions, tachycardia, myocardial metabolism, dog model, subendocardial hemorrhage

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, abnormal myocardial metabolism alone is insufficient to cause structural heart damage; instead, high heart rates during shock are essential for the development of characteristic zonal myocardial lesions and subendocardial hemorrhage that may drive irreversible cardiac failure.
key_points: Prolonged hemorrhagic shock in dogs produces characteristic microscopic "zonal" myocardial lesions, especially in the inner third of the ventricles and papillary muscles.
During hemorrhagic shock, myocardial oxygen extraction increases while lactate and pyruvate extraction fall markedly toward zero or negative values, indicating abnormal myocardial energy metabolism.
The presence and severity of myocardial zonal lesions depend strongly on heart rate during shock rather than on systemic hypotension or metabolic abnormalities alone.
Dogs with complete heart block and low ventricular rates are relatively protected from myocardial zonal lesions and subendocardial hemorrhage during shock.
Artificially increasing the heart rate in heart‑block dogs during shock restores the full pattern of myocardial lesions despite similar hemodynamic and metabolic changes.
Induced tachycardia in otherwise normal, non‑shocked dogs alters myocardial oxygen extraction but does not reproduce the metabolic derangements or extensive zonal lesions seen in shock.
Zonal lesions likely contribute cumulatively to myocardial dysfunction and the irreversibility of hemorrhagic shock–associated cardiac failure.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In hemorrhagic shock, preserving coronary perfusion markedly delays myocardial depression and death, but progressive late cardiac failure still develops due to shock-altered blood, highlighting distinct early ischemic and later humoral/metabolic mechanisms of cardiac injury.
key_points: The study isolated the effects of systemic hemorrhagic shock on the heart while maintaining normal coronary perfusion and cardiac output.
Dogs were placed in profound hemorrhagic shock, but the heart was kept non-ischemic using a custom aortic–atrium reservoir circuit.
Under these conditions, myocardial tension declined only slightly, while stroke work increased as heart rate slowed.
In contrast, control dogs whose hearts were also exposed to low perfusion showed rapid, marked myocardial depression and early death.
Findings support reduced coronary perfusion as a major early driver of myocardial failure in hemorrhagic shock.
A slower, progressive decline in function despite good coronary flow suggests additional late injury from shock-altered blood (acidosis, lactate, depressant factors).

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A Random Forest model using only arterial blood pressure waveform features outperformed pulse pressure variation in predicting fluid responsiveness in porcine models of circulatory shock, highlighting the potential of machine-learning–driven waveform analysis to enable more precise, automated fluid resuscitation.
key_points: The study developed a machine-learning fluid responsiveness algorithm (MLFRA) that predicts stroke volume response to fluid boluses using only arterial blood pressure waveforms.
Data came from 394 fluid challenges in 58 pigs subjected to hemorrhagic and distributive shock models with continuous blood pressure and cardiac output monitoring.
Fluid responsiveness was defined as a ≥15% increase in stroke volume after a fluid bolus.
Across 29 pig-level train/test splits, MLFRA achieved an average AUROC of ~0.82, outperforming pulse pressure variation (PPV) which had an AUROC of ~0.73.
MLFRA showed higher specificity, precision, and overall accuracy than PPV, with slightly lower sensitivity.
Calibration analysis showed that MLFRA’s predicted probabilities aligned well with observed fluid responsiveness across deciles of risk.
Results suggest that ML models based on passively collected arterial waveforms could support automated, precision-guided fluid resuscitation in shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: 13N-ammonia PET can reproducibly quantify resting and pharmacologically induced hyperemic myocardial blood flow in healthy humans—especially when resting flow is normalized to rate–pressure product—supporting its use for serial assessment of therapeutic and physiological effects on coronary perfusion and flow reserve.
key_points: 13N-ammonia PET can reproducibly quantify myocardial blood flow (MBF) at rest and during pharmacologic hyperemia in healthy humans.
Normalization of resting MBF to rate–pressure product (RPP) significantly improves reproducibility of measurements.
Hyperemic MBF during adenosine or dipyridamole stress shows relatively low interstudy variability and strong baseline–follow‑up correlation.
Reproducibility is adequate for serial PET studies assessing effects of therapies or physiological interventions on MBF and vasodilator reserve.
Regional variability is greater than global variability, particularly in the right coronary artery territory.

docs.title: LV Function & Tissue Hypoxia in Irreversible Shock

raw_front_matter.title: LV Function & Tissue Hypoxia in Irreversible Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In canine hemorrhagic and endotoxin shock, left ventricular contractile function is maintained or enhanced by sympathetic activation well beyond the point of so-called irreversible systemic oxygen de…
raw_front_matter.authors: Allan V. N. Goodyer
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endotoxin shock, left ventricular function, cardiac contractility, oxygen debt, beta-blockade, myocardial metabolism, lactate, pyruvate, dog model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic and endotoxin shock, left ventricular contractile function is maintained or enhanced by sympathetic activation well beyond the point of so-called irreversible systemic oxygen debt, with irreversibility arising primarily from peripheral rather than early cardiac failure, while true myocardial dysfunction appears only late after prolonged, severe shock.
key_points: In anesthetized dogs, left ventricular contractile capacity remained normal or increased during early and mid phases of both hemorrhagic and endotoxin shock, even beyond the point of "irreversible" systemic oxygen debt.
Irreversibility of hemorrhagic shock (as classically defined by an oxygen debt >140 ml/kg and failure to restore circulation with transfusion) occurred without primary early myocardial failure.

Sympathetic activation plays a central role in maintaining ventricular performance during shock; transient ventricular depression appeared when beta-adrenergic receptors were blocked with propranolol.

Metabolic indices (coronary lactate and pyruvate extraction, excess lactate, and lactate/pyruvate redox) showed no evidence of significant myocardial anoxia up to and at the point of critical oxygen debt.
Myocardial contractile failure appeared only late, at very high oxygen debts and prolonged shock duration, and was occasionally associated with myocardial lactate production.
Endotoxin shock similarly showed preserved or enhanced ventricular contractility despite reduced cardiac output and blood pressure, with lower systemic oxygen debts than hemorrhage.
Findings point to peripheral circulatory and tissue factors, rather than early intrinsic cardiac failure, as primary determinants of shock irreversibility.

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock Resuscitation and Posttraumatic MOF
raw_front_matter.description: The development of posttraumatic multiple organ failure after hemorrhagic shock is tightly linked to whole-body ischemia/reperfusion injury driven by aggressive normoxemic resuscitation, and emerging…
raw_front_matter.authors: Emmanuel E. Douzinas
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, multiple organ failure, trauma, resuscitation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, reactive oxygen species, cytokines, critical care

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: The development of posttraumatic multiple organ failure after hemorrhagic shock is tightly linked to whole-body ischemia/reperfusion injury driven by aggressive normoxemic resuscitation, and emerging evidence suggests that limited-volume, controlled-oxygen resuscitation may mitigate oxidative and inflammatory damage and alter the trajectory of MOF.
key_points: Posttraumatic multiple organ failure (MOF) remains a major cause of morbidity and late mortality after severe trauma.
Early MOF in trauma is driven by a systemic inflammatory response and can resolve rapidly under modern standard operating procedures (SOPs).
The classic “second hit” model—where nosocomial infection triggers late MOF—is challenged by data showing infections without subsequent late MOF.
Large-volume, rapid, normoxemic resuscitation may intensify whole-body ischemia/reperfusion injury via oxidative burst and inflammatory activation.
Limited-volume and controlled-oxygen (hypoxemic) resuscitation strategies attenuate oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and end-organ injury in experimental models.
Optimizing resuscitation requires matching oxygen delivery to cellular energetic status to avoid triggering excessive reactive oxygen species generation.
Developing “tolerance” to subsequent infectious insults may depend on minimizing early reperfusion-related tissue injury.

docs.title: Wearables + Compensatory Reserve in Trauma

raw_front_matter.title: Wearables + Compensatory Reserve in Trauma
raw_front_matter.description: Continuous machine-learning analysis of wearable-derived arterial waveforms as a Compensatory Reserve Measurement offers a more accurate, earlier indicator of impending circulatory collapse than trad…
raw_front_matter.authors: Victor A. Convertino, Steven G. Schauer, Erik K. Weitzel, Sylvain Cardin, Mark E. Stackle, Michael J. Talley, Michael N. Sawka, Omer T. Inan
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, trauma, critical care, compensatory reserve, CRM algorithm, wearable sensors, photoplethysmography, arterial waveform analysis, machine learning, hemodynamic monitoring, prehospital care, military medicine

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Continuous machine-learning analysis of wearable-derived arterial waveforms as a Compensatory Reserve Measurement offers a more accurate, earlier indicator of impending circulatory collapse than traditional vital signs, and can be operationalized via robust wearable sensor systems for trauma and critical care, especially in austere and prehospital environments.
key_points: Traditional vital signs (BP, HR, SpO2, etc.) change late and have poor specificity and accuracy for early detection of hemorrhagic shock and inadequate oxygen delivery.
Compensatory Reserve Measurement (CRM) uses machine-learning analysis of arterial waveform morphology to quantify remaining physiological reserve during central hypovolemia.

Across LBNP and controlled human hemorrhage models, CRM outperforms all standard vital signs and hemodynamic/metabolic markers in sensitivity, specificity, ROC AUC, and Youden’s J for predicting decompensated shock.
Noninvasive waveform sources suitable for CRM include PPG, tonometry, wearable ultrasound, and cardiogenic vibration signals; each has distinct tradeoffs for field and transport use.
Motion artifact, sensor placement, and signal quality are major challenges for field deployment and must be addressed through sensor design, auxiliary signals, and automated signal-quality indices.
Wearable CRM-capable systems could enable early triage, goal-directed resuscitation, and autonomous fluid management in civilian and military prolonged field care.
The CRM framework can be extended beyond hemorrhage to other low-flow states (sepsis, dehydration, heart failure) and performance monitoring under stress.

raw_front_matter.journal: European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of rapid, controlled hemorrhage, advanced analysis of arterial waveform morphomics—especially increasing variance in harmonic frequency and power—detected progressive hemorrhage severity when conventional blood pressure and heart rate measures had largely plateaued.
key_points: In a swine model of rapid, volume-controlled hemorrhage, hypotension developed early and plateaued after ~20% blood volume loss.
Most arterial waveform features changed in parallel with systolic and diastolic blood pressure and showed sigmoidal (non-linear) behavior with progressive hemorrhage.
The primary antegrade systolic wave (P1) was relatively preserved while reflective waves from the renal (P2) and iliac (P3) beds were progressively attenuated.
The P1:P3 amplitude ratio changed approximately linearly with blood loss but had only moderate explanatory power.
Short-time Fourier transform analysis showed increasing variance in frequency and power spectrum density of the first three harmonics during hemorrhage.
Variance measures of harmonic frequency and power (hemodynamic variability) demonstrated strong linear associations with progressive hemorrhage.
Waveform-derived variability metrics may discriminate between moderate and severe hemorrhage when conventional blood pressure measures have plateaued.
