raw_front_matter.authors: George C. Kramer, Jin-Oh Hahn, Ghazal ArabiDarrehDor, Ali Tivay, Ramin Bighamian, Chris Meador, Christopher Scully, Jose Salinas, and colleagues
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, burn shock, trauma, hemodynamics, cardiovascular modeling, volume kinetics, renal function, urinary output, closed-loop resuscitation, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, phenylephrine, swine model, sheep model, virtual patients, in silico trials
raw_front_matter.journal: US Army CDMRP Annual Report / Associated publications in Burns and American Control Conference

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Mechanistic multi-compartment models of burn and hemorrhagic shock, rigorously calibrated to animal and human data and compressed into realistic virtual patient populations, provide a credible foundation for designing and validating closed-loop fluid and drug resuscitation systems in trauma.
key_points: The project develops mechanistic mathematical models of hemorrhage, burn shock, and resuscitation specifically to design and test closed-loop fluid and drug resuscitation algorithms.

A multi-compartment burn model couples plasma–tissue volume kinetics, protein transport, and renal control of urinary output, including burn-induced perturbations to capillary permeability and tissue pressures.
A lumped-parameter hemorrhage model represents arterial/venous blood volumes, hematocrit, cardiac output, and systemic vascular resistance regulation under bleeding and fluid therapy.
Models are calibrated and validated using extensive large-animal datasets (swine for hemorrhage, sheep for burns) and human burn cohorts, with individualized parameter estimation.
The burn model accurately predicts plasma volume, urinary output, lymph flow, and albumin distributions with low normalized errors and physiologically plausible parameter values.

Analysis of hemorrhage data identified systematic hematocrit undershoot/rebound phenomena, likely related to delayed RBC mixing and dynamic f-cell ratio changes that are not captured by standard models.
Compressed latent parameterization enables generation of realistic virtual patients for hemodynamic simulations while avoiding physiologically implausible behaviors.

docs.title: The Bellamy Challenge and Next-Gen Battlefield Resuscitation

raw_front_matter.title: The Bellamy Challenge and Next-Gen Battlefield Resuscitation
raw_front_matter.description: The Bellamy challenge remains unmet because current battlefield fluids like HES neither safely protect the heart and endothelium nor provide optimal small-volume, permissive hypotensive resuscitation…
raw_front_matter.authors: Geoffrey P. Dobson, H. L. Letson, D. Tadaki
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, battlefield medicine, damage control resuscitation, hydroxyethyl starch, Hextend, permissive hypotension, hypertonic saline, ALM therapy, cardiac failure, endothelium, coagulopathy, trauma
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of the Royal Army Medical Corps

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: The Bellamy challenge remains unmet because current battlefield fluids like HES neither safely protect the heart and endothelium nor provide optimal small-volume, permissive hypotensive resuscitation, underscoring the need to develop and clinically validate novel physiologically targeted solutions such as hypertonic saline–ALM for early hemorrhagic shock care.
key_points: Up to half of combat trauma deaths and a large fraction of civilian trauma deaths are due to catastrophic hemorrhage, many of them potentially preventable.
Hydroxyethyl starch (HES) solutions such as Hextend were adopted for battlefield resuscitation because of logistical advantages, but accumulating evidence now questions their safety.
The authors argue that resuscitation research has underemphasized two critical pillars: rescuing and stabilizing the heart/brain and protecting the vascular endothelium.
Permissive hypotensive, small-volume resuscitation is favored over aggressive, large-volume crystalloid strategies that can worsen bleeding, inflammation, and coagulopathy.

An "ideal" battlefield fluid must buy biological time with minimal volume, support cardiac output and vascular tone, blunt inflammation and coagulopathy, and avoid a second "shock" from the resuscitation itself.

The adenosine–lidocaine–magnesium (ALM) approach, delivered in small-volume hypertonic saline, shows promising preclinical data in severe hemorrhagic shock models, including correction of acute coagulopathy and 100% survival in extreme blood loss in animals.

Despite promising animal data and concerns about HES safety, translation of novel fluids like hypertonic saline–ALM to human prehospital care remains incomplete, so the Bellamy challenge is still unresolved.

docs.title: Mitochondrial depolarization during cardiac ischemia

raw_front_matter.title: Mitochondrial depolarization during cardiac ischemia
raw_front_matter.description: Simultaneous mapping of mitochondrial and sarcolemmal potentials in rabbit and human hearts shows that ischemic mitochondrial depolarization is patchy, partly reversible, and associated with APD shor…
raw_front_matter.authors: Matthew S. Sulkin, Bas J. Boukens, Megan Tetlow, Sarah R. Gutbrod, Fu Siong Ng, Igor R. Efimov
raw_front_matter.tags: ischemia, mitochondria, mitochondrial membrane potential, electrophysiology, optical mapping, arrhythmia, ventricular fibrillation, rabbit heart, human heart, cardiac metabolism
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Simultaneous mapping of mitochondrial and sarcolemmal potentials in rabbit and human hearts shows that ischemic mitochondrial depolarization is patchy, partly reversible, and associated with APD shortening but not conduction slowing or focal arrhythmia origins, indicating that ΔΨm collapse is not directly responsible for ischemia-induced arrhythmias.
key_points: A dual-camera optical mapping system was developed to simultaneously measure mitochondrial inner membrane potential (ΔΨm) and sarcolemmal transmembrane potential (Vm) in intact hearts.
During ischemia, mitochondrial depolarization is sporadic, spatially heterogeneous, and often reversible, rather than a fast, unidirectional propagating wave.
Changes in ΔΨm occur asynchronously with ischemia-induced electrophysiological changes such as action potential duration (APD) shortening and conduction slowing.
Regions with greater mitochondrial depolarization are spatially associated with stronger APD shortening late in ischemia but not with conduction velocity slowing.
Transmural human ventricular recordings show regionally distinct, partly reversible ΔΨm changes during low-flow ischemia, with subepicardium depolarizing more than subendocardium.

The mitochondrial potential at focal arrhythmia origins does not differ from the rest of the myocardium, arguing against a direct causal link between local ΔΨm collapse and focal ischemic arrhythmias.
Apparent propagating waves of ΔΨm collapse seen in some prior wide-field studies can be artifacts caused by ischemia-induced changes in heart shape and motion.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In severely injured trauma patients, plasma succinate is a robust, rapidly changing marker of post-shock metabolic derangement that predicts mortality at least as well as, and possibly better than, lactate, making it a promising biomarker to guide resuscitation in hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Plasma succinate rises sharply after severe trauma and correlates strongly with mortality.
Succinate showed higher predictive accuracy for death than lactate in critically injured patients.
Deceased patients had markedly higher succinate levels than survivors, especially at the last available time point.
Normalization of early elevated succinate levels was associated with survival after resuscitation.
Succinate appears more specific for hemorrhagic/traumatic death than lactate in this cohort.
Rapid, high-throughput mass spectrometry methods can quantify succinate alongside lactate in clinical samples.

raw_front_matter.title: Stone Heart Syndrome
raw_front_matter.description: Stone heart syndrome is a rare but often fatal ischemic myocardial contracture driven by calcium overload and ATP depletion during severe cardiac stress, and emerging experimental data suggest that o…
raw_front_matter.authors: Summary of multiple sources including Cooley DA et al. (1972) and Li M et al. (2023)
raw_front_matter.tags: stone heart syndrome, ischemic myocardial contracture, cardiac surgery, ischemia-reperfusion injury, calcium overload, myocardial contracture, cardiogenic shock, heart failure, ECMO, myosin inhibitors
raw_front_matter.journal: Overview based on Wikipedia entry and cited primary literature (Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine; American Journal of Cardiology; Journal of Thoracic Disease; Scandinavian Cardiovascular Journal; Surgery)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Stone heart syndrome is a rare but often fatal ischemic myocardial contracture driven by calcium overload and ATP depletion during severe cardiac stress, and emerging experimental data suggest that optimized myocardial protection and myosin inhibition may offer a path to prevention in high-risk cardiac surgery.
key_points: Stone heart syndrome (ischemic myocardial contracture) is a rare, often fatal state of extreme myocardial rigidity that typically occurs during high‑risk cardiac surgery or after severe myocardial infarction.
The syndrome is driven by ischemia-induced calcium overload, ATP depletion, and hypercontractility of cardiomyocytes, producing a rigor-like, non-relaxing myocardium that cannot pump blood.
Clinically it presents with sudden hypotension, loss of effective pulse, respiratory distress, and precipitous collapse in cardiac output, often progressing to cardiac arrest.
Risk is highest in older patients with pre-existing heart disease, myocardial hypertrophy, or undergoing complex open-heart procedures.
Prevention focuses on minimizing ischemia-reperfusion injury and myocardial stress (e.g., hypothermia, optimized cardioplegia, calcium antagonism, beta-blockade, advanced surgical techniques).
Emergency management may require mechanical circulatory support such as ECMO; prognosis remains poor once full stone heart is established.

Experimental data in pig hearts suggest that cardioplegia plus rapid cooling and a myosin inhibitor (MYK-461/mavacamten) can prevent or reverse ischemic contracture and represent a promising preventive strategy.

raw_front_matter.authors: Pedro Cabrales, Amy G. Tsai, Marcos Intaglietta
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, microcirculation, blood viscosity, oxygen delivery, red blood cell transfusion, hemodilution, cardiac output, functional capillary density, methemoglobin

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Resuscitation from hemorrhagic shock in this model is limited more by loss of blood viscosity than by reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, with restoration of rheological properties alone markedly improving systemic and microvascular perfusion despite persistent anemia.
key_points: In a hamster hemorrhagic shock model, resuscitation with red blood cells (RBCs) restored systemic and microvascular function better than plasma alone.
RBC transfusion improved outcomes even when hemoglobin was rendered unable to carry oxygen (methemoglobin), implicating viscosity rather than oxygen capacity.
Blood viscosity after resuscitation was higher with RBCs than with plasma and closely associated with better mean arterial pressure, cardiac output, and organ perfusion.
Functional capillary density and microvascular flows were substantially better with RBC-based resuscitation than with plasma-only volume replacement.
Organ blood flow (especially to liver and spleen) and overall oxygen delivery were poorest after plasma resuscitation.
Restoration of blood rheological properties alone could correct the consequences of 50% hemorrhage despite significant anemia.
Findings suggest transfusion benefits in acute shock may derive largely from viscosity and shear-stress effects rather than immediate increases in oxygen transport.

raw_front_matter.title: Computational Modeling of Trauma, Hemorrhagic Shock, and Risk
raw_front_matter.description: By coupling a multiscale cardiovascular–microvascular bleeding model with data-driven machine learning predictors, this work shows how vascular geometry, shear-dependent hemostasis, hemodilution, and…
raw_front_matter.authors: Evangelos (Evan) Tsiklidis
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, hemorrhagic shock, hypovolemia, coagulopathy, trauma-induced coagulopathy, hemostasis, multiscale modeling, vascular networks, cardiovascular modeling, shock physiology, platelet function, machine learning, risk prediction, ICU outcomes, National Trauma Data Bank, MIMIC-III, gradient boosting, SHAP, von Willebrand factor, hemodilution, transcapillary refill
raw_front_matter.journal: PhD Dissertation, University of Pennsylvania (Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering)

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: By coupling a multiscale cardiovascular–microvascular bleeding model with data-driven machine learning predictors, this work shows how vascular geometry, shear-dependent hemostasis, hemodilution, and a small set of bedside variables jointly govern hemorrhagic shock trajectories and trauma mortality risk.
key_points: Develops a multiscale trauma model that couples a global cardiovascular (0D) system with a detailed branching vascular network to predict pressure-driven hemorrhage and hemostasis from specified wound geometries.
Shows that rapid local depressurization of upstream vasculature after vessel severing is a key, often overlooked regulator that limits bleeding in arterial/arteriolar injuries.

Demonstrates that shear rates at traumatic wound exits routinely reach ~10,000 s⁻¹, sufficient to unfold and multimerize von Willebrand factor, profoundly affecting clot mechanics under hemorrhagic conditions.

Quantifies how trauma-induced coagulopathy, modeled as loss of shear-dependent sealing, leads to catastrophic blood loss (>2 L in 2 h) versus near-complete hemostasis (<100 mL in ~2 min) in healthy clotting for comparable vascular injuries.

Identifies hemodilution from transcapillary refill (and reduced hematocrit) as a driver of increased blood loss and impaired seal rates, implicating it as a mechanistic contributor to trauma-induced coagulopathy.
Trains gradient boosting models on NTDB and MIMIC-III data to predict mortality and dynamic risk in trauma patients using small, clinically accessible feature sets, achieving ~92% ROC-AUC.

Uses partial dependence and SHAP analyses to reveal global and patient-specific determinants of trauma mortality risk, highlighting Glasgow Coma Score, age, and systolic blood pressure as dominant predictors.

raw_front_matter.authors: Arnold M. Seligman, Howard A. Frank, Jacob Fine
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, traumatic shock, liver perfusion, cross-circulation, irreversible shock, canine model, microcirculation, hepatic injury

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of hemorrhagic shock deemed irreversible to transfusion, prolonged cross‑circulation that specifically perfuses the injured liver with donor arterial blood reliably restores peripheral vascular tone and survival, demonstrating that hepatic integrity is pivotal to reversing advanced shock.
key_points: Dogs in advanced hemorrhagic shock deemed irreversible to blood transfusion can be rescued by cross‑circulation perfusion of the liver with arterial blood from a healthy donor.
Effective treatment requires directing donor blood to the recipient's liver via the splenic vein; similar cross‑circulation via a systemic vein (femoral) fails to reverse shock.
Liver‑targeted perfusion leads to recovery of peripheral vascular tone, cessation of progressive blood pooling (“taking‑up”), and restoration of systemic blood pressure.
Metabolic markers measured in arterial blood (lactate, glucose, amino nitrogen, urea) do not correlate with ultimate survival, despite changes during cross‑circulation.
The data support a central, causative role for hepatic cellular integrity in the pathogenesis and reversibility of advanced hemorrhagic shock.
The benefit of cross‑circulation is attributed specifically to adequate arterial blood flow to the injured liver rather than general systemic support from the donor.

raw_front_matter.authors: Jean-Philippe Tessier, Bernhard Thurner, Eberhard Jüngling, Andreas Luckhoff, Yvan Fischer
raw_front_matter.tags: sepsis, endotoxemia, lipopolysaccharide, cardiac metabolism, glycolysis, glycogen, insulin resistance, ketone bodies, citrate, sphingomyelin-ceramide pathway, cyclooxygenase-2, thromboxane A2, rat heart, Langendorff preparation, cardiac dysfunction

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Endotoxin-induced systemic inflammation impairs cardiac glucose metabolism primarily by amplifying ketone/fatty-acid–mediated inhibition of glycolysis and blocking insulin-driven glycogen synthesis via a ceramide–COX‑2–thromboxane A2 pathway, changes that may exacerbate septic cardiodepression under metabolic stress.
key_points: Systemic inflammation induced by endotoxin (LPS) produces marked cardiac contractile depression and selective defects in myocardial glucose handling.
With glucose as the sole substrate, overall cardiac glycolysis and glucose uptake are largely preserved 6 hours after LPS, despite clear mechanical failure.
In the presence of the ketone body β-hydroxybutyrate, LPS markedly potentiates inhibition of cardiac glycolysis, associated with increased myocardial citrate.
LPS treatment strongly blunts insulin-stimulated net glycogen synthesis in the heart, indicating profound myocardial insulin resistance at the level of glycogen metabolism.
Pharmacologic inhibition of ceramidase, COX‑2, or thromboxane A2 receptors prevents the LPS-induced potentiation of β-hydroxybutyrate’s anti-glycolytic effect.
The data implicate a sphingomyelin–ceramide–COX‑2–thromboxane A2 signaling cascade in mediating inflammation-related impairment of cardiac glycolysis.

Reduced glycolytic capacity under high alternative-fuel availability may contribute to contractile dysfunction during sepsis or endotoxemia, particularly when energy demand or oxygen limitation increase reliance on glycolysis.

docs.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Post-Traumatic Cardiac Dysfunction

raw_front_matter.title: Molecular Mechanisms of Post-Traumatic Cardiac Dysfunction
raw_front_matter.description: Post-traumatic cardiac dysfunction arises from a complex interplay of direct injury, systemic inflammation, DAMP and complement activation, catecholamine excess, structural remodeling, and metabolic…
raw_front_matter.authors: Birte Weber, Ina Lackner, Florian Gebhard, Theodore Miclau, Miriam Kalbitz
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, multiple trauma, blunt cardiac injury, post-traumatic cardiomyopathy, inflammation, complement system, DAMPs, cardiac metabolism, traumatic brain injury, burn injury, fracture, stress cardiomyopathy

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Post-traumatic cardiac dysfunction arises from a complex interplay of direct injury, systemic inflammation, DAMP and complement activation, catecholamine excess, structural remodeling, and metabolic disturbance, making the heart a central but often under-recognized target in trauma and hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Post-traumatic cardiac dysfunction is common after blunt chest trauma and multiple trauma and is a major determinant of morbidity and mortality.
Cardiac injury after trauma includes systolic and diastolic dysfunction, arrhythmias, valve insufficiency, structural remodeling, and metabolic derangements.

Biomarkers such as troponins and heart-type fatty acid binding protein (HFABP) are useful for detecting myocardial damage but have important limitations, especially in multi-trauma and renal dysfunction.
Inflammation, DAMPs (e.g., HMGB1, extracellular histones, midkine) and complement activation (C3a, C5a) are central molecular drivers of post-traumatic cardiac injury.
Secondary/indirect cardiac damage occurs after non-cardiac trauma (TBI, burns, fractures, psychosocial stress) largely via catecholamine excess and systemic inflammation.
Trauma induces alterations in connexins and Z-disc proteins and disrupts calcium handling and mitochondrial function, promoting arrhythmias and contractile failure.
Experimental therapies targeting HMGB1/histones, complement, cytokines, or downstream signaling pathways show promise but lack robust clinical validation.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model, hemorrhagic hypotension induces characteristic, often initially reversible myocardial zonal lesions and focal hypercontraction necrosis driven by combined hypoxia and shock-related metabolic/catecholamine disturbances, offering a structural basis for low cardiac output in hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Hemorrhagic hypotension in dogs produces characteristic myocardial lesions, especially focal subendocardial hemorrhages and mural "zonal lesions" around intercalated discs.
Systemic metabolic acidosis with markedly increased lactate occurs during the hypotensive period and correlates with lesion severity and extent.
Many myocardial alterations appear potentially reversible acutely, but in severe/prolonged hypotension they progress to irreversible hypercontraction-type necrosis with rapid calcification.
Subendocardial changes are mainly hypoxic, whereas mural zonal lesions likely reflect combined effects of hypoxia, catecholamine surge, and shock-related metabolic/toxic factors.
The structural disorganization of myofilaments in affected cells can impair contractility and provides a morphologic basis for low cardiac output in hemorrhagic shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Mild-to-moderate hypothermia directly enhances ventricular myocyte contractility before and after ischemia by augmenting intracellular Ca2+ transients and Ca2+ sensitivity, thereby mitigating ischemia-induced contractile depression despite some slowing of relaxation.
key_points: Cooling ventricular myocytes from 37°C down to 30°C progressively increased contractility under normal perfusion.
A 10-minute ischemic insult markedly depressed myocyte contractility, but hypothermic reperfusion significantly mitigated this impairment.
Hypothermia enhanced intracellular Ca2+ transients both before and after ischemia.
Myocyte sensitivity to extracellular Ca2+ was greater at 30°C than at 37°C, with a steeper contractile response to increasing Ca2+ concentrations.
The inotropic benefits of hypothermia were accompanied by slower contraction and relaxation kinetics (prolonged time-to-peak shortening and relengthening).
Temperature reduction and myocyte contractility were strongly correlated in both non-ischemic and post-ischemic conditions.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A standardized 48-hour porcine polytrauma model with two levels of hemorrhagic shock reliably induces clinically relevant shock and organ dysfunction while maintaining survivability, providing a robust platform to evaluate post-traumatic intensive care therapies.
key_points: The authors established a reproducible 48-hour porcine polytrauma model combining chest, abdominal, and musculoskeletal injuries with controlled hemorrhagic shock.
Two shock severities were compared: ~44% blood loss with MAP ~30 mmHg for 90 min (group L) vs. ~50% blood loss with MAP ~25 mmHg for 120 min (group H).
Both trauma groups developed metabolic acidosis, elevated lactate, and organ injury markers consistent with severe shock, while all control animals remained stable.
More severe hemorrhagic shock increased cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) frequency and indicators of organ damage but did not significantly change overall 48 h mortality.
The model permitted standardized ICU-style management (ventilation, fluids, vasopressors, emergency interventions) over 48 h without blood transfusion.
Physiologic responses and complication profile (shock, coagulopathy trends, organ dysfunction, need for CPR, respiratory failure) paralleled key features of human polytrauma.
The protocol is proposed as a platform to test post-traumatic therapeutic strategies during the intensive care phase.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In conscious animals, severe hemorrhage triggers an abrupt, opioid-mediated withdrawal of sympathetic drive that precipitates rapid hypotension, indicating that decompensated hemorrhagic shock arises from an active central switch rather than passive failure of compensatory mechanisms.
key_points: Early hemorrhage elicits a strong sympathetically mediated compensatory response that maintains arterial pressure via increased heart rate and vascular resistance.
Beyond a critical degree of blood loss (~20% of total blood volume), animals abruptly transition to marked hypotension with loss of sympathetic drive.
The transition to the decompensated phase appears to be an active centrally mediated process rather than simple exhaustion of sympathetic neurotransmitter stores.
Plasma norepinephrine levels and overall sympathetic activity fall in parallel with the onset of hypotension in severe hemorrhage.
Naloxone attenuates the hypotensive response to severe blood loss and restores sympathetic activation, implicating endogenous opioids.
Endogenous opioid signaling is a major contributor to the withdrawal of sympathetic tone during the decompensated phase of hemorrhagic shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Absolute quantitation of plasma lactate and succinate in hemorrhagic shock demonstrates that larger mammals—especially non-human primates—more faithfully reproduce human metabolic derangements than rodents, supporting their preferential use for translational shock research.
key_points: Absolute plasma levels of lactate and succinate in hemorrhagic shock differ substantially between rodents, swine, non-human primates, and humans.
Rats exhibit markedly higher baseline and post-shock lactate and succinate than larger mammals and humans, despite comparable target MAP.
Macaques show baseline and post-shock metabolite levels most similar to humans; pigs are intermediate.
Post-shock lactate and succinate levels in pigs (lactate) and macaques (succinate) are directly comparable to those in severely injured patients.
Shock-to-baseline ratios for lactate and succinate resemble human patterns in pigs and macaques but not in rats.
Lactate and succinate concentrations are tightly and positively correlated across all species, with exponential succinate rises at higher lactate levels.
Findings support preferential use of larger mammals over rodents for modeling metabolic derangements of severe hemorrhage.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: During dobutamine-induced demand ischemia with fixed coronary stenosis, metabolic stress and glycolytic activity shift predominantly to the better-perfused subepicardium, and inhibition of glycolysis leads to global energetic compromise and myocardial edema despite maintained or elevated flow in outer layers.
key_points: Dobutamine-induced high cardiac work with coronary stenosis produces transmural metabolic abnormalities that are most pronounced in the subepicardium, despite higher blood flow there.
During pure dobutamine stimulation without flow limitation, high-energy phosphate levels are preserved and no clear transmural energetic gradient develops.
With coronary stenosis plus dobutamine and 2-deoxyglucose infusion, PCr/ATP falls and Pi/PCr rises across the wall, indicating global energetic compromise in the ischemic zone.
2-deoxyglucose-6-phosphate accumulates in all layers but is highest in the subepicardium, indicating greater glycolytic flux or limitation of reducing-equivalent transfer there.
Myocardial oxygen consumption and lactate uptake increase with dobutamine alone and return toward baseline when stenosis and glycolytic inhibition are imposed.
The ischemic region develops significant myocardial edema when glycolysis is inhibited during demand ischemia, implicating glycolytic ATP in maintaining ion and volume homeostasis.

docs.title: Internal State of the Severely Wounded on Forward Hospital Entry

raw_front_matter.title: Internal State of the Severely Wounded on Forward Hospital Entry
raw_front_matter.description: In severely wounded WWII soldiers arriving at forward hospitals, shock was a largely reversible, quantitatively hemorrhage‑driven state—often with massive but survivable blood and hemoglobin losses—a…
raw_front_matter.authors: Beecher HK, Simeone FA, Burnett CH, Shapiro SL, Sullivan ER, Mallory TB
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, battlefield trauma, blood loss, cardiovascular physiology, resuscitation, liver function, renal function, electrolytes, WWII, forward surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In severely wounded WWII soldiers arriving at forward hospitals, shock was a largely reversible, quantitatively hemorrhage‑driven state—often with massive but survivable blood and hemoglobin losses—accompanied by early but graded metabolic and organ dysfunction, best treated by prompt hemostasis and whole blood transfusion rather than delayed attempts at full physiologic “normalization.”
key_points: In severely wounded WWII soldiers arriving at the most forward hospital, the dominant driver of shock was quantitative blood loss rather than mysterious or irreversible cardiovascular failure.

Young, otherwise healthy casualties often tolerated loss of 50–75% of calculated blood volume and large hemoglobin deficits, yet could still survive if hemorrhage was controlled and whole blood was given.

Hemoconcentration was uncommon; most shocked patients showed hemodilution (hematocrit falling far more than plasma proteins), reflecting rapid recruitment of protein‑rich interstitial fluid into the circulation.
Severity of clinical shock correlated closely with extent of extremity injuries involving major bone fractures or traumatic amputations, which produced the largest blood and hemoglobin losses.

Biochemical disturbances on arrival included rising nonprotein nitrogen, creatinine, phosphorus, magnesium, lactic acidosis, hyperglycemia, and depressed bromsulfalein excretion, particularly in more severe shock.

Electrocardiograms were usually normal even in severe shock; overt primary myocardial failure was rarely demonstrable, and most cases of poor response to transfusion were explainable by ongoing hemorrhage or other complications.

The authors argue that so‑called “irreversible shock” was essentially not observed at the bedside when hemorrhage and correctable lesions were aggressively treated with timely whole blood transfusion.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, myocardium, glycolysis, enzymes, transmural gradients, dog model, oxygen supply, catecholamines, metabolic remodeling

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In prolonged hemorrhagic hypotension in dogs, left ventricular glycolytic enzymes become globally upregulated and transmural gradients are disrupted without evidence of myocardial oxygen deficit, implicating structural, catecholamine- or toxin-mediated injury rather than hypoxia as the main driver of cardiac failure.
key_points: In anesthetized, ventilated dogs subjected to prolonged hemorrhagic hypotension, left ventricular glycolytic enzyme activities and transmural gradients were analyzed.
Global myocardial oxygen deficit could not be demonstrated despite severe systemic acidosis and advanced shock.
Most glycolytic enzymes showed increased activities after shock, while pyruvate kinase, LDH, and α-HB-DH did not follow this pattern.
Transmural activity gradients present in normal myocardium were partially lost, altered, or reversed after shock, especially in the inner (subendocardial) layer.
The data argue against myocardial hypoxia as the primary cause of cardiac deterioration in this shock model.
Findings are more consistent with functional consequences of structural derangements linked to catecholamine excess or circulating toxic factors.
Enzyme distribution patterns are proposed as sensitive indicators of subcellular myocardial injury in shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, characteristic reversible myocardial "zonal" lesions arise primarily from mechanically stressful conditions—tachycardia, reduced ventricular volume, and heightened beta-adrenergic drive—acting on the hypovolemic heart, suggesting that protecting cardiac rate and loading conditions is crucial to limiting shock-induced myocardial damage.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in dogs produces characteristic, potentially reversible myocardial "zonal" lesions, distinct from overt subendocardial hemorrhage and necrosis.
Zonal lesions represent localized bands of extreme sarcomere contraction at intercalated discs with mitochondrial redistribution, especially in subendocardial and papillary regions.
Tachycardia and reduced ventricular volumes during shock are critical for lesion formation; eliminating tachycardia or blocking beta-adrenergic stimulation markedly reduces myocardial damage.

Myocardial metabolic abnormalities (increased O2 extraction, reduced or negative pyruvate and lactate extraction) occur even when lesions are prevented, indicating dissociation of metabolism from structural injury.

Experiments with separated cardiopulmonary and systemic circulations show that "heart shock" (cardiac hypovolemia/hypotension) is far more important than systemic shock alone in producing zonal lesions.
Sympathetic stimulation alone does not create zonal lesions in normovolemic hearts but amplifies damage when combined with cardiac shock conditions.
Mechanical factors—small ventricular volume, vigorous rapid contraction, and subendocardial stress—are implicated as key drivers of zonal lesion formation.

docs.title: Can Outflow Obstruction Be Induced in the Normal LV?

raw_front_matter.title: Can Outflow Obstruction Be Induced in the Normal LV?
raw_front_matter.description: In normal dog hearts, the large left ventricular–aortic pressure gradients reported during hemorrhagic shock and inotropic stimulation largely reflect catheter-position artifacts rather than true out…
raw_front_matter.authors: Andrew G. Morrow, John S. Vasko, R. Peter Henney, Robert K. Brawley
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, left ventricular outflow tract, cardiac catheterization, measurement artifact, inotropic drugs, isoproterenol, experimental cardiology, dog model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In normal dog hearts, the large left ventricular–aortic pressure gradients reported during hemorrhagic shock and inotropic stimulation largely reflect catheter-position artifacts rather than true outflow obstruction, challenging prior interpretations of cardiac function in experimental shock.
key_points: Previous dog studies suggested that hemorrhagic shock and inotropic stimulation could induce left ventricular outflow obstruction in structurally normal hearts.
This study reproduced ventriculo-aortic gradients when LV pressure was measured via retrograde aortic or transatrial catheters.
Simultaneous apical LV measurements showed that many of these gradients were artifactual rather than true outflow obstruction.
Catheter position within small muscular recesses of the LV wall could sequester the catheter tip and record non-cavitary (intramyocardial) pressures.
Controlled venous return and isoproterenol greatly increased the likelihood of recording spurious gradients from non-apical LV catheters.
Hemodynamic responses to premature beats were inconsistent with true dynamic muscular subaortic stenosis.
The authors conclude there is no valid hemodynamic evidence that true outflow obstruction can be experimentally induced in the normal dog left ventricle under these conditions.

raw_front_matter.authors: Donald B. Hackel, Walter T. Goodale

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In intact dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock causes intense sympathetic-driven myocardial stress with preserved coronary flow but high oxygen extraction, severely impaired pyruvate utilization, and frequent subendocardial injury, resulting in profoundly inefficient cardiac performance and contributing to circulatory failure.
key_points: In intact anesthetized dogs, prolonged hemorrhagic shock profoundly alters myocardial carbohydrate metabolism, especially pyruvate handling.
Despite severe systemic hypotension and low cardiac output, coronary blood flow and total myocardial oxygen consumption are largely maintained.
Myocardial oxygen extraction increases to very high levels, indicating relative myocardial hypoxia during shock.
Mechanical efficiency of the left ventricle falls markedly, with high oxygen use for very little external work.
Subendocardial hemorrhage or necrosis of the left ventricle develops in a subset of animals after severe or prolonged shock.
The observed pattern is attributed to intense sympathetic activation and elevated circulating catecholamines rather than anesthesia or catheterization alone.

raw_front_matter.title: Respiratory Changes in Haemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a canine model of severe haemorrhagic shock, respiratory failure and lethal organ damage were prevented only when extracellular osmolarity and metabolic acidosis were actively corrected—most effec…
raw_front_matter.authors: D.K. Brooks; W.G. Williams; R.W. Manley; P. Whiteman
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, respiratory failure, osmolarity, acid–base balance, dog model, hypertonic resuscitation, ventilation, cardiorespiratory physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a canine model of severe haemorrhagic shock, respiratory failure and lethal organ damage were prevented only when extracellular osmolarity and metabolic acidosis were actively corrected—most effectively with hypertonic sodium bicarbonate or hypertonic saline—underscoring that successful shock resuscitation must target biochemical as well as haemodynamic stability.
key_points: In severe haemorrhagic shock, dogs develop profound metabolic acidosis, falling plasma osmolarity, hyperventilation, and ultimately respiratory failure and death if untreated.
Spontaneous ventilation under hydroxydione anaesthesia shows marked hyperventilation during shock, yet oxygenation can still fail when biochemical derangements progress.
Infusion of hypertonic sodium bicarbonate or hypertonic saline during controlled hypotension prevented respiratory failure and tissue necrosis and allowed consistent survival.
Hypertonic glucose alone was less reliable: despite marked hyperglycaemia, many animals still developed haemorrhagic bowel necrosis and multi-organ infarction.
Isotonic saline, isotonic bicarbonate, or isotonic glucose infusions failed to prevent organ damage and death, indicating that hypertonicity, not simple volume expansion, is critical.
Falling plasma osmolarity and bicarbonate concentration preceded the onset of respiratory failure, suggesting these as early biochemical markers of impending irreversibility.
Intercurrent infection/endotoxin-like states abolished the protective effect of hypertonic solutions, emphasizing the interaction of shock with sepsis.

docs.title: Cardiac vs Peripheral Failure in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog)

raw_front_matter.title: Cardiac vs Peripheral Failure in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog)
raw_front_matter.description: In canine hemorrhagic shock under closed-chest conditions, the immediate post-transfusion decline in cardiac output is usually driven by progressive loss of effective circulating volume and cardiac u…
raw_front_matter.authors: Carl F. Rothe, Ewald E. Selkurt
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac output, cardiac failure, peripheral circulatory failure, hypovolemia, dog model, pulmonary hypertension, venous pressure, fluid shifts, massive transfusion

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock under closed-chest conditions, the immediate post-transfusion decline in cardiac output is usually driven by progressive loss of effective circulating volume and cardiac underfilling, with overt myocardial failure emerging primarily after more extreme or prolonged hypotension.
key_points: In most cases of severe hemorrhagic hypotension in dogs, the immediate post-transfusion decline in cardiac output is due more to reduced cardiac filling than to primary myocardial failure.

Central venous and atrial filling pressures often fail to return to control values after blood reinfusion, indicating significant loss of effective circulating volume and/or increased vascular capacity.

Clear myocardial depression can develop, but typically only after extreme oligemic hypotension or when moderate hypotension is combined with prior cardiac damage or a second prolonged hypotensive period.
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises markedly during prolonged hypotension, producing pulmonary hypertension even while systemic pressure and cardiac output remain low.
Progressive hemoconcentration (increased hematocrit and plasma proteins) during late hypotension and after transfusion suggests substantial net fluid loss from the intravascular space.
Massive repeated transfusions can maintain filling pressures and substantially prolong survival, yet do not fully prevent later myocardial depression or fatal gastrointestinal and systemic injury.
The data challenge the view that acute primary cardiac failure is the dominant cause of irreversibility in hemorrhagic shock under closed-chest conditions with initially normal hearts.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a goat model of hemorrhagic hypovolemia with limb ischemia-reperfusion, substituting pyruvate for lactate in Ringer’s resuscitation fluid markedly reduced myocardial oxidative stress, preserved creatine kinase and high-energy phosphate status, and durably stabilized cardiac electrical activity compared with standard lactated Ringer’s.
key_points: In a goat model of hemorrhagic hypovolemia plus hindlimb ischemia-reperfusion, replacing lactate with pyruvate in Ringer’s solution markedly stabilized cardiac electrical activity.
Pyruvate-enriched Ringer’s reduced myocardial oxidative stress, preserved creatine kinase activity, and enhanced myocardial energy state compared with standard lactated Ringer’s.
Anti-arrhythmic and metabolic benefits of pyruvate resuscitation persisted for at least 3.5 hours after cessation of infusion.
Pyruvate resuscitation improved mean arterial pressure recovery more than lactated Ringer’s during active resuscitation.

Lactated Ringer’s resuscitation was associated with increased QTc variability, elevated myocardial 8-isoprostane, and reduced creatine kinase activity, indicating a more pro-arrhythmic, energy-compromised state.

docs.title: Hemorrhage, Cardiac Output & Organ Flow in Rats

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhage, Cardiac Output & Organ Flow in Rats
raw_front_matter.description: In anesthetized rats, moderate hemorrhage triggers a selective redistribution of a greatly reduced cardiac output to brain, adrenals, heart, and lungs via vasoconstriction in muscle, kidney, skin, an…
raw_front_matter.authors: Leo A. Sapirstein, Elizabeth H. Sapirstein, Antonie Bredemeyer
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac output, organ blood flow, vascular resistance, rat model, regional perfusion, shock pathophysiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized rats, moderate hemorrhage triggers a selective redistribution of a greatly reduced cardiac output to brain, adrenals, heart, and lungs via vasoconstriction in muscle, kidney, skin, and splanchnic beds, but with severe hemorrhage these compensatory patterns break down—no organ maintains flow, renal/splanchnic resistances surge, skeletal muscle ceases to adequately constrict, and systemic vascular collapse ensues.
key_points: Moderate (10 ml/kg) and severe (21–25 ml/kg) hemorrhage in anesthetized rats cause large falls in cardiac output and arterial pressure, with compensatory rises in total peripheral resistance.

In moderate hemorrhage, blood flow is preferentially redistributed to brain and adrenal glands, partially preserving myocardial and pulmonary perfusion at the expense of skeletal muscle, kidney, skin, and splanchnic organs.
In severe hemorrhage, no organ maintains normal flow; brain, heart, lungs, and adrenals still receive a larger fraction of the cardiac output but in absolute terms are markedly underperfused.
Renal, splanchnic, and cutaneous vascular resistances rise substantially with hemorrhage, especially at severe levels, whereas cerebral and adrenal resistances fall (vasodilation).
Skeletal muscle (“carcass”) shows strong vasoconstriction in moderate hemorrhage but fails to further increase resistance in severe hemorrhage and instead receives an excessive flow fraction.
The authors suggest that failure of skeletal muscle vasoconstriction in severe hemorrhage may contribute to loss of compensatory redistribution and final vascular collapse.
Methodologically, organ flow fractions were quantified by indicator fractionation (Rb-86 and iodo-131 antipyrine), focusing on functional (exchanging) rather than shunt flow.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhagic shock is driven less by a single toxin than by complex interactions among volume loss, hormonally mediated volume restitution, cellular depolarization with Na/K ATPase inhibition, and sys…
raw_front_matter.authors: Donald S. Gann, William R. Drucker
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, circulatory shock, trauma, cardiac failure, resuscitation, coagulopathy, shock index, Na/K ATPase, damage control resuscitation, hypertonic saline, hypothermia, multiple organ failure, bacterial translocation
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhagic shock is driven less by a single toxin than by complex interactions among volume loss, hormonally mediated volume restitution, cellular depolarization with Na/K ATPase inhibition, and systemic inflammation, and its optimal management now centers on controlled, blood-product–focused resuscitation strategies that aim to restore perfusion while limiting coagulopathy and organ failure.
key_points: The concept of a single "shock toxin" was replaced by a volume-loss and peripheral perfusion failure model, making fluid resuscitation the central therapy for circulatory shock.

Hemorrhagic shock triggers complex metabolic and hormonal responses aimed at restoring blood volume and energy homeostasis, with cortisol‑dependent glucose mobilization and extracellular hyperosmolality playing key roles.
Restitution of blood volume after hemorrhage is biphasic and fails beyond ~25–26% blood loss, coinciding with widespread cellular depolarization and Na/K ATPase inhibition.

A circulating low–molecular-weight Na/K ATPase inhibitor and protective purine nucleosides (e.g., adenosine, inosine) may constitute a shared mechanistic pathway across hemorrhagic and septic shock and contribute to cardiogenic failure.

Modern resuscitation emphasizes judicious, often delayed or hypotensive fluid strategies plus early plasma-rich transfusion (damage control resuscitation) to limit coagulopathy, acidosis, and organ failure.
Hypertonic saline, controlled hypothermia, and careful choice of crystalloids/colloids can modulate immune activation, cerebral physiology, and microvascular injury in severe shock.

Bacterial translocation, systemic inflammation, and impaired oxygen utilization underlie multiple-organ failure after trauma, but the exact contribution of gut-derived sepsis in humans remains unresolved.

raw_front_matter.authors: Yuma Morishita, Shoko Tamura, Kentaro Mochizuki, Yoshinori Harada, Tetsuro Takamatsu, Hajime Hosoi, Hideo Tanaka

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In perfused rat hearts, irreversible sarcolemmal permeabilisation drives agonal Ca2+ waves and contraction bands, but contraction bands arise not directly from the waves themselves, rather from Ca2+-overload–driven calpain activation and ATP-dependent cross-bridge interactions characteristic of reperfusion-type injury.
key_points: Irreversible sarcolemmal permeabilisation with saponin in perfused rat hearts triggers extremely high-frequency "agonal" Ca2+ waves and contraction band formation in cardiomyocytes.
Agonal Ca2+ waves slow and eventually disappear over ~10 minutes as Ca2+ overload and mitochondrial depolarisation progress, culminating in high static cytosolic Ca2+.
Contraction bands form despite pharmacologic suppression of Ca2+ waves from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, indicating they are not a direct consequence of the waves themselves.
Mechanical arrest of myocytes with 2,3-butanedione monoxime (BDM) completely prevents contraction band formation, despite persistence or enhancement of Ca2+ waves.
Calpain inhibition partially preserves Z-disc α-actinin structure but does not prevent actin aggregation, implicating Ca2+-dependent proteolysis in structural disintegration.
ATP depletion via mitochondrial uncoupling with FCCP abolishes both Ca2+ waves and contraction bands, highlighting the requirement for preserved energetics and cross-bridge cycling.
The model supports a mechanistic link between Ca2+ overload, calpain activation, and active cross-bridge interactions in generating contraction band necrosis typical of reperfused myocardium.

docs.title: Matrix Oxidative Stress Drives Post-ischemic Mitochondrial Instability

raw_front_matter.title: Matrix Oxidative Stress Drives Post-ischemic Mitochondrial Instability
raw_front_matter.description: In reperfused ventricular myocytes, bursts of oxidative stress confined to the mitochondrial matrix, rather than Ca2+ overload, drive transient mitochondrial membrane potential oscillations that dest…
raw_front_matter.authors: Soroosh Solhjoo, Ting Liu, Agnieszka Sidor, Dong I. Lee, Brian O’Rourke, Charles Steenbergen
raw_front_matter.tags: ischemia-reperfusion, ventricular myocyte, mitochondria, oxidative stress, reactive oxygen species, mitochondrial membrane potential, calcium handling, arrhythmias, heart failure mechanisms

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In reperfused ventricular myocytes, bursts of oxidative stress confined to the mitochondrial matrix, rather than Ca2+ overload, drive transient mitochondrial membrane potential oscillations that destabilize energetics and promote arrhythmogenic substrate, while later Ca2+-dependent mPTP opening mediates irreversible depolarization and cell death.
key_points: Post-ischemic mitochondrial inner membrane potential (ΔΨ) in cardiomyocytes exhibits unstable oscillations that are tightly linked to bursts of oxidative stress within the mitochondrial matrix.
Cytosolic redox changes do not track individual ΔΨ oscillations, whereas mitochondrial matrix glutathione oxidation (GSSG:GSH) does.
Pharmacologic enhancement of glutathione buffering (GSH monoethyl ester) and acute inhibition of complex IV with cyanide both suppress ΔΨ oscillations during reperfusion.
ΔΨ oscillations occur largely independently of changes in mitochondrial or cytosolic Ca2+, including under Ca2+-depleted conditions.
Sustained ΔΨ collapse is preceded by mitochondrial and cytosolic Ca2+ overload and progressive whole-cell oxidative stress, consistent with opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore.
Transient, ROS-driven mitochondrial instability is proposed to involve a Ca2+-independent inner membrane anion channel, distinct from classical mPTP-mediated depolarization.
IR-induced mitochondrial instability and oxidative stress create an energetically and electrophysiologically heterogeneous substrate that promotes post-ischemic arrhythmias.

raw_front_matter.tags: pulseless electrical activity, sudden cardiac arrest, nonshockable rhythms, cardiac arrest epidemiology, cardiac mechanics, resuscitation, heart failure, ischemia-reperfusion injury, inflammation and cytokines, hypothermia, vasopressors, mechanical CPR, NHLBI workshop, research priorities

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Pulseless electrical activity is an increasingly prevalent, mechanistically heterogeneous, and highly lethal form of cardiac arrest for which current care is largely nonspecific, prompting an NHLBI-endorsed roadmap to develop better models, mechanistic understanding, monitoring, and targeted resuscitation strategies over the next decade.
key_points: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) is increasingly common as an initial rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest while ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia (VF/VT) are declining.

The workshop defines PEA as organized cardiac electrical activity without a palpable pulse in an unconscious patient, excluding ventricular tachyarrhythmias and transient low-flow states like vasovagal syncope.
PEA has markedly worse survival than VT/VF but recent data suggest modest improvement with advances in resuscitation practice.
Primary PEA (initial rhythm) and secondary PEA (postshock or due to noncardiac causes) likely involve different mechanisms and prognoses.
Potential mechanisms include acute contractile failure from ischemia, metabolic stress, immune/inflammatory activation, drug effects, and advanced structural heart disease.
Current management is nonspecific (high-quality CPR, vasopressors, search for reversible causes), and evidence for many pharmacologic or device interventions is limited or mixed.
The NHLBI group proposes a research roadmap emphasizing better models, mechanistic studies, real-time hemodynamic monitoring, and early testing of PEA-specific interventions.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of complete proximal SMA occlusion, maintaining MAP >90 mmHg with norepinephrine increased gastroduodenal collateral flow and significantly delayed progression to irreversible small bowel ischemia without evidence of harm, supporting induced hypertension as a potential temporizing strategy before revascularization.
key_points: Acute proximal SMA occlusion causes rapid, lethal intestinal ischemia and needs temporizing strategies while awaiting revascularization.
In swine with complete proximal SMA occlusion, inducing and maintaining MAP >90 mmHg with norepinephrine increased GDA collateral flow.
A MAP push prolonged time to both clinically threatened bowel and histologically irreversible ischemia compared with conventional therapy.
Norepinephrine did not worsen bowel survival despite its known splanchnic vasoconstrictive effects at the microvascular level.
The intrinsic, transient MAP rise after SMA occlusion in untreated animals suggests a compensatory physiologic response to mesenteric malperfusion.
These data support short-term induced hypertension as a potential bridge to definitive treatment in proximal SMA occlusion.

docs.title: Complication-Associated Mortality After Trauma

raw_front_matter.title: Complication-Associated Mortality After Trauma
raw_front_matter.description: In a large population of trauma patients, empirically defined post-admission ICD-9 complications—especially a small set of acute cardiopulmonary, renal, neurologic, and septic events—accounted for ro…
raw_front_matter.authors: Turner Osler, Laurent G. Glance, David W. Hosmer
raw_front_matter.tags: trauma, complications, mortality, ICD-9, risk adjustment, critical care, epidemiology, quality of care

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a large population of trauma patients, empirically defined post-admission ICD-9 complications—especially a small set of acute cardiopulmonary, renal, neurologic, and septic events—accounted for roughly two-thirds of deaths, highlighting both the central role and practical limits of complication prevention in improving trauma survival.
key_points: Using a large California trauma cohort, the authors empirically defined complications as ICD-9 diagnoses not present on admission that significantly increased mortality.
Eighty-two distinct ICD-9 codes met criteria as mortality-related complications, with odds ratios ranging from ~1 to >40.
About 24% of trauma patients experienced at least one complication; each additional complication increased mortality by roughly 8%.
An estimated 64% of all trauma deaths were statistically attributable to these complications, representing an upper bound on potentially preventable mortality.
A small subset of complications (25 codes) accounted for 80% of complication-attributable deaths, with acute respiratory failure alone responsible for 9%.
Hospitals varied substantially (≈37–65%) in the proportion of deaths attributable to complications, even after risk adjustment.
Classic low-lethality surgical complications (e.g., wound infections) did not appear as mortality drivers, underscoring that high-mortality complications are largely acute physiologic failures.

docs.title: Modern Treatment of Shock Based on Physiologic Principles

raw_front_matter.title: Modern Treatment of Shock Based on Physiologic Principles
raw_front_matter.description: Across diverse experimental and clinical settings, irreversible shock emerges from prolonged catecholamine-driven visceral vasoconstriction and intestinal injury, is worsened by vasopressors, and can…
raw_front_matter.authors: Richard C. Lillehei, Jerrold K. Longerbeam, Jack H. Bloch, William G. Manax
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endotoxin shock, septic shock, cardiovascular physiology, microcirculation, catecholamines, intestinal ischemia, vasopressors, adrenergic blockade, corticosteroids, phenoxybenzamine, hydrocortisone, experimental shock models, Gram-negative sepsis

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Across diverse experimental and clinical settings, irreversible shock emerges from prolonged catecholamine-driven visceral vasoconstriction and intestinal injury, is worsened by vasopressors, and can be prevented or reversed most effectively by combining aggressive volume replacement with physiologic modulation of peripheral vascular tone using adrenergic blockade or high-dose corticosteroids plus definitive infection control.
key_points: Irreversible shock from hemorrhage, endotoxin, epinephrine, or mesenteric ischemia shares a common hemodynamic mechanism: severe, prolonged visceral vasoconstriction leading to intestinal mucosal necrosis and loss of circulating volume.

Endogenous catecholamines and exogenous vasopressors worsen visceral ischemia; adrenergic blockade (phenoxybenzamine) or high-dose corticosteroids (hydrocortisone) combined with aggressive volume replacement markedly improve survival in dogs.
Plasma volume loss, rising hematocrit, and increasing plasma free hemoglobin after an initial hypotensive insult are reliable harbingers of the irreversible phase of shock.

Experimental perfusion of the superior mesenteric artery during hemorrhagic shock preserves gut integrity and prevents the development of irreversible shock, whereas perfusion of other organs does not.
Bowel bacterial load and intravascular coagulation appear secondary: gut sterilization or high-dose heparin do not prevent lethal shock, and bacteremia is uncommon and low-grade in these models.

In clinical Gram-negative or postoperative shock, the authors advocate hydrocortisone, generous plasma/blood replacement guided by central venous pressure, appropriate antibiotics, and surgical source control, while avoiding vasopressors whenever possible.
Pre-emptive modulation of vascular reactivity (e.g., phenoxybenzamine before high-risk procedures such as cardiopulmonary bypass) is proposed to prevent shock-related organ injury.

docs.title: Hemorrhagic-Hypotension Shock in Locally Anesthetized Dogs

raw_front_matter.title: Hemorrhagic-Hypotension Shock in Locally Anesthetized Dogs
raw_front_matter.description: In dogs under only local anesthesia, prolonged controlled hemorrhagic hypotension produces irreversible, fatal shock more readily than in barbitalized animals, with a distinct pressure-decline sign m…
raw_front_matter.authors: Harold C. Wiggers, Raymond C. Ingraham, James Dille
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, hypotension, cardiovascular failure, microcirculation, intestinal injury, experimental shock model, dog model, anesthesia and shock

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In dogs under only local anesthesia, prolonged controlled hemorrhagic hypotension produces irreversible, fatal shock more readily than in barbitalized animals, with a distinct pressure-decline sign marking irreversibility and a 40–45 mmHg, 60-min protocol defining a useful threshold for survivable but severe hemorrhagic insult.
key_points: Standardized hemorrhagic-hypotension protocols that cause irreversible shock in barbital-anesthetized dogs are even more lethal in dogs under only local anesthesia.
Locally anesthetized dogs showed 100% mortality with combined moderate and drastic hypotension, despite sometimes shorter low-pressure exposure than in earlier barbitalized series.
A modified, milder protocol (40–45 mmHg for 90 min) produced irreversible shock in ~77% of locally anesthetized dogs and allowed some survivals.
A further abbreviated hypotension period (40–45 mmHg for 60 min) was usually survivable, with 9 of 10 dogs recovering after full blood reinfusion.
A critical sign of irreversible shock was a persistent spontaneous decline of arterial pressure below the set hypotensive level despite repeated blood/saline infusions.
Severe intestinal and cardiac capillary damage with hemorrhage and plasma leakage occurred after prolonged hypotension, particularly after reinfusion raised blood pressure.
Barbital anesthesia, when properly administered, does not appear to facilitate the onset of hemorrhagic shock and may not make dogs more vulnerable than local anesthesia alone.
