raw_front_matter.title: Endogenous Opiates and NE Release in Hemorrhage
raw_front_matter.description: In conscious rabbits, progressive hemorrhage triggers an endogenous opioid–mediated limit on sympathetic norepinephrine release that contributes to hypotension, and naloxone reverses this by enhancin…
raw_front_matter.authors: James C. Schadt, Ronald R. Gaddis
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, endogenous opioids, naloxone, sympathetic nervous system, norepinephrine, epinephrine, rabbit model, vascular resistance
raw_front_matter.journal: Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In conscious rabbits, progressive hemorrhage triggers an endogenous opioid–mediated limit on sympathetic norepinephrine release that contributes to hypotension, and naloxone reverses this by enhancing norepinephrine-dependent vascular resistance without altering adrenal epinephrine output.
key_points: In conscious rabbits, moderate hemorrhage increased plasma norepinephrine and heart rate without affecting blood pressure or epinephrine.
With progression to severe hypotensive hemorrhage, plasma epinephrine rose sharply while norepinephrine plateaued rather than increasing further.
Naloxone administered during hemorrhagic hypotension restored arterial pressure and further increased plasma norepinephrine but did not alter epinephrine.
Findings support a role for endogenous opiate peptides in limiting sympathetic norepinephrine release during acute hemorrhage.
The naloxone-induced pressor response appears to be mediated primarily via increased vascular resistance through sympathetic activation.
Adrenal catecholamine content in rabbits is overwhelmingly epinephrine, so plasma epinephrine reflected adrenal output whereas norepinephrine reflected sympathetic nerve release.

docs.title: Acidosis, Ischemia, and Ca2+ Alternans in Intact Rat Heart

raw_front_matter.title: Acidosis, Ischemia, and Ca2+ Alternans in Intact Rat Heart
raw_front_matter.description: Global acidosis and low-flow ischemia in intact rat hearts similarly disturb Ca2+ cycling—raising diastolic Ca2+, prolonging Ca2+ transient decay, and thereby shifting both cellular Ca2+ transient al…
raw_front_matter.authors: Sunil Kapur, J. Andrew Wasserstrom, James E. Kelly, Alan H. Kadish, Gary L. Aistrup
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, ischemia, acidosis, ventricular arrhythmias, calcium handling, T-wave alternans, repolarization alternans, calcium transient alternans, Langendorff heart, confocal microscopy, rat heart
raw_front_matter.journal: American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Global acidosis and low-flow ischemia in intact rat hearts similarly disturb Ca2+ cycling—raising diastolic Ca2+, prolonging Ca2+ transient decay, and thereby shifting both cellular Ca2+ transient alternans and repolarization alternans to slower heart rates—implicating acidosis-driven Ca2+ instability as a key, preconditionable mechanism of ischemia-induced ventricular arrhythmogenesis.
key_points: Global acidosis and low-flow global ischemia similarly raise diastolic Ca2+, prolong Ca2+ transients, and reduce relative transient amplitude in intact rat hearts.
Both acidosis and ischemia shift the onset of Ca2+ transient alternans and repolarization alternans to slower heart rates, increasing alternans susceptibility.
Spatially concordant and discordant Ca2+ transient alternans (including subcellular alternans within single myocytes) are promoted by acidosis and ischemia.
The cycle length shifts for Ca2+ transient alternans and repolarization alternans are nearly identical, supporting a causal link between Ca2+ instability and ECG alternans.
Repeated episodes of either acidosis or ischemia abolish the increased alternans susceptibility, mimicking ischemic preconditioning.
Prolonged Ca2+ transient decay, rather than altered rise time, is most strongly associated with increased alternans vulnerability.
Findings implicate acidosis-driven Ca2+ cycling changes as a major contributor to ischemia-induced proarrhythmic states and a potential target for modulation.

docs.title: Factors Determining Coronary Blood Flow

raw_front_matter.title: Factors Determining Coronary Blood Flow
raw_front_matter.description: In an isolated dog heart–lung preparation, coronary sinus measurements show that coronary blood flow is chiefly governed by aortic pressure and powerful local metabolic vasodilation (enhanced by adre…
raw_front_matter.authors: Josef Markwalder, Ernest H. Starling
raw_front_matter.tags: coronary circulation, cardiac physiology, heart-lung preparation, arterial pressure, adrenaline, carbon dioxide, asphyxia, metabolic regulation, coronary sinus catheterization, experimental dog model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In an isolated dog heart–lung preparation, coronary sinus measurements show that coronary blood flow is chiefly governed by aortic pressure and powerful local metabolic vasodilation (enhanced by adrenaline, CO₂, and asphyxia), such that a large and variable fraction of ventricular output is devoted to perfusing the myocardium itself.
key_points: Morawitz's coronary sinus catheterization method can be adapted to an isolated heart–lung preparation in dogs, allowing direct measurement of coronary venous outflow under tightly controlled conditions.
Only about three-fifths of total coronary flow is collected from the coronary sinus, but sinus flow changes reliably track overall coronary circulation.
Coronary blood flow is highly dependent on aortic (arterial) pressure, and low arterial pressures in heart–lung preparations result in markedly inadequate perfusion of the myocardium.
Adrenaline (adrenalin) consistently dilates coronary vessels and accelerates coronary flow, with no demonstrable vasoconstriction even at very small doses when an effect is present.
Raised blood CO₂ tension causes coronary vasodilation and cardiac dilation, with reduced systemic output but increased coronary flow as the heart fails.
Asphyxia and accumulation of non-volatile cardiac metabolites are powerful stimuli for coronary vasodilation, often driving maximal coronary flow just before pump failure.
Metabolic products generated by the contracting myocardium appear to provide a local feedback mechanism that augments its own blood supply when its functional demands increase.

docs.title: Postmortem Metabolite Changes in Rabbit Myocardium

raw_front_matter.title: Postmortem Metabolite Changes in Rabbit Myocardium
raw_front_matter.description: In rabbit hearts subjected to warm ischemia, the preservation of high‑energy phosphates and key metabolites—and thus potential for organ resuscitation—depends strongly on the mode of cardiac arrest,…
raw_front_matter.authors: W. Schilt, A. Büchler, A. Lemeunier, P. Lundsgaard-Hansen
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac arrest, myocardial metabolism, ischemia, warm ischemia, ATP, ADP, AMP, lactate, glycogen, animal model, rabbit heart, organ preservation, transplantation

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In rabbit hearts subjected to warm ischemia, the preservation of high‑energy phosphates and key metabolites—and thus potential for organ resuscitation—depends strongly on the mode of cardiac arrest, with exsanguination being metabolically most favorable and asphyxia most detrimental.
key_points: The study quantified high‑energy phosphates and key metabolites in rabbit myocardium after death, comparing three modes of cardiac arrest: asphyxia, exsanguination, and ether overdose.
Warm ischemia times of 15, 30, and 60 minutes were examined post‑cardiac arrest in 63 rabbit hearts.
Asphyxial cardiac arrest led to the most rapid depletion of ATP, ADP, glycogen, and glucose, indicating the greatest energy store consumption.
Cardiac arrest by controlled exsanguination best preserved myocardial energy stores and substrates across ischemia intervals.
Ether overdose produced intermediate patterns of high‑energy phosphate and metabolite depletion.
AMP levels rose markedly during ischemia, particularly after exsanguination, and remained high even after 60 minutes of warm ischemia.
The authors relate AMP preservation and overall energy status to the potential for successful resuscitation and use of cadaver organs for transplantation.

docs.title: Modeling Hypoxia and Hypothermia in Ventricular Myocytes

raw_front_matter.title: Modeling Hypoxia and Hypothermia in Ventricular Myocytes
raw_front_matter.description: A refined ToR-ORd–based ventricular model with realistic β-adrenergic kinetics and targeted temperature-dependent channel modulation reveals that hypoxia becomes proarrhythmic only in the presence of…
raw_front_matter.authors: Jakub Tomek, John Green, Alan Garfinkel
raw_front_matter.tags: computational cardiology, ventricular myocyte, hypoxia, hypothermia, beta-adrenergic signaling, early afterdepolarizations, ionic currents, calcium handling, arrhythmia mechanisms
raw_front_matter.journal: Unpublished internal modelling report / email summary

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: A refined ToR-ORd–based ventricular model with realistic β-adrenergic kinetics and targeted temperature-dependent channel modulation reveals that hypoxia becomes proarrhythmic only in the presence of sympathetic activation and that properly modeled hypothermia increases both Ca transients and arrhythmia vulnerability in a mechanistically consistent way.
key_points: Refines a ToR-ORd–based ventricular cell model to incorporate mechanistic effects of hypoxia and hypothermia on key ionic currents and Ca handling.
Shows that hypoxia alone is not strongly proarrhythmic, but becomes proarrhythmic when combined with beta-adrenergic (β-AR) activation.
Implements realistic β-AR signaling kinetics, revealing a transient window of heightened vulnerability to early afterdepolarizations (EADs).
Demonstrates that simple Q10-based temperature scaling fails to reproduce experimental hypothermia phenotypes, especially Ca transient augmentation.
Introduces targeted temperature-dependent modifications (ICaL, IKr, INaL, NCX) that yield larger Ca transients and prolonged APD at lower temperatures.
Provides a mechanistic framework to link transient β-AR surges (e.g., sleep apnea) and therapeutic/mild hypothermia to arrhythmia risk and contractility changes.

docs.title: AV PCO₂ and pH as Hypoxia Markers in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: AV PCO₂ and pH as Hypoxia Markers in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In anesthetized dogs with progressive hemorrhage, abrupt widening of arteriovenous PCO₂ and pH gradients identifies the same critical fall in oxygen delivery that triggers VO₂ decline and lactate ris…
raw_front_matter.authors: Philippe Van der Linden, Isabelle Rausin, Annie Deltell, Yamina Bekrar, Eric Gilbart, Jan Bakker, Jean-Louis Vincent
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, tissue hypoxia, oxygen delivery, cardiac output, arteriovenous gradients, carbon dioxide, pH, lactate, animal model, perioperative monitoring

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In anesthetized dogs with progressive hemorrhage, abrupt widening of arteriovenous PCO₂ and pH gradients identifies the same critical fall in oxygen delivery that triggers VO₂ decline and lactate rise, supporting these gradients as simple global indicators of tissue hypoxia in hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: In anesthetized, mechanically ventilated dogs undergoing progressive hemorrhage, tissue hypoxia emerged when oxygen delivery (DO₂) fell below a critical value of ~9 mL·min⁻¹·kg⁻¹.
At this critical DO₂, oxygen uptake (VO₂) became supply-dependent and blood lactate rose abruptly, indicating onset of anaerobic metabolism.
Arteriovenous gradients for PCO₂ (AV PCO₂) and pH (AV pH) widened sharply at the same critical DO₂ as VO₂ and lactate.
Critical DO₂ values derived from AV PCO₂, AV pH, and lactate were statistically indistinguishable from those derived from VO₂.
AV PCO₂ and AV pH correlated strongly with blood lactate during hemorrhage (r = 0.84 and 0.78, respectively).
End-tidal CO₂ (PETCO₂) fell abruptly and alveolar dead space increased when DO₂ passed below the critical threshold.
The study supports AV PCO₂ and AV pH as simple, global indicators of tissue hypoxia during hemorrhagic low-flow states.

docs.title: Total Vascular Resistance in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog)

raw_front_matter.title: Total Vascular Resistance in Hemorrhagic Shock (Dog)
raw_front_matter.description: In canine hemorrhagic shock, total peripheral resistance initially rises and later partially wanes but does not collapse; the ultimate fatal fall in blood pressure is chiefly due to persistent depres…
raw_front_matter.authors: Carl F. Rothe, James R. Love, Ewald E. Selkurt
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, total peripheral resistance, cardiac output, vascular resistance, dog model, irreversible shock, hemodynamics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, total peripheral resistance initially rises and later partially wanes but does not collapse; the ultimate fatal fall in blood pressure is chiefly due to persistent depression of cardiac output rather than generalized loss of vascular tone.
key_points: Rapid hemorrhage to 50 mm Hg in anesthetized dogs causes a profound drop in cardiac output but a marked increase in total peripheral resistance (TPR).

During prolonged oligemic hypotension, TPR progressively declines from its early high level, accompanied by falls in heart and respiratory rates, suggesting partial failure of neurogenic vasoconstrictor control.
After reinfusion of shed blood, arterial pressure usually remains below control largely because cardiac output remains depressed, while TPR returns to around control values.
During the post-transfusion deterioration phase, TPR typically rises as blood pressure falls, indicating compensatory vasoconstriction rather than vascular collapse.
Terminally, with very low arterial pressures (<~60 mm Hg), TPR may fall in some animals, but this represents a late and secondary event.
Across the shock course, failure of cardiac output, not generalized loss of peripheral resistance, is the primary cause of circulatory collapse and irreversibility.

docs.title: Cardiac Metabolism in Hemorrhagic Shock

raw_front_matter.title: Cardiac Metabolism in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In experimental canine hemorrhagic shock with preserved systemic oxygen transport, post-shock cardiac failure reflects functional and structural disorganization of myocardium—likely driven by catecho…
raw_front_matter.authors: Lundsgaard-Hansen P, Meyer C, Riedwyl H, Zierott G
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac metabolism, myocardial oxygen supply, lactate/pyruvate, glycolytic enzymes, catecholamines, subendocardial injury, dog model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In experimental canine hemorrhagic shock with preserved systemic oxygen transport, post-shock cardiac failure reflects functional and structural disorganization of myocardium—likely driven by catecholamines and circulating toxins—rather than a primary or hidden myocardial oxygen deficit.
key_points: In anesthetized dogs subjected to prolonged hemorrhagic shock, myocardial dysfunction after retransfusion is not primarily explained by an oxygen supply deficit when ventilation, hemoglobin, and coronaries are normal.
Coronary sinus oxygen saturation remains above the critical threshold for myocardial anaerobiosis at shock blood pressures around 40 mmHg, indicating preserved global oxygenation of the heart.
Myocardial lactate/pyruvate handling during shock generally shows continued lactate uptake and pyruvate output, inconsistent with significant cardiac anaerobic metabolism.

Transmural and apico-basal gradients of glycolytic enzyme activities in the left ventricle are altered after shock, especially in subendocardial layers, suggesting functional and structural disorganization rather than uniform hypoxia.
The data do not support a hidden subendocardial oxygen deficit as the main cause of post-shock cardiac failure under otherwise normal oxygen transport conditions.

Excessive catecholamine activity and/or circulating toxic factors from hypoxic peripheral tissues are proposed as key contributors to myocardial structural damage and metabolic disorganization in prolonged hemorrhagic shock.
Adequate ventilation, avoidance of marked hemodilution, and caution in coronary disease are emphasized to prevent myocardial hypoxia during shock resuscitation.

docs.title: pH and Cardiac Contractile Function

raw_front_matter.title: pH and Cardiac Contractile Function
raw_front_matter.description: Acidosis exerts a complex, predominantly negative effect on cardiac contractility by depressing myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity and SR/L‑type Ca2+ handling while simultaneously altering intracellular Na…
raw_front_matter.authors: C. H. Orchard; J. C. Kentish
raw_front_matter.tags: acidosis, intracellular pH, cardiac muscle, excitation–contraction coupling, intracellular calcium, sarcoplasmic reticulum, myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity, ion transport, mitochondria

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Acidosis exerts a complex, predominantly negative effect on cardiac contractility by depressing myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity and SR/L‑type Ca2+ handling while simultaneously altering intracellular Na+, Ca2+, and metabolism, so that the observed force results from a shifting balance between impaired responsiveness and partially compensatory increases in [Ca2+]i.
key_points: Acidosis depresses cardiac contractility despite often increasing the systolic Ca2+ transient and diastolic [Ca2+].
pH changes affect essentially every step of excitation–contraction coupling: action potential, Ca2+ influx, SR uptake/release, cytosolic buffering, and myofilament function.
Intracellular pH (pHi), more than extracellular pH, is the dominant determinant of the inotropic response to acidosis.
Acidosis inhibits L‑type Ca2+ current, Na+–Ca2+ exchange, SR Ca2+ uptake, and gap‑junction conductance, while activating Na+–H+ exchange when pHi falls.
Myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity and maximum force are both reduced by acidosis, largely via reduced Ca2+ binding to troponin C and direct effects on cross‑bridges.
The net force during acidosis reflects a balance between negative effects on Ca2+ delivery and myofilament function and partially compensatory rises in [Ca2+]i.
Acidosis alters arrhythmia vulnerability via effects on spontaneous SR Ca2+ release, transient inward current, and conduction.

raw_front_matter.title: Stellate Ganglion Blockade in Hemorrhagic Shock–Induced Gut Injury
raw_front_matter.description: In a rat model of hemorrhagic shock, stellate ganglion blockade markedly improves survival and intestinal barrier integrity by reducing gut permeability and preserving epithelial cytoskeletal and jun…

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of hemorrhagic shock, stellate ganglion blockade markedly improves survival and intestinal barrier integrity by reducing gut permeability and preserving epithelial cytoskeletal and junctional proteins, highlighting sympathetic modulation as a promising therapeutic strategy.
key_points: Stellate ganglion blockade (SGB) significantly improved 96-hour survival in rats subjected to hemorrhagic shock and resuscitation.
Hemorrhagic shock caused marked structural damage to intestinal villi and loss of mucus coverage, which were attenuated by SGB.
Shock increased intestinal permeability (FD4 flux, plasma D-lactate), and SGB largely normalized these permeability markers.
Shock reduced expression of key cytoskeletal and junctional proteins (F-actin, Claudin-1, E-cadherin) in intestinal tissue; SGB reversed these decreases.
Findings support a role of sympathetic overactivation in gut barrier failure during hemorrhagic shock and identify SGB as a potential modulatory intervention.

docs.title: Overview of Animal Hemorrhagic Shock Models

raw_front_matter.title: Overview of Animal Hemorrhagic Shock Models
raw_front_matter.description: Animal models of hemorrhagic shock—fixed-pressure, fixed-volume, and uncontrolled—each offer distinct trade-offs between experimental control and clinical relevance, and their thoughtful selection an…
raw_front_matter.authors: J. L. Lomas-Niera, Mario Perl, Chun-Shiang Chung, Alfred Ayala
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, animal models, fixed-pressure hemorrhage, fixed-volume hemorrhage, uncontrolled hemorrhage, resuscitation, trauma, immunology, sex differences, aging

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Animal models of hemorrhagic shock—fixed-pressure, fixed-volume, and uncontrolled—each offer distinct trade-offs between experimental control and clinical relevance, and their thoughtful selection and standardization are crucial for elucidating mechanisms of organ failure and immune dysfunction and for translating therapies to trauma patients.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock is a leading cause of early death after trauma and contributes to later multiple organ failure and infection.
Three main experimental hemorrhage paradigms are used: fixed-pressure, fixed-volume, and uncontrolled hemorrhage, each with distinct advantages and limitations.
Controlled (especially fixed-pressure) models maximize reproducibility but are less clinically realistic than uncontrolled hemorrhage models.
Anesthesia, resuscitation strategies, and heparin use are major confounders that can significantly alter cardiovascular and immune responses in these models.
Sex, hormonal status, and age strongly influence immune function and survival after trauma-hemorrhage in animals.
Species choice (mouse, rat, larger animals, primates) reflects trade-offs between clinical comparability, genetic tools, reagent availability, and cost.
Optimizing and better understanding these models is critical to improving translation of preclinical hemorrhagic shock research to clinical therapies.

docs.title: ED POCUS in Cardiac Arrest

raw_front_matter.title: ED POCUS in Cardiac Arrest
raw_front_matter.description: In ED cardiac arrests with PEA or asystole, point-of-care ultrasound–defined cardiac activity is the strongest predictor of survival and helps identify reversible causes amenable to targeted interven…
raw_front_matter.authors: Gaspari R, Weekes A, Adhikari S, Noble VE, Nomura JT, Theodoro D, Woo M, Atkinson P, Blehar D, Brown SM, Caffery T, Douglass E, Fraser J, Haines C, Lam S, Lanspa M, Lewis M, Liebmann O, Limkakeng A, Lopez F, Platz E, Mendoza M, Minnigan H, Moore C, Novik J, Rang L, Scruggs W, Raio C

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In ED cardiac arrests with PEA or asystole, point-of-care ultrasound–defined cardiac activity is the strongest predictor of survival and helps identify reversible causes amenable to targeted interventions, while absence of activity—especially in asystole—signals very poor but not zero likelihood of meaningful survival.
key_points: In a 20-center prospective cohort of 793 non-traumatic PEA/asystole arrests, sonographic cardiac activity in the ED was the strongest predictor of survival at all time points.
Patients with cardiac activity on initial ultrasound had substantially higher ROSC (51% vs 14%), survival to admission (29% vs 7%), and survival to discharge (3.8% vs 0.6%).
Absence of cardiac activity, especially when combined with asystole, was highly predictive of non-survival, though rare survivors (0.6%) still occurred.
POCUS identified reversible causes (notably pericardial effusion) that led to non-ACLS interventions with markedly higher survival than the cohort as a whole.

About 10% of patients in monitor asystole had cardiac activity on ultrasound, and 45.6% of PEA patients had no mechanical activity, indicating frequent electromechanical dissociation misclassification.
Integrating ultrasound into ACLS did not prolong pulse-check pauses and was associated with similar epinephrine dosing intervals between activity/no-activity groups.
Findings support using POCUS to risk-stratify cardiac arrest patients and to guide targeted interventions, but not as a sole criterion to terminate resuscitation.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, regional blood flow, oxygen consumption, mesenteric circulation, hepatic circulation, microcirculation, intestinal failure, animal model, cardiac output, irreversible shock

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In experimental hemorrhagic shock, irreversible collapse is linked less to persistent hypoperfusion and more to a critical, time-dependent failure of intestinal tissues to utilize oxygen even after blood flow and oxygen delivery are restored.
key_points: A new technique was developed to directly measure hepatic blood flow in dogs using an internal shunt of infrahepatic blood.
During hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock, limb, mesenteric, and hepatic blood flows are markedly reduced, but their proportional contribution to total cardiac output remains similar to baseline.
Irreversible hemorrhagic shock is associated with a failure of the intestine to utilize oxygen despite restoration of blood flow and oxygen delivery.
Post-transfusion, non-surviving dogs showed markedly depressed intestinal oxygen consumption despite hyperemic mesenteric blood flow.
Hepatic oxygen consumption reflected oxygen delivery rather than predicting outcome; high hepatic O2 uptake did not correlate with survival.
Portal venous pressure and flow changes after transfusion did not simply reflect mesenteric back-pressure or hepatic resistance alone.
There appears to be a critical time–flow threshold beyond which intestinal oxidative metabolism cannot be rescued by restoring circulation.

raw_front_matter.title: Transmural Glycolytic Gradients in Shocked LV Myocardium
raw_front_matter.description: In prolonged hemorrhagic shock in dogs, left ventricular glycolytic enzyme activities and transmural gradients are markedly altered despite preserved coronary sinus oxygenation, indicating that cardi…
raw_front_matter.authors: P. Lundsgaard-Hansen, C. Meyer, H. Riedwyl
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac failure, myocardium, glycolysis, enzymes, transmural gradients, dog model, catecholamines, coronary sinus, metabolism

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In prolonged hemorrhagic shock in dogs, left ventricular glycolytic enzyme activities and transmural gradients are markedly altered despite preserved coronary sinus oxygenation, indicating that cardiac failure arises more from structural and regulatory derangements—potentially catecholamine- or toxin-mediated—than from primary myocardial hypoxia.
key_points: In anesthetized, ventilated dogs subjected to prolonged hemorrhagic hypotension, coronary sinus blood did not show evidence of an overall myocardial oxygen deficit despite severe systemic acidosis.

Activities of most glycolytic and related enzymes in left ventricular myocardium were increased after shock, while pyruvate kinase, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and α‑hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase (α‑HB‑DH) did not increase or were reduced.
Transmural enzyme activity gradients across the left ventricular wall, previously present under normal conditions, were altered or lost after shock, particularly in the subendocardial (inner) layer.
New base‑to‑apex enzyme activity differences appeared after shock, most prominently in the inner layer for G‑6‑P‑dehydrogenase, pyruvate kinase, and LDH.
The pattern of enzyme changes and preserved coronary sinus oxygenation argue against myocardial hypoxia as the primary cause of cardiac deterioration in prolonged hemorrhagic shock.

Findings are more consistent with functional consequences of structural myocardial derangements, potentially related to excessive catecholamine activity or toxic mediators from hypoxic peripheral tissues.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, hepatic deamination and amino acid clearance are largely preserved and recover quickly with transfusion, indicating that elevated blood amino nitrogen and altered amino acid handling are consequences of reduced hepatic blood flow rather than primary drivers of irreversible shock.
key_points: Seven common amino acids and an amino acid mixture were injected into dogs before, during, and after hemorrhagic shock to study amino acid handling and deamination.
Clearance of injected amino acids from blood was slowed in the oligemic phase of shock but generally returned to near-normal after transfusion, even in animals that remained in irreversible shock.
Blood urea levels rose after amino acid administration in both normal and shocked dogs, indicating preserved deamination capacity.
Overall blood amino nitrogen remained elevated in shock and often persisted after transfusion, despite normal clearance of the experimentally injected amino acids.
Slowed amino acid clearance in early shock is attributed to reduced hepatic blood flow rather than irreversible injury to hepatic deaminating enzymes.
Protein synthesis or amino acid storage appears to occur even in shocked animals given large amino acid loads, as urea production was insufficient to account for amino acid disappearance.
No relationship was found between amino acid clearance or blood amino nitrogen levels and reversibility of hemorrhagic shock to transfusion.

raw_front_matter.title: ALM Therapy and Autonomic Shift in Hemorrhagic Shock
raw_front_matter.description: In a rat model of non-compressible hemorrhagic shock, ALM resuscitation improves survival by shifting autonomic control from sympathetic hyperactivity to parasympathetic dominance, preserving cardiop…
raw_front_matter.authors: Hayley L. Letson, Erik Biros, Jodie L. Morris, Geoffrey P. Dobson
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, non-compressible hemorrhage, cardiac failure, autonomic nervous system, ALM therapy, adrenergic receptors, cholinergic receptors, inflammation, rat model, adiponectin

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of non-compressible hemorrhagic shock, ALM resuscitation improves survival by shifting autonomic control from sympathetic hyperactivity to parasympathetic dominance, preserving cardioprotective receptor expression, limiting myocardial inflammation and injury, and maintaining cardiac pump function.
key_points: In a rat model of non-compressible hemorrhagic shock, ALM (adenosine–lidocaine–magnesium) resuscitation improved 72 h survival compared with hypertonic saline.
Mortality was associated with marked loss of cardiac adrenergic (β1, α1A) and muscarinic M2 receptor expression, high sympathetic drive, and severe myocardial inflammation and injury.
ALM survivors exhibited a strong shift toward parasympathetic dominance (high M2/β1 ratio, higher HF HRV), better cardiac output and stroke volume, and minimal cardiac histopathology.
Cardiac α1A-adrenergic receptor expression was dramatically upregulated in ALM survivors and may play a protective inotropic and cardioprotective role during shock.
Saline-treated rats showed greater cardiac cytokine expression (IL-1α, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-4, IL-10, IL-13), chemokines, and histologic evidence of ischemia, edema, and inflammatory infiltrates.

Systemic adiponectin rose more in ALM-treated animals and tracked with survival, whereas saline animals showed paradoxically high cardiac adiponectin gene expression suggestive of intra-cardiac synthesis in ischemic injury.

The authors interpret death after severe hemorrhage as a systems-level CNS–cardiac autonomic failure, with survival linked to restoration of parasympathetic dominance and controlled sympathetic activity.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Ischemia-driven disruption of myocardial calcium handling underlies contractile failure and electromechanical dissociation in cardiac arrest, while targeted monitoring (echocardiography, ETCO2), intra-CPR hypothermia, and ischemic postconditioning can significantly improve resuscitation success and post-arrest cardiac and neurological outcomes in experimental and clinical settings.
key_points: SR calcium release, force development, and the calcium transient amplitude during each heartbeat are tightly regulated by trigger calcium entry through L-type calcium channels and couplon recruitment.

Ischemia rapidly alters high-energy phosphate metabolism and ionic milieu, which together blunt myofilament calcium responsiveness, disrupt coordinated SR calcium release, and reduce contractile force.

Progressive metabolic derangements (H+, Pi, Mg2+, high ADP/ATP) during ischemia impair L-type Ca channel behavior, RyR sensitivity, and SERCA function, causing diminished and dyssynchronous calcium transients.
In human cardiac arrest resuscitation, residual echocardiographic cardiac activity and higher ETCO2 values during CPR are strongly associated with survival to hospital admission.

Intra-CPR therapeutic hypothermia—particularly via endovascular right atrial cooling—can improve ROSC rates and markedly limit infarct size, whereas simple cold-volume loading alone lowers coronary perfusion pressure.

Ischemic postconditioning applied at CPR initiation, combined with post-resuscitation mild hypothermia, facilitates functional cardiac and neurological recovery after prolonged untreated ventricular fibrillation in animal models.

These mechanistic and experimental insights link cellular calcium dysregulation in ischemia to macroscopic hemodynamics and highlight monitoring and hypothermic/postconditioning strategies to improve resuscitation outcomes.

docs.title: Human Hemorrhage & Compensation

raw_front_matter.title: Human Hemorrhage & Compensation
raw_front_matter.description: Hemorrhage tolerance and progression to shock are governed not by blood pressure alone but by the integrated capacity of multiple compensatory mechanisms—capturable as a “compensatory reserve” from a…
raw_front_matter.authors: Victor A. Convertino, Natalie J. Koons, Mithun R. Suresh
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, central hypovolemia, oxygen delivery, compensatory mechanisms, baroreflex, cerebral perfusion, autonomic nervous system, compensatory reserve, hemostasis, trauma resuscitation, environmental stress, sex differences, aging, cardiovascular physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Hemorrhage tolerance and progression to shock are governed not by blood pressure alone but by the integrated capacity of multiple compensatory mechanisms—capturable as a “compensatory reserve” from arterial waveforms—which offers a sensitive, individualized tool for early detection and targeted treatment of hemorrhagic shock.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock is defined as inadequate tissue oxygenation occurring when systemic oxygen delivery (DO2) falls below tissue oxygen consumption (VO2) required for aerobic metabolism.

Compensation for hemorrhage relies on integrated mechanisms: oxygen extraction from blood and tissue reserves, autonomic and neuroendocrine activation, baro- and chemoreflexes, cerebrovascular control, respiration, and auto-resuscitation via transcapillary refill.
Tolerance to blood loss varies markedly between individuals and is influenced by sex, aerobic fitness, race in women, and environmental stressors (heat, altitude, cold).

The concept of a critical DO2 (DO2crit) marks the transition to hemorrhagic shock, after which anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation, and endotheliopathy drive hemorrhagic blood failure and coagulopathy.

Animal hemorrhage models (rat, dog, pig, nonhuman primate) show important quantitative and mechanistic differences from humans, particularly in compensatory capacity and DO2crit, limiting direct clinical translation.

The compensatory reserve—quantified via machine-learning analysis of arterial waveform features—captures the integrated status of all compensatory mechanisms and detects significant blood loss earlier and more specifically than conventional vital signs or single biomarkers.

Continuous compensatory reserve monitoring can guide early triage and goal-directed resuscitation and has shown clinical utility in trauma, sepsis, hemorrhagic conditions, and fluid/blood product therapy.

raw_front_matter.authors: Luciano Curcio, Valerio Cusimano, Laura D’Orsi, Jiraphat Yokrattanasak, Andrea De Gaetano
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiovascular modeling, Guyton model, Zenker model, hemodynamics, baroreflex, transcapillary refill, computational physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: The Guyton model, with its rich multi-timescale regulatory mechanisms, more accurately reproduces experimental hemodynamic responses to hemorrhagic shock than the simpler Zenker model, but a suitably enhanced Zenker-like framework may offer a better balance between realism and practical usability for clinical and research applications.
key_points: The paper compares the complex Guyton model and the compact Zenker model for simulating fixed-volume hemorrhagic shock across ATLS hemorrhage classes I–IV.

Guyton’s model includes multi-timescale regulatory mechanisms (baroreflex, renal control, renin–angiotensin system, transcapillary refill) and can reproduce both short- and long-term responses to hemorrhage.
Zenker’s model is a 0D lumped-parameter, 5-ODE system with baroreflex control only, designed for simplicity and parameter identifiability in acute scenarios.
Under identical hemorrhage protocols, both models show similar qualitative behavior during the bleeding phase, but diverge substantially in post-bleed compensation and recovery.
Guyton simulations qualitatively match experimental animal data for MAP, HR, and CO during and after hemorrhage better than Zenker’s model.
Zenker’s lack of a transcapillary refill mechanism leads to no recovery of blood volume or MAP after hemorrhage, making it inadequate for modeling longer-term shock evolution.
The authors suggest that adding transcapillary refill and related mechanisms to a Zenker-like framework could yield a clinically useful yet tractable shock model.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, cardiac metabolism, myocardial oxygen consumption, coronary blood flow, lactate, pyruvate, redox potential, canine model, irreversible shock, conscious animal model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In conscious dogs with hemorrhagic shock, coronary perfusion and redox markers indicate that the myocardium generally remains aerobically supplied even at irreversible shock levels, implying that shock-induced cardiac failure is driven more by non-hypoxic factors than by global myocardial oxygen deprivation.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in conscious dogs reduces coronary blood flow and myocardial oxygen consumption only when arterial pressure falls to very low (near-irreversible) levels.
Despite profound systemic hypotension, myocardial redox state (ΔEh), lactate/pyruvate ratio, and excess lactate do not indicate a shift to anaerobic metabolism in the heart.
Coronary blood flow is relatively preserved compared with systemic (aortic) flow, suggesting preferential perfusion of the myocardium during shock.
Anesthesia itself markedly depresses myocardial oxygen consumption and alters redox potential compared with conscious conditions, potentially confounding earlier shock studies.
Systemic lactate and pyruvate levels rise markedly in late shock, but coronary sinus data indicate adequate overall myocardial oxygenation relative to reduced cardiac work.

The authors propose that cardiac damage and shock irreversibility are driven more by non-hypoxic factors (e.g., catecholamines, circulating inhibitors from hypoxic tissues) than by global myocardial oxygen deficit.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Traumatic hemorrhage–induced endotheliopathy and coagulopathy are driven by endothelial succinate metabolism that triggers oxidative membrane remodeling, bringing membrane MMPs into contact with the glycocalyx to cause rapid shedding—a process that can be interrupted by targeting SDH, PLA2, or membrane organization.
key_points: Acute traumatic hemorrhage causes rapid endothelial glycocalyx shedding (‘endotheliopathy’) that contributes to coagulopathy and organ dysfunction.
Endothelial succinate accumulation and its metabolism via succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) drive mitochondrial ROS production during hypoxia–reoxygenation.
Succinate-driven ROS induces lipid oxidation, PLA2-dependent lysophospholipid generation, and plasma membrane reorganization.
These membrane changes increase colocalization and interaction of membrane-tethered MMP24 and MMP25 with glycocalyx constituent syndecan-1, promoting its shedding.

In a rat hemorrhagic shock model, pharmacologic inhibition of SDH, mitochondrial ROS, PLA2, or membrane reorganization prevents glycocalyx damage and coagulopathy, and improves survival and organ injury markers.

In trauma patients, plasma succinate levels correlate strongly with syndecan-1 (glycocalyx shedding), prothrombin time, and creatinine, and MMP24–syndecan-1 interaction is increased in endothelial extracellular vesicles.
Succinate-dependent glycocalyx damage is also triggered by LPS and influenza in vitro, suggesting a shared mechanism across critical illnesses.

raw_front_matter.title: Pressure-Volume Curves of Interstitial Space

raw_front_matter.authors: Arthur C. Guyton
raw_front_matter.tags: interstitial fluid pressure, pressure-volume relationship, tissue compliance, edema, microcirculation, lymphatics, vascular physiology

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: Across multiple experimental approaches and a physical model, interstitial spaces in dogs exhibit very low compliance at negative pressures and sharply increased compliance just above atmospheric pressure, providing a key mechanical safety factor that delays but then sharply accelerates edema formation once interstitial pressure becomes positive.
key_points: Interstitial fluid pressure in normal tissues is negative (about −6 to −7 mm Hg) and becomes positive as edema develops.
Compliance of the interstitial space is very low in the negative pressure range but increases sharply once pressure crosses atmospheric (0 mm Hg).
A small change in interstitial volume at negative pressures causes a large pressure change, whereas large volume changes in edema cause only small pressure increases.
Multiple independent in vivo and ex vivo methods yielded similar interstitial pressure-volume curves, supporting the robustness of the findings.
A physical model mimicking cells, fibers, and skin reproduced the characteristic pressure-volume behavior and delayed compliance observed in tissues.
The shape of the pressure-volume curve explains a major “safety factor” that delays edema formation despite substantial changes in Starling forces.

raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, shock heart syndrome, ventricular arrhythmias, electrical remodeling, optical mapping, Connexin43, hemoglobin vesicles, artificial oxygen carriers, washed red blood cells, ischemia-reperfusion injury, Langendorff heart preparation, rat model

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a rat model of severe hemorrhagic shock, liposome-encapsulated hemoglobin prevents structural and electrical ventricular remodeling and almost completely abolishes inducible VT/VF, providing anti-arrhythmogenic protection comparable to washed red blood cell transfusion and far superior to saline or albumin resuscitation.
key_points: Severe hemorrhagic shock with prolonged hypotension induces a "Shock Heart Syndrome" characterized by structural and electrical remodeling that promotes lethal ventricular arrhythmias.
Optical mapping showed marked action potential duration dispersion (APDd) and abnormal ventricular conduction patterns after shock when resuscitation used saline or 5% albumin.
Resuscitation with liposome-encapsulated hemoglobin (hemoglobin vesicles, HbV) preserved myocardial conduction properties and APDd similarly to autologous washed red blood cells (wRBCs).
Sustained ventricular tachycardia/fibrillation (VT/VF) was easily inducible after saline or albumin resuscitation, but was absent with wRBCs and nearly absent with HbV.
Histology revealed pronounced myocardial cell damage and Connexin43 degradation with saline/albumin, which were markedly attenuated by HbV and wRBC transfusion.
The data implicate APD dispersion and gap-junction (Connexin43) remodeling as key arrhythmogenic substrates in hemorrhagic shock hearts.
Artificial oxygen carriers such as HbV may substitute for RBCs to prevent post-shock lethal arrhythmias by preserving myocardial structure and electrical stability.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a swine model of hemorrhagic shock, dimethyl malonate blunted succinate accumulation, reduced endothelial oxidative damage, preserved pulmonary glycocalyx, and improved cardiac recovery while lowering fluid requirements during resuscitation, supporting its potential as a targeted therapy against ischemia-reperfusion injury.
key_points: Dimethyl malonate (DMM), a succinate dehydrogenase inhibitor, attenuates plasma succinate accumulation during resuscitation from hemorrhagic shock in swine.
DMM-treated animals showed improved cardiac output and cardiac index recovery, along with higher filling pressures, despite similar mean arterial pressure targets.
DMM reduced endothelial reactive oxygen species in the myocardium and preserved pulmonary endothelial glycocalyx integrity.
DMM-treated pigs required significantly less crystalloid fluid to maintain target blood pressure during resuscitation.
Ionized calcium levels rose during resuscitation in DMM-treated animals, suggesting a potential effect on calcium handling.
Global markers of shock and organ injury (lactate, creatinine, pH) and short-term survival were not different between groups in this small study.
Findings support DMM as a potential adjunctive therapy to limit ischemia-reperfusion injury after hemorrhagic shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a murine trauma-hemorrhage model, both genetic deletion and pharmacologic antagonism of TLR4 preserve cardiac function by sustaining PI3K/Akt activity and suppressing NF-κB–driven inflammation, highlighting TLR4 blockade as a promising strategy to prevent hemorrhagic shock–induced cardiac failure.
key_points: TLR4 signaling is a key mediator of cardiac dysfunction following trauma-hemorrhage (TH) in mice.
TLR4-deficient mice are protected from the early depression of left ventricular function seen after TH.
Pharmacologic TLR4 blockade with Eritoran (E5564) dose-dependently attenuates TH-induced cardiac dysfunction, with 3 mg/kg showing near-complete protection.
TLR4 inhibition prevents TH-induced decreases in myocardial Akt phosphorylation and reduces NF-κB binding activity.
Blocking TLR4 also diminishes lung neutrophil infiltration and TNFα production after TH, indicating attenuated systemic inflammation.
The cardioprotective effects of TLR4 inhibition likely involve PI3K/Akt activation and suppression of TLR4–NF-κB inflammatory signaling.

raw_front_matter.authors: Hiltrud Mueller, Stephen M. Ayres, James T. Mazzara, Stanley Giannelli Jr., E. Foster Conklin, William J. Grace, Thomas Nealon
raw_front_matter.tags: coronary shock, cardiogenic shock, myocardial infarction, coronary blood flow, myocardial metabolism, intraaortic counterpulsation, norepinephrine, hemodynamics

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In human coronary shock after myocardial infarction, coronary blood flow is tightly linked to mean aortic pressure and myocardial metabolism, and intraaortic counterpulsation optimally improves oxygenation and performance while reducing myocardial work compared with norepinephrine-driven pressure support.
key_points: In human coronary (cardiogenic) shock after acute myocardial infarction, coronary blood flow is closely coupled to mean aortic pressure, especially at lower pressures.
The coronary flow–pressure relationship is nonlinear, with a critical no-flow point at a mean aortic pressure of about 30 mm Hg.
Above ~65–70 mm Hg mean aortic pressure, the coronary flow–pressure curve flattens, while it steepens markedly as pressure falls below this range.
Coronary blood flow strongly determines myocardial oxygen extraction and lactate metabolism during coronary shock.
Both norepinephrine infusion and intraaortic counterpulsation improve myocardial metabolism and mean aortic pressure in coronary shock.
Norepinephrine increases myocardial work substantially, whereas intraaortic counterpulsation improves oxygenation while reducing myocardial workload.
Therapeutic strategies that raise perfusion pressure and flow while minimizing cardiac work, such as intraaortic counterpulsation, are particularly favorable in coronary shock.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In canine hemorrhagic shock, marked elevations in blood lactate, pyruvate, and the lactate/pyruvate ratio primarily reflect anoxic overproduction and reduced perfusion rather than intrinsic failure of lactate–pyruvate metabolic enzymes, and they are not responsible for the development of irreversibility to transfusion.
key_points: Hemorrhagic shock in dogs causes marked elevations in blood lactate, pyruvate, amino acid nitrogen, and the lactate/pyruvate (L/P) ratio, reflecting a shift toward anaerobic metabolism.
Transfusion rapidly normalizes lactate, pyruvate, and the L/P ratio, even when it fails to reverse the shock state and the animal subsequently dies.
Clearance of exogenous lactate and pyruvate remains largely intact in shock and after transfusion, indicating that key enzymatic pathways for their metabolism are not severely damaged.
The magnitude of lactate and pyruvate abnormalities in shock cannot be explained by endogenous epinephrine, adrenal cortical hormones, or systemic acidosis alone.
Reduced clearance of glucose and pyruvate during the hypotensive phase of shock is attributed primarily to decreased blood flow, particularly through the liver, rather than intrinsic enzyme failure.
Development of irreversibility to transfusion is not due to an inability of the liver to metabolize lactate and pyruvate and is not directly driven by these carbohydrate abnormalities.

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In traumatic brain injury, recurrent malignant ventricular arrhythmias can be driven by raised intracranial pressure and may resolve completely after surgical decompression, so persistent resuscitative efforts and early neurosurgical intervention are crucial and can yield good long-term neurological outcomes.
key_points: Recurrent ventricular tachycardia can occur after traumatic brain injury as a manifestation of neurogenic cardiac dysfunction.
In the reported case, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias ceased after surgical evacuation of an extradural haematoma.
Raised intracranial pressure and brain shift may impair neuro-autonomic cardiovascular regulation and trigger malignant arrhythmias.
Elevated cardiac biomarkers and ECG changes are common after severe head injury and may reflect neurogenic, not primary cardiac, pathology.
Repeated CPR and defibrillation in this setting do not necessarily portend a poor long-term neurological outcome if intracranial pathology is definitively treated.
Early neurosurgical decompression combined with intensive care aimed at limiting intracranial pressure can reverse brain injury–induced cardiac dysfunction.

raw_front_matter.description: In a controlled cat model, 2 hours of continuous severe hemorrhagic hypotension produces largely irreversible depression of left ventricular contractility that is only modestly responsive to digitali…
raw_front_matter.authors: Howard W. Siegel; S. Evans Downing
raw_front_matter.tags: hemorrhagic shock, left ventricular function, myocardial contractility, metabolic acidosis, digitalis, animal model, cat, cardiac failure, reversibility of shock

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In a controlled cat model, 2 hours of continuous severe hemorrhagic hypotension produces largely irreversible depression of left ventricular contractility that is only modestly responsive to digitalis and not solely explained by acidosis, whereas brief periodic restoration of normal aortic pressure prevents permanent myocardial failure despite equivalent cumulative shock duration.
key_points: Sustained severe hemorrhagic shock at an aortic pressure of ~30 mmHg causes a marked, progressive reduction in left ventricular contractility in areflexic cats.
After 2 hours of continuous hypotension, left ventricular function is depressed to about half of its initial value and is largely not reversible by restoration of normal aortic pressure.

Metabolic acidosis develops progressively during shock, but similar levels of acidosis do not cause irreversible depression when aortic pressure is periodically normalized, implicating factors beyond pH alone.
Digitalis (Cedilanid-D) yields only a modest, transient improvement in contractility and does not restore function to control levels in shock.
Intermittent re-elevation of aortic pressure to normotensive levels every 30 minutes prevents permanent loss of contractility despite the same cumulative duration of hypotension.
The data support a primary, shock-induced myocardial contractile defect that contributes to irreversibility in prolonged hemorrhagic shock.

raw_front_matter.authors: Chu-Jeng Chiu; Alice H. McArdle; Rea Brown; Henry J. Scott; Fraser N. Gurd

docs.one_sentence_takeaway: In low-flow states, the intestinal villus microcirculation and ongoing absorption create a subepithelial transport barrier that depletes epithelial ATP and mechanically lifts otherwise viable cells from their capillary supply, leading to rapid, flow-dependent loss of mucosal barrier integrity and systemic consequences in shock.
key_points: Intestinal mucosal injury in low-flow states progresses through a reproducible sequence that is strongly flow-dependent.
The earliest and pivotal lesion is epithelial disruption at the infranuclear (basal) region with formation of subepithelial Gruenhagen’s space.
Epithelial cells initially remain structurally and metabolically relatively intact despite being lifted from the lamina propria.
Mucosal ATP levels fall disproportionately to the reduction in oxygen utilization, implicating substrate deprivation rather than intrinsic mitochondrial failure.
Loss of epithelial integrity (denudation) is required before large, normally excluded molecules such as d-tubocurarine cross the mucosa.
The villus microcirculation and countercurrent exchange system promote a local transport barrier during hypoperfusion, worsening epithelial injury.
Lysosomal rupture appears to be a late event, occurring after epithelial separation, challenging models that ascribe primary injury to early lysosomal breakdown.
